Research has examined the correlations of charges in particle interactions within Pb-Pb collisions, specifically looking at whether evidence of the Chiral Magnetic Effect (CME) exists in the collision data collected at 2.76 and 5.02 TeV. The study considered all charged particles within specific pseudorapidity and transverse momentum ranges, with particular emphasis on peripheral collisions. A signal related to CME was observed in specific correlator calculations and found to intensify with increasing collision peripherality. Calculations accounting for effects of background that arise from charge and anisotropic flow patterns, while able to partially explain observed results, did not capture the entirety of the CME signal measurements. A comparison of the CME and mixed-harmonics correlator signals further highlighted the significant influence of background contributions. Finally, the study found that the observed CME effect is consistent with a local charge separation concept, with relevant parameters tracked across different collision peripherality. The study found that the influence of CME on specific correlator calculations does not exceed 10% of the measured value in the most peripherally occurring Pb-Pb collisions. The research also found that the influence of CME on tri-hadron correlations does not modify its intensity relative to charged pion measurements but does introduce a signal intensity difference (in relation to charged pions) of up to 30% for lowest collision peripherality and 10% for most peripherally occurring collisions. The research presents these and other significant observations related to the study of CME signal and background interactions within Pb-Pb collision data collected at the LHC. The research sets constraints for the strength of CME effects measured in relation to charged pion and all charged particle signals, with relevant parameters quantified across various collision peripherality. The research also outlines necessary steps for further investigation in this area of research. The research further remarks on the importance of collecting more data in lower collision peripherality ranges with higher precision to distinguish CME effects from background influences from charge and anisotropic flow patterns. The research presents alternative approaches to eliminate background influences from charge and anisotropic flow patterns, with relevant data collected in higher collision peripherality ranges. The research also calls for further investigation in this area of research. The research further remarks on the importance of examining the influence of CME on observed results with various assumptions for the influence of CME. The research presents significant observations related to the study of CME effects measured in relation to all charged particle signals, with relevant parameters quantified

The surge in online fundraising (or "crowdfunding") research focuses on understanding the crowd dynamics that predict the success of crowdfunded projects. Differing from prior studies that concentrated on project characteristics, our analysis takes a more holistic approach and is less dependent on the specific crowdfunding platforms being used. By combining various research methods, we explored the impact of features describing crowd behavior on project success. Through a multi-platform investigation of fundraising in online markets, our findings reveal the common crowd dynamics that ultimately decide which projects will succeed. Consistently across our analysis, the behaviors of funders are highly correlated with fundraising success. They offer more accurate predictions of project success compared to traditional approaches that rely solely on project characteristics. These behaviors, captured by our novel crowd dynamics features, provide valuable insights into the social processes underlying crowd decision-making, processes that have previously been overlooked in the crowdfunding literature. As a result, these new variables can be utilized to develop predictive models of project success and potentially other crowd-funded projects. Additionally, our work may be adapted to the evaluation and prediction of other types of collective tasks. The code used for our research is publicly accessible at https://github.com/jmmele/crowdSuccess. The data used in our research are publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/jmmele/crowdSuccess-data. (For the complete abstract, please refer to the attached paper)

Machine learning (ML) based detection of network attacks has shown effectiveness when tailored to a single organisation, but combining data from multiple sources is challenging due to data format inconsistencies and privacy concerns. To address this issue, this paper introduces a collaborative federated learning framework, allowing multiple organisations to co-create and train a robust ML-based intrusion detection system without compromising their data's privacy. A key feature of the proposed framework is the ability to collect and process network traffic data in a common format to reveal meaningful patterns. Moreover, the federated learning mechanism allows organisations to benefit from shared cyber threat intelligence without needing to share sensitive information, by sharing only model updates through the averaging process. To evaluate the proposed framework, two NetFlow datasets were used and compared with traditional training methods involving local data exchange or centralised training, demonstrating its efficiency and effectiveness in training a universal ML model to classify benign and intrusive traffic from multiple organisations without requiring data exchange. The results show the federated learning framework produces comparable or superior classification performance to traditional methods, particularly in training a robust model on distributed data without requiring data exchange. Furthermore, the employed cyber threat intelligence sharing mechanism offers a more secure alternative to direct data sharing, significantly reducing the risk of data exposure and privacy breaches. The source code of the proposed framework has been made available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/wh9/FLIDSS. To ensure fairness in the evaluation process, the federated learning framework and its performance were presented to the research community with no restrictions. Experimental results can be reproduced by downloading the NetFlow datasets and implementing the proposed framework using the provided code. The employed datasets can be obtained from the following sources: \cite{taxii2} and \cite{flow-mine}. The used traffic generation tool 'NetFlow' and its source code can be accessed at: \url{https://i-am-trace.github.io/NetFlow/} and \url{https://github.com/wh9/NetFlow/blob/main/README.md}, respectively. The federated learning framework presents a novel method for cyber threat intelligence sharing and ML model collaboration that addresses the aforementioned challenges, thereby enabling the co-development of a robust ML-based intrusion detection system among multiple organisations without exchanging sensitive information while ensuring the privacy and security of the shared cyber threat intelligence. The proposed framework has been successfully evaluated, producing comparable or superior results to traditional training methods, and its source code has been made available for reproducibility. The federated learning framework offers a versatile solution for cyber defence, enabling multiple organisations to collaborate

The issue of scheduling a multi-point robotic manipulator over time is an important issue in domains such as service robotics and computing grids. The basic variant of this problem, which involves a given time interval, a set of tasks, and corresponding time requirements, can be solved using a simple greedy algorithm. The essence of this problem is characterized by the need to perform tasks at multiple facilities using a multi-point robotic manipulator, where each task can be handled by a particular robot. We consider the basic variant of this problem as a facility layout problem, where each facility corresponds to a particular time segment. The proposed algorithm demonstrates its efficiency by showing that its time complexity is directly proportional to the number of tasks and facilities. The developed solution has been successfully tested using a comprehensive set of synthetic data. The results of these experiments confirm the effectiveness of the suggested approach, which in many cases outperforms other traditional optimization techniques. The presented work is a continuation of a research on a basic variant of a multi-point robotic manipulator scheduling problem. The novel aspect of the current study involves a dynamic environment, characterized by the emergence and disappearance of tasks and facilities at random time moments. The proposed solution incorporates these changes, which in many cases significantly outperforms other optimization techniques, both in simulations and practical scenarios. The presented work is publicly available at https://github.com/ag-td/multi-robot-manipulator-scheduling. The detailed description of the source code can be found at https://ag-td.github.io/multi-robot-manipulator-scheduling/. The study provides a practical solution for service providers, facilitating their transition to a multi-point robotic manipulator scheduling system. The essence of the suggested approach involves introducing a new resource, capable of handling tasks, and initially devoid of any attributes or costs. The system is then adjusted to prefer assignments that leverage this new resource. The effectiveness of the proposed solution has been confirmed using a comprehensive set of synthetic data, demonstrating its superiority over alternative optimization techniques. The study offers a practical solution, applicable to real-world scenarios characterized by dynamic tasks, facilities, and multi-point robotic manipulators. In complex networks, a phenomenon occurs where different clusters of oscillators, comprised of distinct systems, synchronize with their own distinct rhythms. When each cluster contains identical systems, synchronized within that group, but operating independently from other groups, this phenomenon is known as group synchronization. Typically, strict conditions need to be met to achieve synchronization, but research has revealed that slight discrepancies between the parameters of the systems do not preclude it. This knowledge has been utilized to design artificial neural networks, where non-identical neurons nonetheless synchronize within respective groups. Interestingly, these groups can exist in multiple configurations and even facilitate the stabilization of unstable systems. Within each group, connections are homogeneous, but differences between the groups give them unique characteristics, raising the concept of intragroup connections where connections within a single group are not all the same. Exploring the possibilities of intragroup connections and adjustments to the standard coupled map lattice model allows for a broader range of applications and a more delicate control over the synchronization patterns. Ultimately, adjusting these connections enables the transition between different group configurations. This work presents a framework for a wide array of artificial neural systems, providing numerous possibilities for implementation and experimentation. Due to its theoretical nature, possible practical implementations are outlined using specific examples. These include the use of group synchronization to improve image processing algorithms and the exploitation of group synchronization and parameter mismatch for secure, robust, and reliable communication systems. Additionally, the concept of group synchronization is used to develop an algorithm for detecting and protecting against artificial intelligence-based threats. These examples serve to showcase the diverse potential applications of group synchronization in real-world projects. Lastly, potential future research directions on group synchronization are proposed. This study provides a comprehensive toolkit for designing complex systems with multiple interconnected components and can serve as a resource for those seeking to utilize group synchronization in their work. Specifically, the intragroup connection feature is highlighted as a versatile tool with vast potential applications and is distinguished from other synchronization phenomena by its adjustable connections within each group. Furthermore, group synchronization is presented as a means of creating artificial neural networks with predetermined characteristics and is examined in conjunction with parameter synchronization. Additionally, the effect of parameter mismatches on group synchronization is explored and renowned mathematician and scientist, Leonid P. Nesi's, work on the topic is mentioned. Lastly, the concept of group synchronization is utilized to develop novel algorithms for reliable quantum computing and fault-tolerant quantum error-correction systems. This study delves into the theoretical and scientific aspects of group synchronization and provides a framework for future research and development, offering numerous possibilities for implementation

Our study examines the existence of domain-level source diversity bias in video search outcomes by utilizing a virtual agent-based method. The approach entails comparing the outputs of five prominent search engines, comprising four Western and one non-Western search engines, for both English and Russian language queries. The research reveals significant variation in source diversity according to language, with English search queries yielding more diverse results. Additionally, our findings indicate that the video-sharing platform YouTube dominates the top search outputs for all Western search engines, excluding Google. Interestingly, we also discovered that the sampled Google search results lack video content from TikTok and Instagram. The outcomes of our study provide valuable insights for designers and researchers aiming to decrease diversity bias in video search outcomes and increase the representation of various video content platforms. Consequently, users may benefit from a more comprehensive understanding of available video content. These precursor studies involve the analysis of two key systems: monodromy defects without supersymmetry, and a Wess-Zumino model with a defect-free ε-expansion. Building on existing research regarding codimension-two conformal blocks and Lorentzian inversion formulas, the monodromy defects study extends its reach to include parity-odd structures, offering a deeper understanding. Meanwhile, the ε-expansion study focuses on bootstrapping four-point functions of chiral operators in the Wess-Zumino model, aiming to provide key spectral information about the model's underlying theory. Following these foundational investigations, the analysis proceeds to two-point functions of chiral operators in the presence of a supersymmetric monodromy defect. The resulting expressions for these two-point functions are expressed through novel, in-depth special functions analysis. Notably, the techniques employed and discoveries made here are versatile and likely applicable to diverse other theoretical frameworks. As a result, the model's global consistency requires the cancellation of any superdefects' contributions. The only exceptions to this cancellation rule are found in sectors of odd supersymmetry. The study then verifies these predictions using known results from the Wess-Zumino model, specifically examining its behavior during a holomorphic stress tensor expansion. The capacity of wireless networks is inherently restricted by interference, and there has been a lack of investigation into the correlation of interference, which has the potential to cause substantial delays in local transmission. This study addresses the query of whether randomizing the Medium Access Control (MAC) layer, using protocols like frequency-hopping multiple access and ALOHA, can mitigate the adverse effects of interference correlation. By deriving precise analytical expressions for the mean and variance of local transmission delays in both protocols, and determining the optimal parameters that minimize these delays, this study proposes two distinct operating modes, correlation-limited and bandwidth-limited. Notably, while both protocols may exhibit identical mean local delays when operating at specific conditions, their variances diverge significantly. Finally, this study evaluates the interplay between delay and variability, and provides crucial design insights for practical wireless systems. Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement the training set with high-confidence, pseudo-labeled nodes in a self-training cycle. Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling techniques have several shortcomings. Primarily, they expand the label set cautiously by choosing only the most confident, yet potentially uninformative nodes, which merely amplify minor improvements. Secondly, they combine pseudo-labels with actual labels using the same loss function, failing to acknowledge their distinct contributions to classification. To address these limitations, we propose InfoGNN, an innovative pseudo-labeling framework. InfoGNN focuses on labeling nodes with the greatest informative value, which effectively represents local neighborhoods through mutual information maximization. By separating pseudo- and actual labeling and incorporating task-driven hard pseudo-labeling, InfoGNN optimizes the trade-off between local informativeness and global generalization. Experimental results on six graph datasets substantiate the effectiveness of our proposed method, which outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and robust self-supervised methods on graph data by a significant margin. Code is available at https://github.com/Chen-56/InfoGNN.

In video processing tasks, precise identification of recognizable objects at a low computational cost enables real-time video analysis on devices. We present PatchNet, a highly efficient neural network model for tracking objects across adjacent frames in videos. Unlike traditional pixel-based approaches, PatchNet leverages patch-wise correlation features. This results in a compact network that runs at a remarkably low computational cost of 58MFLOPs, approximately $5\times$ simpler than MobileNetV2. Our research showcases the effectiveness of PatchNet on object detection in videos and visual tracking through a simple and efficient re-design of the classification head. Specifically, the former application is similar to traditional object detection tasks but requires tracking objects across frames. Conversely, the latter focuses on tracking a target within a single image. We employ PatchNet as a sub-network within a larger framework that utilizes video clues like optical flow and temporal information. This combination enables robust object tracking in videos. We have conducted extensive experiments and analyses on various video datasets and benchmarks and found that the model excels at several video-based tasks while requiring minimal parameters and processing resources. Furthermore, the model has been adapted for real-time object detection and tracking in videos and has demonstrated a substantial reduction in computational complexity compared to other state-of-the-art approaches while producing comparable or superior performance. Our research presents a novel application of the patch-wise correlation, a widely known image processing concept, within deep neural network models for efficient video analysis. This technique has been successfully incorporated in several other video processing tasks like high-speed tracking and video denoising where there is often a significant data disparity. We have conducted a detailed study and found that the model combines the effectiveness of hand-crafted video features with the flexibility of CNNs, resulting in superior performance and a significant reduction in computational complexity. Our research has successfully addressed the long-standing issue of high computational cost associated with video analysis tasks and has demonstrated the model's efficacy on various challenging video datasets and benchmarks in real-time. This real-time analysis has been achieved through a delicate design of the model's head and the clever incorporation of patch-wise correlation features. We examine the one-dimensional discrete-time asymmetric exclusion process with periodic boundaries, using parallel updating rules. For the exclusion process with a variety of starting conditions, we obtain a formula for a multi-time distribution. This involves complex mathematical calculations based on integrals of determinant functions. Under specific assumptions about the initial conditions, we are able to determine how this distribution evolves over large time and distances in the system, particularly in situations where geometry impacts the system's behavior. These assumptions are verified for certain basic starting conditions. As a consequence, we are able to determine the probability distribution of the exclusion process on the entire integer lattice by considering large enough systems, effectively removing boundary effects. Furthermore, we calculate the probability distribution of the exclusion process on the lattice at large times for a specific starting condition. These calculations require determining the eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors of the exclusion process's generator, which are initially complicated by the system's geometry but are later simplified by removing boundary effects. Due to space limitations, some of these results are presented in an accompanying letter. It is shown that the exclusion process's macroscopic behavior is similar to a system of interacting particles whose equations of motion are defined by a certain Hamiltonian, which has been studied by other mathematicians. As a consequence, we are able to determine the time at which the exclusion process's macroscopic observables reach their equilibrium values. Finally, we make conjectures about how the probability distribution of the exclusion process evolves over large times and distances in the system and verify these conjectures for certain basic starting conditions. These conjectured results can be found in the appended notes. It is shown that the exclusion process's microscopically maintained periodic patterns are maintained on an even larger scale as a consequence of the system's geometry. Due to space limitations, some of these results are presented in an accompanying letter. The study of the exclusion process's probability distribution has been extended to include systems with additional features, such as irregularly shaped particles and particles that interact nonlocally. Some of these results can be found in the appended notes. The eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors of the exclusion process's generator are found to extend continuously from systems with regularly shaped boundaries to those with irregularly shaped boundaries. A new method of efficient wireless communication is proposed in a novel SWIPT system, enabling faster and more sustainable mobile data networks. The system, utilizing energy-harvesting technology from access points without the need for a splitter, allocates part of the frequency spectrum for information transmission and the remaining for energy capture. To analyze performance improvements, an optimization problem was created that maximizes energy gain and maintains a minimum data rate in a multi-user OFDMA network with multiple users and subcarriers. Due to the complex nature of these problems, an iterative algorithm combining binary search and column generation was designed to solve the challenging optimization issues efficiently. The results show significant improvements in output limits and reduced energy consumption, confirming the effectiveness of the proposed solution. The implementation of this method on SWIPT networks enables more prudent allocation of frequency subbands to users for data and energy transmission. The proposed solution validates the potential of higher data rates and increased system performance, demonstrating a $16.8\%$ increase in output limit and $58.3\%$ decrease in energy consumption. Additionally, the method achieves nearly optimal performance with minimal computational complexity. The efficient energy-harving capabilities of SWIPT provide a more sustainable solution for future mobile data networks, enabling better resource allocation and a lower carbon footprint. In Fermi gases with low concentrations of magnetic properties, a particular phenomenon occurs at specific points beyond the applicability of second-order approximations in mathematical modeling. To address this issue, researchers revisited third-order approximations for systems with multiple magnetic components and developed expressions incorporating both a universal model and one that accounts for detailed pairings. Unlike similar models at the second-order level, the new expressions show varying results for systems with one, two, or three magnetic components. These results are comparable to computer-simulated predictions and exhibit similar trends as the magnetic properties of one component become highly influenced by the others. Furthermore, the variations in these models are most pronounced at the point where the magnetic properties of one component become highly influenced by the others and the magnetic properties of the other components are minimal. Additionally, the variations in these models are related to detailed pairings and can be eliminated under certain theoretical conditions. Lastly, the variations in these models could potentially be measured in upcoming experiments at the Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory, specifically using a type of experiment involving a magnetic field, a particular element, and a highly advanced magnetic material. This could help clarify the underlying physics of the Fermi gases with low concentrations of magnetic properties and potentially apply to these gases when they become universal. Finally, the variations in these models are related to an important property in which the relationships between different magnetic components are the same in both the universal model and the detailed model. However, this does not apply to the portion of the phase diagram where the magnetic properties of one component become highly influential of the others and the magnetic properties of the other components are minimal. In this part of the phase diagram, the phase transitions in systems with one, two, or three magnetic components exhibit a unique characteristic where the relationships between these components are the same as those in the universal model and the detailed model. Analytical derivations are developed, incorporating fundamental aspects like the back-action force, input-output relationships, and corresponding spectral densities, all situated within a purely classical framework. These derivations align with the established quantum optomechanics when both the cavity and mechanical oscillator have high occupation numbers. Additionally, the derived analysis equates optical elements with their electronic counterparts, a necessity for accurate measurements and design requirements. Lastly, a direct comparison between the quantum and classical treatments helps to distinguish the boundaries between these two regimes, thus identifying the genuinely quantum characteristics from those of the classical realm. All calculations are symbol-based, facilitating easy reproduction and extension of the presented findings. Our work is tailored to provide a thorough understanding of optomechanics' underlying principles, a necessary foundation for pioneering new experiments. Specifically, the research outlined here focuses on the conventional setup featuring a single tone but also introduces methods to incorporate multiple tones, envelope modulation, and hybrid schemes within the classical framework. These basic yet versatile models are anticipated to broaden the scope of microwave optomechanics, encompassing both classical and quantum aspects. This study is the first to examine chaotic behavior in a simplified model of a robot that follows the wall in an environment with obstacles. The research involves analyzing a system with two interacting dynamical elements, one of which is inherently stable, representing a robot that can perfectly replicate its surroundings. The authors employ and expand upon the Arshad-Tanaka model, incorporating a control strategy that mimics human error correction mechanisms. To investigate chaotic characteristics, the researchers apply and interpret various analytical tools, including Lyapunov exponents, dimension calculations, and a complex non-linear correlation integral. The study reveals that the presence of obstacles can induce chaotic behavior in a robot that otherwise operates predictably. The authors discovered a threshold beyond which the robot's error corrections become increasingly complex and less predictable. A crucial finding shows that a robot can learn and adapt from its own mistakes in a chaotic environment. The research provides grounds for future exploration of a robot that can learn from its own errors in a dynamic environment. The proposed model also offers a potential approach for the theoretical modeling of a robot that can learn from its own errors. Laparoscopic surgery has limitations due to a narrow field of view. Smoke produced by laser ablation in such operations obstructs the surgeon's visibility, highlighting the need for smoke removal to ensure a clear view. To apply smoke removal techniques effectively, it's essential to accurately distinguish between smoke and non-smoke images, which poses a challenge as current methods are incomplete. To overcome this issue, we have developed an image enhancement technique that extracts crucial information from RGB images to differentiate between smoke and non-smoke content. Leveraging a weighted least squares optimization framework, we employ statistical features derived from bivariate histograms and specific image characteristics, which are then used to train a classifier for binary classification of smoke or non-smoke content. We have tested our approach on the Cholec80 dataset and achieved notable results, demonstrating a 4% improvement in accuracy and F1-score over standard RGB image performance, as well as a 2% improvement in accuracy and 1% improvement in F1-score when compared to existing methods. Furthermore, our technique avoids the need for additional channels or processes, making it an efficient and effective solution. We have also showcased the effectiveness of our approach in real-world laparoscopic surgery scenarios through qualitative analysis. This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian amplitude modulation and a consistent laser frequency. We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, particularly for long chains of ions. A demonstration of this method is performed on a chain of three ions, achieving an average reduction of under one percent from peak precision within a twenty kilohertz range of frequency deviation, and the efficiency of this gate design is examined through numerical simulations on chains consisting of two to thirty-three ions. The results show that it can withstand average frequency deviations of around ten hertz for even longer chains. Additionally, this gate design is compared to other more complex implementations that utilize only a single motional mode to realize more robust gates, highlighting its practical advantages in terms of complexity and performance. Consequently, this work presents a straightforward yet effective approach to creating highly resilient MS gates suitable for larger-scale ion-trap quantum computers. Experimental verification is needed. These variables offer the potential for refined laboratory implementations tailored to specific applications. The researchers also recognize the connection between this work and other relevant findings, particularly a different method for creating robust gates where only a single motional mode is employed, which is more complex and challenging to execute than the approach presented here. This approach also fails to yield the high level of robustness against frequency errors achieved with the proposed method when the number of ions exceeds a certain threshold. Therefore, this work presents a straightforward yet effective means of creating highly resilient MS gates, and the researchers provide numerical simulations to support their claims and compare the performance of the two methods.

Existing quantum processors are prone to errors and have limited lifespan due to
imperfect gate applications. To work effectively with these processors, compilers
must optimize programs to run within the device's coherence time, translating them
into the most efficient version possible to extract maximum value from the hardware.
We have developed new, deterministic methods to efficiently optimize quantum programs
by taking advantage of patterns that repeat within the programs. Specifically, we
have created two innovative algorithms. The first algorithm identifies the longest
repeating pattern in a program, while the second algorithm finds all the patterns
in a program and applies them efficiently. Both algorithms have a linear time
complexity and are resistant to errors, especially when compared to other approaches.
We have successfully tested these algorithms on a real-world quantum circuit used for
computing eigenvalues and observed a substantial reduction in program size, amounting
to a factor of 5 to 10 times over other effective methods, and even up to a factor
of as much as 350 times over a standard approach known as Quantum Assembly Language. 
Additionally, we have measured how these algorithms compare to other effective methods
called Tracking and Reordering, finding a substantial reduction in program size, with
some cases improved by as much as 2 orders of magnitude. We have drawn these
conclusions based on data obtained from various datasets, including random programs and programs derived from a real-valued solver called QPXS. We have established that our novel method is indeed better than other effective methods by conducting statistical analysis on these results. Furthermore, we have analyzed the performance of these algorithms under conditions of partial error resilience. As hardware coherence times continue to improve, our algorithm promotes the fullest possible exploitation of the quantum hardware by reducing the number of gate applications required. We have made the source code of our compiler, known as Quantum Circuit Optimizer, and the generated programs and size metrics publicly available under a permissive license at our website. We expect this work to contribute positively to the research in quantum software and hardware optimization. A recent approach to optimizing techniques employs average-case analysis, enabling more nuanced convergence assessments than conventional worst-case results, yet this analysis demands more specific assumptions about the data generation process than typically found in statistical learning theory. We present a novel framework for evaluating the convergence of stochastic gradient descent under minimal moment assumptions and show that (i) its condition number aligns with that of the population risk, (ii) a specific adaptation of Nesterov's method achieves an optimal convergence rate and is resilient to modifications in its step size and data arrival pattern, and (iii) a minor deviation in its smoothness results in an almost optimal convergence rate that is both robust to data permutations and achievable in the population regime. We also propose a statistical learning framework that quantifies the sample complexity required for successful generalization and provide empirical support for our theoretical framework. Moreover, we offer an infinite-dimensional geometric interpretation of our results, which emphasizes the relationship between the convex function's parameterized family and the path traced by its iterative optimization process. Our findings yield novel understanding and solutions to previously intractable optimization problems and offer a general approach to addressing the complexity of optimal solutions in the population risk. Additionally, our results can be extended to non-convex functions and yet still provide rigorous guarantees. The presented work follows a comprehensive arXiv report that also covers the reproduction of known results for completeness and further generalizes our findings to non-convex scenarios. We have developed a message-passing algorithm designed to accurately determine the location of mobile devices within buildings. The system relies on data from multiple FMCW radar sensors located throughout a building, whose radar signals are reflected by the mobile device being tracked. The positioning process is complicated by the mobile device's two-dimensional movement, hidden radar visibility, and adverse environmental conditions like radar signal blocking and multi-path interference. To effectively locate the mobile device, our adaptive probabilistic algorithm incorporates factors like the mobile device's motion, hidden areas, and environmental obstacles, utilizing a message-passing technique that takes into account the risks of blocked signals, resulting in a reliable estimate of the mobile device's position. The algorithm is tested using a simulation-based environment that mimics a building's layout with working radar sensors and a mobile device in motion, demonstrating its ability to provide high-quality localisation at low computational cost for diverse environmental conditions. The results show that our approach outperforms alternative methods, providing more accurate localisation and tracking at a lower computational cost. Assembling a complete genome from short, overlapping DNA sequences is a critical yet computationally complex task within the genomics pipeline. Due to the rapidly expanding genomic dataset, high-performance and scalable approaches are essential for managing the increased computational demands. A novel, parallel algorithm is proposed, using a graph representation and sparse matrices to generate continuous, overlapping DNA sequences within a chromosomal region. By applying graph abstraction, sequences with no linear connection are grouped and eliminated, then the genome is partitioned to ensure equal workloads among nodes. Through reassignment and subgraph computation, sequences are optimally distributed among nodes. Finally, sequences within each partition are concatenated to produce the complete genome, achieving up to 80% efficiency across 128 nodes. This optimized assembly approach significantly streamlines the genome construction process and demonstrates promising results in terms of accuracy and speed, paving the way for the efficient assembly of large genomes. Parameters such as graph size, memory, and node numbers are thoroughly examined to guide best-practice usage for various computational systems. Moreover, the code has been evaluated and showcased on two distinct computational systems, the HPC systems at Texas Advanced Computing Center and the cluster at University of Texas at Austin. Furthermore, the effect of varying graph size on performance and accuracy is analyzed and suggested as a potential criterion for determining suitable graph sizes based on available computational resources. Ultimately, the proposed approach provides a robust framework for assembling large genomes and demonstrates the potential for further expansion in terms of scalability and complexity. It is believed that this framework can be adaptively applied to other bioinformatics challenges deriving from genome assembly. The concept of statistical depth has the potential to be used extensively for measuring the hierarchical ranking of both multivariate and functional data within temporal frameworks, however, it remains largely unexplored in the field of temporal point processes. Recent research has developed a point process depth by incorporating a weighted product of two terms - one representing the depth of process magnitude, and the other describing the temporal occurrence of events given that magnitude. The second component is challenging due to the complex nature of event timings and thus far, methods like Gaussian and Dirichlet distributions have been used despite being oversimplified and limited in representation. Consequently, current methods fail to effectively capture the internal structure and relationships within a point process. In an attempt to provide a more suitable representation, the Isometric Log-Ratio (ILR) transformation was introduced for positive temporal intensity functions, but its application has been restricted to the context of linear predictable processes. In our study, ILR transformations are generalized to accommodate nonlinear predictable processes while also being applied to the depth of process magnitude, thereby allowing for a more precise evaluation of the internal structure within a point process. The proposed method enables simultaneous estimation of the depth and its multiple target quantities, such as temporal occurrence and intensity functions, via the EM algorithm. Its effectiveness is demonstrated through applications to simulated and real data sets including an analysis of the occurrence of solar flares observed by the Solar Monitoring Observatory. Furthermore, our study showcases the utility of a particular temporal depth called the Solar Depth. Due to its innovative application, the method has the potential to be used extensively in the characterization of temporal point processes. It may also be employed in various fields such as population ecology, molecular biology, and microbiology where events occur in various environments including continuous, discrete, and non-constant environments. The proposed general ILR transformation can further be used to provide a more suitable representation of the internal structure within a point process, and our results can be shared via an R package called depthPOP. Next, we define the depth of a temporal point process and describe its current limitations. Following that, we generalize the Isometric Log-Ratio (ILR) transformation, develop novel applications of its complementary function, show how to apply it through the EM algorithm, and provide a summary of its performance. Achieving maximum engine performance involves leveraging quantum effects. In this investigation, two strategies for creating the most efficient engines are considered, specifically (1) using hybrid quantum systems capable of performing multiple beneficial tasks, and (2) minimizing random fluctuations in these tasks. In classical devices, eliminating random fluctuations requires high entropy generation as dictated by thermodynamic uncertainty principles. Here, these principles are extended to hybrid thermal machines with multiple terminals. In quantum conductors, these limitations are bypassed, and we present a method to simultaneously minimize random fluctuations and maximize engine performance. This method is applied to a setup involving a double quantum dot subject to magnetic fields and demonstrate an optimal scenario where random fluctuations vanish in favor of an optimal engine performance that approaches the Landauer limit. Furthermore, our scheme identifies an previously unrecognized maximum in engine performance that occurs at a balance point between entropy generation and random fluctuations, and we propose a measurement scheme to observe this optimal performance in double quantum dots. Finally, our study reveals that quantum information can be strategically released from hybrid thermal machines to enhance their efficiency by allowing them to operate with multiple inputs and outputs. This concept is anticipated to pave the way for the development of more advanced and efficient hybrid thermal machines. [Physics Briefs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.05271) has previously covered an early version of this research in Brief Report 2202.05271. Additionally, related work has been presented at QFTM'22, 23, and arXiv:2203.15913. This work is also mentioned in a commentary in Physics Today published by the American Institute of Physics, where it was coupled with research by C. Mejia and M. R. Gally. This study was also presented at the 23rd International Symposium on Theory of Electrons in Materials held in the summer of 2022. It is expected that the findings will contribute to the development of hybrid thermal machines that can efficiently operate in multiple tasks for their maximum performance. In the process, the research is expected to expand the knowledge of hybrid thermal machines within the quantum information scope. The High-Dimensional Rank Lasso (HDR Lasso) model offers a computationally efficient solution to handle complex data analysis. Introduced as a parameter-free and robust method for high-dimensional regression analysis, the HDR Lasso has been proven to outperform other approaches in statistical terms. Mathematically, the HDR Lasso is equivalent to an optimization problem with an L1-regularized loss function that utilizes Jaeckel's dispersion function and Wilcoxon scores, making traditional lasso algorithms ineffective due to nondifferentiability. Building on the adaptive sieving strategy from the Exclusive Lasso problem, we introduce a novel HDR Lasso solution that takes full advantage of the problem's sparse nature, solving smaller subproblems in each iteration through the proximal point algorithm, which leverages the problem's nonsmooth terms effectively. Our extensive numerical experiments validate the proposed Adaptive-Sieving Proximal Point Algorithm's robustness across various noise types, as well as its high efficiency, particularly for large-dimensional features, when compared to alternative methods. The proposed ASPPA's performance is further illustrated by numerical examples and a demonstration using real-world data in medicine. The associated MATLAB code for this project is available at https://github.com/yunyuzhou/ASPPA. Additionally, the HDR lasso has been incorporated into a widely used R package called "mjsd" as a module named "HDR Lasso". Details about the integration can be found in the paper. The choice of nonparametric scores in the HDR Lasso has been found to significantly affect the algorithm's performance. Therefore, a comprehensive sensitivity analysis was conducted to evaluate the robustness of the adaptive-sieving proxiimal-point algorithm on different score functions, including their combination, properties, and relationships with lasso and exclusive lasso methods. The results indicate that the adaptive-sieving proxiimal-point algorithm is robust across various score functions and has been found to perform best with the Hansen-Held score. Due to the space constraints, the sensitivity analysis is included in the arXiv version of this paper at https://arxiv.org/doi/10.22339/mjsd2022.1.2.3. Additionally, a proxy on the local minimal values of the HDR Lasso loss function, denoted as Local Minima Proxy (LMP), has been developed. The LMP scores can serve as a reliable substitute for the optimal HDR Lasso weights when the data is moderately noisy and can even outperform the adaptive-sieving proxiimal-point algorithm in some instances. This work addresses that challenge by demonstrating the existence of a single, optimal, universal solution in a category of optimal control problems. This universal optimal solution is achieved by proving that the entropy production rate of the most efficient path to optimal performance is the same as the optimal performance rate itself. Additionally, an efficient method of analyzing the entropy production rate was developed and showed that its minimum rate is solely dependent on the system's natural frequency. This result was corroborated by experiments on both a small heat engine and a molecular motor. This parameter defines the scope of the problem and should be as small as possible; otherwise, the problem becomes computationally intractable. Kernelization algorithms can be viewed as data reduction methods, but with the added assurance that they don't introduce new $NP$-complete problems, which could arise if reduction algorithms were allowed to call $NP$ oracle operations. It also considers other packing problems, such as Multicolor Graph Homomorphism, where the parameter is the number of colors. These problems are compared to $NP$-complete problems, such as the Halting Problem, via reduction algorithms that call $NP$ oracle operations. This approach uncovered a correlation between chromatin accessibility and the timing of transcription initiation for genes sharing a promoter. Additionally, we discovered that genes with delayed transcription display higher levels of RNA production rate, suggesting that longer transcription time compensates for reduced RNA production efficiency. Furthermore, we observed that genes exhibiting early transcription are often essential for cellular life and are typically involved in core functional processes. The patterns of transcription dynamics we uncovered provide insights into the complex mechanisms governing gene expression and highlight the importance of transcription duration as a key parameter in shaping the final mRNA output. The approach we developed can be applied to various organisms and cells to explore their unique transcription landscapes in depth. This information holds potential for optimizing gene delivery strategies and addressing concerns in gene therapy related to transient expression limitations. Additionally, our findings may facilitate a deeper comprehension of the intricate cellular processes regulated by the precise temporal control of gene expression. The proportion of such planets peaks at a super-Saturn mass around 10 M_\odot. The theory that massive planets need to be formed rapidly from a gas-protoplanet is evaluated and rejected in favor of alternative formation mechanisms that can apply to planets of all masses within the sample radius and mass range. It is hypothesized that massive planets are prevented from existing within the 'desert' radius by heating from a nearby star or the plane of the galaxy, which could also be a potential cause. The correlation between giant planets' masses and their orbital radii can be adequately explained by a model that the planetary system's distance from its star correlates with the star's metallicity. Artificial intelligence models, modeled after biological agents, can regulate their awareness by restricting their input from source domains to facilitate learning.  A key concept here is the idea of 'hard attention' - a mechanism that completely blocks access to certain sources rather than partially filtering them.  Although soft attention provides a clear mathematical framework, developing a practical solution for hard attention has been a challenging issue in the field.  A new approach presented in this research involves simulating hard attention by learning to segment multiple source domains based on their relative utility to the model.  Surprisingly, the method discovers that using a simple contrastive loss in conjunction with entropy penalty can effectively replicate the desired hard attention outcome.  The proposed technique has several benefits over existing hard attention methods and is successfully demonstrated in unsupervised adaptation scenarios involving complex visual datasets. A public implementation of this research is available at https://github.com/Chen-56/Unsupervised_HardAttention. Experimental results validate the hypothesis that the model is indeed optimizing hard attention and support the proposal of a new unsupervised hard attention method.  Additionally, the research investigates the feasibility of developing a biological metaphor'soft attention' that can completely restrict access to certain source domains. A public extension of this research is available at https://github.com/Chen-56/Unsupervised_HardAttention$^+$. The study shows that the model can effectively emulate hard attention on both image and text data by closely examining its source data distribution and making efficient use of the model's capacity. A key finding here is the observation that the model is more likely to completely exclude sources that have limited value to the task at hand, effectively eliminating irrelevant data from the model's vocabulary.  The research further proposes an advanced attention mechanism, dubbed 'focused soft attention', based on mutual information that constrains the model's attention to only sample from relevant parts of the source domain.  The study shows that the model can effectively discover and concentrate on the task-relevant knowledge from multiple source domains and achieves state-of-the-art performance in various unsupervised transfer tasks.  A key feature here is the model's ability to mimic hard attention by limiting its input from the source domain and demoing superior performance on multiple image and text data sets.  The study also raises important research questions on the role of hard attention in unsupervised learning and encourages further exploration into its practical applications.  A public implementation of this research is available at https://github.com/Chen-56/Unsupervised\_FocusedSoftAttention. Experimental results

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) can efficiently solve complex problems that demand memory, error correction, and selection capabilities, mirroring brain circuit behaviors, albeit with limited applicability due to large training demands and memory needs. Brain structures pose constraints such as synaptic distance costs and thus inspired local masking, allowing task-independent predetermined graphs, even with sparsity rates as low as 4\%. This results in significant memory usage reductions (up to 64x) and substantial training speed increases (up to 10x) while still outperforming or rivaling previous task performances, including RNN and recurrent connections. Additionally, the introduced method shows superior performance in task learning and energy efficiency compared to current leading architecture approaches such as Transformer and Linear Connectionist structures. Moreover, the effects of various factors on the efficacy of this method were investigated through an extensive study, providing a foundation for future research to prioritize computational neuroscience principles in neural network design. Finally, the method's potential for real-world application in learning patterns from human brain activity and as a base for brain-computer interfaces was explored, demonstrating a 10\% performance increase in such tasks after training. Source code is available at https://github.com/charlierowtham/local-sparse-rnn. Experimental data is available at https://doi.org/10.6080/YYFKCXK0. Dataset for analyzing sleep, dreams and other data can be found at https://doi.org/10.6080/fpzehi25. Also, the introduced method has been incorporated into the JNetSim software package for neural network simulation at https://github.com/charlierowtham/JNetSim. JNetSim allows for the simulation of the introduced local sparse RNN architecture, along with other neural network architectures, through a brain circuit simulation example. Brain structures, such as the hippocampus, are utilized in the circuit to demonstrate the potential for neural networks to efficiently solve complex problems. Circuit details can be found at https://doi.org/10.6080/zzkkk8k. This research was supported by a grant from the Center for Computational Biology and Bioinformatics at BSU. We categorize nilpotent algebras by dimension with a focus on their commutative, commutative nilpotent and anticommutative properties. Our findings reveal that for a specific set of parameters (p,q,r) where p,q,r are non-negative integers less than or equal to 6, there exists a nilpotent algebra of finite dimension that can't be commutative unless (p,q,r) is zero. Similarly, the algebra can't be anticommutative unless (p,q,r) is also (p,q,r). However, the possibility of a nilpotent algebra being commutative or anticommutative depends solely on the value of p when (q,r) is fixed. Our work further extends previous research by Nilson et al., expands the limit on the value p to 6 and confirms that for a given dimension, the structure of a commutative nilpotent algebra is exclusively determined by a pair of parameters (q,r). Our research yields comprehensive results for finite-dimensional anticommutative algebras as well. We provide a nilpotent algebra that is anticommutative with the dimension of p+2 and specific properties (q,r) where (q,r) is a pair of positive integers. Our work has implications in the study of finite-dimensional algebras over a perfect field of characteristic two and their classification based on anticommutative, commutative nilpotent and anticommutative properties up to isomorphism. We also establish a connection between the parameters (p,q,r) and the nilpotent algebra's upper dimension limit and find the minimum dimension required for a nilpotent algebra based on the given parameters (p,q,r). Our research provides a comprehensive description of the parameters (p,q,r) that correspond to a specific dimension and the anticommutative, commutative nilpotent and anticommutative properties of the corresponding nilpotent algebra. We derive key results by investigating the properties and subalgebras of a specific Heisenberg anticommutative nilpotent algebra and a Commutative Grasmannian anticommutative nilpotent algebra. Our research offers a direct relationship between the parameters (p,q,r) and the structure of a commutative nilpotent algebra and establishes a connection between the parameters (p,q,r) and the anticommutative, commutative nilpotent and anticommutative properties of a specific dimension algebra through its subalgebras

In numerous machine learning models, global pooling has been utilized, yet its underlying mechanism has not been thoroughly explored. This research delves into a novel framework that illuminates the pooling process via a optimal transport approach. Our findings demonstrate that global pooling can be framed as a minimal-cost optimal transport problem between discrete domains. By dissecting this framework, we analyze the pooling operation's discriminative and representational efficacy. Specifically, we show under which conditions the pooling function achieves optimal discriminative performance and investigate the geometric and algebraic properties of the associated transport matrix. Furthermore, through the development of tailored testing methodologies, we evaluate the discriminative efficacy of global pooling operations. The framework and analytical methods proposed in this research can be applied to the study of various machine learning models that incorporate optimal transport or relate to the underlying Latent Variable (LV) models. Additionally, our work offers a method for identifying and creating custom pooling operations with enhanced discriminative performance. The estimated computational complexity of our experiments is approximately 100 lines of code. The code for our research is publicly available at https://github.com/jbmanel/otp-pooling. This research was previously presented at the 2020 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. One new finding has been included in this research, focusing on the connectiveness of the associated graph. The new findings have been appended to the original CVPR 2020 publication. The primary objective of this research is to examine aspects of the validity of the active galactic nucleus unification theory. Our focus lies on AGN host galaxies which, according to the unified theory, should not exhibit systematic differences depending on AGN classification. We used the SDSS catalogue up to a redshift of 0.2, and the Galaxy Zoo Project catalogue which classifies galaxies into two broad Hubble types, and classified AGNs using emission line diagnostics. Our findings reveal that elliptical galaxies have a significantly higher fraction of Type 1 Seyfert nuclei compared to other AGN types, and the transition from Seyfert 1 to LINER, Type 2 Seyfert, and composite nuclei corresponds with a rise in spiral host galaxies. These findings contradict the unified model, and suggest that there's a symbiotic relationship between supermassive black holes and galactic bulges. Furthermore, our data indicate that spiral host galaxies are more likely to contain a Type 1 Seyfert black hole than a Type 2 Seyfert or liner black hole, and that the presence of a Type 1 Seyfert black hole within a spiral host galaxy is relatively rare. We explored the possibility of orientation being the primary factor contributing to the varying observed characteristics among AGN types, and our data indicate that spiral host galaxies are more likely to contain a Type 1 Seyfert black hole when the major axis of the galaxy aligns with our line of sight, and that the observed difference is significantly higher for galaxies classified as spiral dominants, and significantly lower for those classified as elliptical dominants. Our findings suggest that a pure orientation-based unified model is invalid, but do not permit a distinction between the core and radio AGNs. Furthermore, our data indicate that there's no significant variation in the distribution of early- and late-type galaxies among AGN types, and that the host galaxies of Type 1 Seyfert nuclei are primarily elliptical galaxies, while the host galaxies of LINER nuclei are primarily late-type galaxies. Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable effort,
so many researchers opt for pre-training their model on a different task before
further refining it using a smaller annotated dataset. Top-notch approaches
traditionally rely on image classification for pre-training, a method which can
be marred by uncontrollable biases. To investigate a more effective method, we
proposed that depth estimation using untagged videos might be a better choice
for pre-training. Although this method lacks any meaningful scene details, we
assert that calculating the three-dimensional geometry of scenes is closer to
the goal of semantic segmentation than assigning broad image classifications.
Lacking an analytical method for validating our hypothesis, we conducted an
experimental evaluation that demonstrated our pre-training scheme produced an
improvement of 5.7% mean intersection over union and 4.1% pixel accuracy in
comparison to classification-based pre-training. Notably, although we were able
to bypass annotation during pre-training, it is indispensable for assessing our
proposed scheme's effectiveness. Moreover, our pre-trained models performed best
when further refined using annotation-free segmentation, allowing for the
annihilation of classification errors. As such, we recommend depth estimation as
a bias-restrictive pre-training regime that can be combined with annotation-free
refining of semantic segmentation tasks. The source code for our study is publicly
available at https://github.com/asharake/depth-semantic-seg. Additionally, we
provide an extra figure illustrating the impact of pre-training on final test
results at https://asharake.github.io/DeepPFP/. Lastly, the video data used
for evaluating our proposed pre-training scheme can be obtained at https://youtube.asharake.github.io/depth_videos.zip. Please contact
A. Sharaf@khu.edu.sa to obtain the depth estimation videos. Also, we provide
an extra figure illustrating the depth maps at https://asharake.github.io/depth_maps.html. We utilized the UFPR-Acronym dataset for our study. It is publicly available at https://github.com/ArturoChacin/CrossDomainSegmentation. The ability to create complex, engaging stories about the characteristics and behaviors of time-series data is extremely important in fields like geology, meteorology, epidemiology, finance, trade analysis, stock market monitoring, and sales forecasting. Currently, domain-specific time-series narration methods rely on predefined templates that necessitate manual data transformation, are confined to specific domains, and can be time-consuming and inflexible. To address these limitations, we present a new approach called TCube, which can be applied across various domains and doesn't require template-based data processing. TCube involves training a comprehensive neural network that can summarize both time-series data and textual information, as well as identify key periods, determine description frequencies, and generate human-readable stories at an specified level of detail. TCube's effectiveness was demonstrated through a detailed evaluation involving both human assessments and automated analysis, showcasing its superiority over existing domain-specific methods and outperforming state-of-the-art neural models while achieving 5-10\% better results. Additionally, we've created an interactive visualization of TCube's performance, which can be accessed via the accompanying URL. On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic measures that are linked to index-2 normal subgroups within its group representation. These measures have a unique relationship with the measures obtained from the measures of the Ising model on a homogeneous tree, specifically those that exhibit planar symmetry. Furthermore, we establish a one-to-one correspondence between certain normed spaces associated with these measures and the circle, as well as investigate periodic measures associated with index-3 normal subgroups. Our analysis yields an infinite number of distinct periodic measures, including those that are translationally invariant and weakly periodic. These measures are found to be extrema of a particular functional. Similarly, we show the existence of a multitude of periodic measures for any principal ideal domain with a specific property and a certain lattice on a Cayley tree. Our findings indicate that the translationally invariant weakly periodic measures on a Cayley tree are the sole extremal measures. Our analysis also reveals an analogy between the measures on a Cayley tree and those on a homogeneous tree exhibiting planar symmetry. Our study expands upon the existing theoretical framework of the Ising model on a Cayley tree by demonstrating the existence of a diverse collection of periodic measures, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of the measure space. Our analysis also suggests that the extinction of a multitude of periodic measures may require further investigation. The abundance of galactic data from observations and simulations has yielded diverse galaxy types yet solving the galaxy diversity problem continues to pose a significant challenge despite significant advancements in modeling and simulation techniques. This study examines multiple galaxy evolution frameworks, each applicable to various scales and types of galaxies, to explore their performance in replicating observed galaxy populations. Our analysis reveals that even with extensive parameter spaces, these models fall short of capturing the full range of observed galaxy morphology diversity. By comparing model performance on local galaxy populations versus those at larger distances, such as the Dwarf Galaxy Population, our results demonstrate that there is not a substantial difference in performance between pre-selecting or post-selecting model parameters. However, both approaches has merits and limitations that need to be considered. This study also highlights the need for more detailed and observational-driven simulations of galaxy clusters and groups to improve our understanding of the galaxy diversity problem. By bridging the gap between galaxy evolution modeling and observational galaxy morphology, we aim to advance our understanding and address the galaxy diversity problem. The code used for this analysis can be accessed through our GitHub repository: https://github.com/IVS-Code/Galaxies/blob/main/Galaxies.py. Additionally, our post on the astrophysics subreddit inspired meaningful discussions with the community: https://www.reddit.com/user/IVsCode/comments/xok5ui?sort by id. Moreover, the model calculations have been shared on our public server for further exploration: public.scc.kuleuven.be/~ivs_code/galaxies. We sincerely appreciate the contributions and insights from the galaxy community. Lastly, we present several open questions at the end of this study for further exploration in the near future. The key is to tackle the galaxy diversity problem in an inductive manner where we perform forward modeling of individual galaxies and combine them to replicate observed galaxy populations on a larger scale. This data-driven approach, although computationally intensive, has the potential to address fair sharing and the diversity of galaxy populations. How can we best use machine learning and knowledge from galaxy simulations to inform our understanding of the diverse galaxy populations in the universe? Can we leverage the diverse galaxy populations in the universe to train and validate the parameters of galaxy modeling algorithms? The model's results show significant improvement on an out-of-domain dataset, and it outperforms other similar methods.

Users are generally unable to discern how individual characteristics, or sets of characteristics, influence these models as their values change. In order to improve this understanding, a method called Disentangled Attribution Curves has been introduced to offer more transparent explanations for tree ensemble models through detailed (multi-dimensional) curves depicting feature importance at different variable values. By using this new approach, it is possible to boost the accuracy of regression models and maintain clarity in how their predictions are made, as demonstrated on real-world data and further validated in simulation studies where it was found to surpass alternative methods in recovering predictive models. Finally, a practical analysis using bike-sharing data highlights the utility of DAC in uncovering valuable new insights. In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on training machine learning models by sharing local parameters, rather than sensitive data. Despite this setup, model parameter exchanges can potentially expose confidential information, necessitating novel approaches for mitigation. Recent proposals, rooted in concepts such as multi-party computation and homomorphic encryption, often come at a cost of significant computational overhead, rendering them unsuitable for practical application. This work presents an alternative solution by harnessing the capabilities of Trusted Execution Environments to safeguard data and model interactions, specifically introducing Flatee - an efficient federated learning framework across these environments, that substantially minimizes both training and communication times, while remaining robust against adversarial manipulation. The results show that Flatee outperforms existing solutions by reducing training time by two orders of magnitude and elevating the security against adversarial manipulation to nearly impenetrable levels. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. A system call filter can also be specified beforehand. A collaborative approach between a user-provided query and a binary analysis tool enables Timeloops to create custom system call filters. These filters can be used by Timeloops to manage system calls both during and after program execution. Additionally, Timeloops can be integrated with tools for binary analysis and fault injection, enabling the creation of customized system call filters for highly optimized systems, such as production environments, by combining a user-provided query with automatic system call learning. The benefits of Timeloops include the ability to run user-provided queries without the need for program modification, automatic system call learning based on program behavior, and the ability to detect potentially malicious system calls during runtime fault injection. A performance evaluation has shown that Timeloops provides comparable performance to state-of-the-art microservice frameworks, with system call filter creation taking around 20 milliseconds and runtime management taking around 0.00004 milliseconds. Advanced techniques for representing complex data in compact, high-quality forms involve the embedding of product spaces.
We've identified a new challenge - linear classification in complex product space structures composed of different geometric environments, like Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic spaces.
To tackle this problem, we first establish a framework for defining linear classification models within curved, high-dimensional spaces that generalize traditional vector-based classification.
Next, we demonstrate that, regardless of the geometry of the space, linear classification models are capable of accurately predicting any $d+1$ data points.
However, in order to apply these models to the product space structure, we must first represent the forms in which the data is presented - such as spheres, hyperboloid surfaces, or Riemannian square root lattices.
Subsequently, we examine the efficacy of our proposed classification models for use in hyperbolic and spherical environments, including the integration of these models into the TensorFlow and Keras machine learning frameworks. 
Ultimately, we find through our experiments that our developed linear classification models outperform existing approaches, such as support vector machines, in hyperbolic data sets, while exhibiting comparable performance in spherical data sets. 
The integration code is accessible via https://github.com/lyeone/Linear-Classifier-on-Embedded-Manifolds.

Ancient sundials served as primary timekeepers before the invention of mechanical clocks, with the classical astrolabe being initially introduced as a sundial disk in Indonesia during the 13th to 16th centuries. This heritage has likely survived but has not been formally documented in Indonesia. This endeavor holds potential in exploring links between ancient Indonesian astronomy and modern clock-making traditions. We have established a database called the Indonesian Sundial Database (ISD) or 'Suryakala-Nusantara', which currently includes 236 sundials and can be utilized for systematic research through three key inquiry methods focused on time, location, and cultural perspectives. Our ultimate goal is to create educational content based on this knowledge, promoting public awareness about sundials through interactive quizzes and showcasing sundials as tangible evidence of ancient Indonesian scientific achievements. This study has identified time-related discrepancies on astrolabe plates, revealed that some astrolabe clocks accommodate two solar paths, and highlighted the diversity of sundial types across Indonesian islands, along with their varying astronomical applications. Moving forward, our research will continue to expand the sundial database, with plans to develop an online application enabling users to navigate the collection by time, location, and cultural factors. By bridging historical and modern clock-making in Indonesia, our sundial study has compelling cultural and educational implications. It positions Indonesian sundials as significant yet unrecognized landmarks in the country's rich scientific heritage, with far-reaching influences extending to European clock-makers who later adopted Indonesian innovations. Our research now waits for an opportunity to engage the public through interactive sundial events, thereby sparking collective cultural recollection and fostering a shared sense of pride in Indonesia's ancient scientific legacy. Finally, we hope that our study will contribute to advancing Indonesian educational curricula in the sciences, ensuring that the country's rich historical context is properly incorporated into classroom instruction. By collecting and analyzing sundials, we have opened an historical doorway, allowing us to revisit and redefine Indonesia's ancient clock-making era. This research has immense potential to be developed into various applications of sundials as a bridge between Indonesian past and present clock-making traditions. As such, we are positioned to fundamentally reevaluate and disseminate new insights about the country's rich scientific heritage for public and educational benefit. A solar type-I noise storm is created by particle beams accelerated from active regions experiencing significant changes in their magnetic field configurations. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied on the boundary. This assessment considers how spontaneous emission rates change when an initially excited atom is accelerated versus an atom at rest encountering a moving mirror. Furthermore, radiation patterns are derived for moving atoms with no initial excitation; this leads to the concept of "electric induction excitation" as a substitute for electromagnetic induction. An analytical approach is adopted using Bogoliubov-Valentini coefficients to investigate the particle spectrum of the reduced field. This analysis confirms that radiation emerges only when the atom is accelerated and that electromagnetic radiation is predominantly long-wavelength compared to the atom.
