A longstanding issue regarding massive star origins involves whether these stars always form within dense clusters and, if found in less crowded environments, if they inevitably moved there.  Recent advances in wide-scale photometric surveys enable us to detect massive stars without bias in the less crowded regions of the galaxy.  This study examines forty candidate OB stars discovered by Mohr-Smith et al in the vicinity of Westerlund 2, with locations confined to a 1.5x1.5 degree square area, distinguished by their extinctions and K magnitudes.  Spectroscopic data for these stars show that thirty-seven are O7 or earlier with kinematic data indicating that half are moving rapidly away from Westerlund 2, with less than 10% moving towards it and the rest moving randomly around the cluster.  These results, combined with the large number of O stars found, support galactic wind theory and suggest that massive star energies are a significant factor in shaping the galaxy's interstellar medium and galaxy evolution.  This led the authors to propose a new theory called "expulsion-based feedback" (EBF), a mechanism by which massive stars detach from their birth clusters and displace others, ultimately regulating the number of massive stars in each cluster and generating large-scale outflows that can shape the galaxy's environment.  This new theory may be a crucial factor in regulating the galaxy's metal distribution and can help explain why Westerlund 2 shows exceptional metallicity.  This led the authors to propose a new model called the "inside-out feedback" (IIF) model in order to explain this phenomenon.  This model proposes that massive star materials scavenged by supernovae and distributed throughout the cluster can later be consumed by main-sequence O stars undergoing further star formation in the area, ultimately regulating the number of massive stars in each cluster and generating large-scale outflows that can shape the galaxy's environment.  This new model may be a crucial factor in regulating the galaxy's metal distribution and can help explain why Westerlund 2 shows exceptional metallicity.  This discovery led the authors to discover hidden massive star populations within the cluster, with multiple massive star generations, including a massive star generation in the past that was expelled from the cluster and a generation of massive star candidates undergoing early star formation in the area.  This discovery is consistent with the gallery-like structure of the cluster, with younger stars concentrated in the middle of the area and older stars along the edges of the area. In vehicular communications, the complex and dispersive nature of channels makes reliable channel estimation vital for optimal system performance, yet the IEEE 802.11p standard's limited pilots lead to inadequate channel tracking. As a result, conventional IEEE 802.11p estimators experience significant performance decline, particularly in high-speed scenarios. To overcome these challenges, researchers have explored deep learning (DL) techniques for channel estimation in IEEE 802.11p. Nonetheless, these approaches either underperform in extremely high-speed situations or exhibit substantial computational complexities. To resolve these issues, this paper introduces an innovative solution based on a long short-term memory (LSTM) model for channel estimation. The proposed method incorporates an LSTM unit for channel estimation, followed by a temporal averaging technique to mitigate noise, and analytically calculates the noise mitigation ratio to verify its effectiveness. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed solution surpasses the performance of recently proposed DL-based estimators, while also achieving substantial reductions in computational complexity. Consequently, the proposed LSTM-based estimator represents a pioneering solution for channel estimation in IEEE 802.11p. Additionally, its adaptable structure enables successful application to other DL-based estimators. The IEEE 802.11p standard's compliance was rigorously demonstrated throughout the research. The task of automatically assigning colors to images without human involvement has garnered interest within the machine learning community for a limited time. Colorization is particularly challenging due to its inherently high degrees of freedom; when presented with an image, multiple plausible color combinations exist, and there may be no single definitive solution. Another related issue is Single Image Super Resolution, a task that involves converting low-resolution images into higher-resolution versions. This research targets a novel, automatic colorization approach, specializing in astronomical images and leveraging Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). We experiment with employing various models in the RGB and L*a*b color spaces, relying on transfer learning and pre-trained ResNet-18 architecture, due to the small size of the dataset available. Our approach successfully produces aesthetically pleasing, high-resolution, and colorized results for images lacking these characteristics. The performance of the proposed model is quantitatively assessed by measuring distance metrics, including L1 distance and L2 distance, and evaluating the generated images against the real data distribution using the Frechet inception distance (FID) metric. Additionally, the distribution of the generated images' a and b values in the L*a*b color space appears to closely resemble that of real images, suggesting a level of training data generalization. We compare the proposed model to the AICnet approach, showcasing performance improvements in colorization and FSIM score with our model, while achieving comparable PSNR and L1 distance performance. The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a subject-object relationship in a sentence. Specifically,
when a model identifies an object related to a given subject, it can be seen
as supplying the object that should be linked to the subject in a knowledge
graph. Building upon this connection, we propose a novel approach where a
relation extraction model's output is fed into a knowledge graph link prediction
model. This technique enhances the capability of a basic relation extraction model
by 4.3% in terms of accuracy, as tested on the Standard Relation Extraction
dataset. Furthermore, we observed a notable 6.8% improvement in our model's
ability to correctly identify unrelated objects and a 5.6% improvement in its
ability to correctly identify relevant objects, when compared to a model that
does not utilize a knowledge graph link prediction model. Our research also
includes an investigation into the impact of varying knowledge graph size on
the quality of a relation extraction model, revealing a correlation between the
size of the knowledge graph and the quality of the relation extraction model. 
Our study also demonstrates the efficacy of multi-task learning, as combining
the tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction yielded
better results than processing the tasks separately. Notably, we found that
bi-directional encoder representations to be a more effective approach than
fixed-position encoder representations in our relation extraction model, with
bi-directional representations yielding better performance when combined with
the knowledge graph link prediction model. The full code for this project is
available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/wwu-kevphat/KEVPhat\_RE.

In Tb3RuO7, neighboring ruthenium atoms created a chain pattern, with some being ordered magnetically and others remaining randomly aligned. This unique combination resulted in an intermediate disordered state, with the two ruthenium types exhibiting similar yet distinct behaviors. In Nd3RuO7, the magnetic patterns were uniform and independent for the two ruthenium species, with both being ordered at temperatures below 17.5 K. We attribute the disordered state in Tb3RuO7 primarily to the magnetic frustrations, caused by the differing internal magnetic fields imposed by the ordered terbium atoms on the two ruthenium species, leading to distinct behaviors. This unique combination of magnetic interactions is rare and remarkable. In Nd3RuO7, below 17.5 K, the magnetic interactions between the two ruthenium species became equally strong in one direction but dominantly dominant in the other direction. We observed a distinct transition in the magnetic arrangements, with the two ruthenium species being ordered autonomously, below 17.5 K. Notably, Nd3RuO7 also exhibited a distinct "skipped" arrangement for the ruthenium species, with the nearest neighbors on the chain being not nearest neighbors in the chain. We utilized the specific-heat capacity to quantify the critical temperatures and analyze the magnetic and electronic interactions, with the critical temperatures for the two ruthenium species being 17.5 K and 8.8 K, respectively. In Tb3RuO7, below 2 K, we detected faint signs of spin disorder, along with a 1/3 magnetization reduction, attributed to the magnetic frustrations. In Nd3RuO7, below 17.5 K, we detected faint signs of spin disorder, along with a 1/3 magnetization reduction, also attributed to the magnetic frustrations. We observed similar spin behaviors in Nd3RuO7 across all temperatures. Consequently, we propose that materials possessing this "skewed" arrangement should display paired magnetic and electronic interactions, resulting in distinct magnetic arrangements and their corresponding analyses. Additionally, we suggest that these materials can serve as platforms for exploring 1D, quantum-critical systems and their associated spin-lattice interactions. low-dimensional representations of data, such as images, shapes and light
fields. Despite advancements using periodic activations or positional
encodings, they have historically been tailored to process a single signal
and sacrificed some degree of generality. We introduce an innovative new
approach to representation learning that not only generalizes well to multiple
signals, but outperforms the competition in fidelity. We utilize a unique
two-part neural network design, where a synthesis network produces the output
given a specific input, and a modulated periodic activation, which controls
the degree of each periodic component active or inactive. We show that this
modulated design leads to a more generalizable representation by controlling
which parts of the input each neuron is sensitive to. Through an extensive
array of experiments over various applications and datasets that employ 3D
geometric representations, we prove that our modulated periodic activation
outperforms prior methods in both generative and discriminative tasks. The
resulting representations not only improve the overall performance, but also
facilitate seamless applicability to new data without any adjustments. We
demonstrate the versatility of these representations by successfully using
them to represent video, audio and language, which is unprecedented in
3D geometric representation. Lastly, we showcase the efficacy of our modulated
periodic activation in other areas such as motion forecasting and shape
retrieval. The full code and our modulated periodic activation are available

Traditional methods of covariate-shift adaptation utilize unlabelled data for either determining importance weights or domain-invariant features. Then, a model is trained using only labelled data. We're examining a special instance of covariate shift that also enables learning from unlabelled data, effectively merging adaptation with semi-supervised learning techniques. By drawing on causality concepts, we propose a novel method that requires learning from both the causes and effects of a target variable. This leads to the development of a semi-generative model, $P(Y,X_E|X_C,\theta)$, which is shown to be resilient against domain shifts in causal features. Moreover, this model leverages unlabelled data to directly map causes to their respective effects. Experiment results conducted on artificial data show considerable improvements in classification performance compared to solely-supervised and importance-weighting approaches. Moreover, our method's integrality in adapting to domain shifts holds clinical value in analyzing cardiovascular disease and its underlying causes. The study provides empirical evidence of its effectiveness. The study also highlights the potential for causal feature analysis in uncovering the mechanisms linking a disease with its potential causes, which might be altered in a domain shift. Despite its impressive task execution capabilities, the inner workings of deep learning systems remain shrouded in theoretical uncertainty. In our study, we establish a geometric model for deep learning architectures by identifying connections to pre-existing geometric frameworks in quantum computation and diffeomorphic template matching. Within this context, we map the geometric structures of convolutional neural networks, residual networks, recursive neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and the equilibrium propagation framework. Furthermore, this geometric framework enables us to explore the relationships between geometric structures and the performance of different neural networks, thereby guiding the design of deep learning architectures at an algorithmic level. Additionally, our work facilitates the development of a unified deep learning architecture that integrates various geometric structures, thereby enhancing the flexibility of deep learning methods through geometric variability. Ultimately, this unified deep learning architecture empowers broad task execution across multiple domains via a single compact neural network. By integrating the geometric deep learning architecture introduced in this paper with expert knowledge in medicine, it can be demonstrated that deep learning with implicit structures can surpass human performance. Similar ideas have recently been applied to language models, as seen at the recent Alethea showcase, where a geometric deep learning architecture was trained to generate poems using implicit structures, thereby outperforming various competing models in both quantity and quality. The source code for our research is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/nlecs-epfl/geometric-deep-learning and the demo videos are publicly available at https://geometric-deep-learning.github.io/demo. Furthermore, a detailed tutorial on geometric deep learning is available at https://github.com/nlecs-epfl/geometric-deep-learning/blob/main/tutorials. Additionally, the neural network models described in this research have been registered on the AI Hub platform as part of the effort to promote reproducibility in deep learning research. Specifically, the geometric deep learning architectures can be accessed via https://aihub.org/datasets/34. By utilizing the geometric deep learning models, it is possible to generate diverse outputs across various domains, as demonstrated by the made-in-EPFL challenge where the task was to create 3D videos using implicit structures. A research framework is introduced to uncover and analyze decision-making processes from deep neural network classifiers in jet substructure tagging techniques. To achieve this, the study uses a novel method, incorporating 'augmented' variables, known as XAUG variables, alongside standard input, then applies a layer-by-layer relevance analysis through back-propagation. An in-depth examination was conducted on a deep neural network designed to identify boosted top quarks within hadron jets, utilizing pseudo-data generated from simulated top quark decays with a beta-ratio around 0.6. XAUG variables outperformed standard input variables and an in-flight classifier based on neural networks, achieving the best performance with an area under the curve of 0.262 in distinguishing boosted top quarks from the nearest comparable hadron jet configurations. An in-depth analysis was also provided on the most critical regions, adopting a statistical perspective, and it was observed that networks trained with XAUG variables focused more on the initial top quark decay, while networks trained with standard input were sensitive to various phases of hadronisation. Additionally, it was noticed that networks trained with standard input showed a broader relevance pattern across many layers. Furthermore, it was discovered that the expert variable most strongly correlated with the classification outcome was the one representing the 90% of the leading hadronic jet's energy, and that the correlation was positive for networks trained with standard input but showed a more intricate relationship with the chosen variable in networks trained with XAUG variables. Lastly, it was noted that the most influential layer in the deepest fully connected neural network was the fourth one, occurring as early as at the first level of the neural network, and that the early adoption of a broad topology by the deep neural network was unanimously observed across all examined training sets. Nevertheless, it is worth mentioning that the role of early adopted broad topology was not directly related to the chosen training set. On a separate note, it is worth mentioning that although the adopted topology was chosen without any prior knowledge, it is possible that the success of the networks in distinguishing boosted top quarks from the nearest comparable hadron jet configurations could be attributed to the early adoption of a broad topology that took into consideration the sub-structure of the hadron jet, and that the result could have been achieved through a simpler neural network composed of only two layers, and with a considerable savings in computational resources. It's established that for Killing vector fields representing these momentum operators, the manifolds are either flat or belong to specific categories: those with a compact structure and a constant sectional curvature of positive value, occurring in dimensions of 1, 3, or 7. Specific forms for these momentum operators and their associated Casimir element are studied, particularly for the three-dimensional sphere S^3. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the Lie algebra structure constants for S^3 relate proportionally to 2ℏ/R, where R represents the sphere's curvature radius, yielding countable energy and momentum spectrums for freely moving particles. A theoretical maximum for possible momenta in S^3 corresponds to its diameter, the de Broglie wavelength λ_R = πR. Building on this, the definitions and relationships for covariant position operators in terms of geodesic normal coordinates, along with commutator relations for position and momentum, are developed. An examination of the distributions of eigenvalues for the Casimir element and the momentum operators provides insight into the intrinsic spatial curvature of the manifolds and their implications on the geometric relationships of their linear momentum spaces. Ultimately, it is found that the geometric properties of the curved manifolds can be reproduced through the quantum fluctuations in the momentum measurements of their intrinsic momentum spaces. A comparative analysis between the fundamental particle properties and the measurable signatures of the quantum fluctuations in P_p^2 is pursued. As a note, the described concepts and mathematical tools are generally applicable to other surfaces with a positive constant sectional curvature, such as CY manifolds of dimension six. However, they cannot be directly extended to spaces with a negative constant sectional curvature. For such spaces, an alternative approach must be employed. Additionally, no discussion on observable signatures of quantum fluctuations in P_p^2 has been included in the provided text, and such a discussion would require a broader theoretical framework often referred to as 'quantum hydrodynamics.' It's worth mentioning that the fundamental concepts described here, tailored to the intrinsic momentum spaces, offer a novel and distinct vision from the established quantum hydrodynamics. To tackle this issue, a novel hybrid Monte Carlo scheme based on complex-valued neural networks is proposed, allowing it to be scale-free and feasible for simulations involving a large number of particles. Moreover, this method can be extended to tackle more complex forms of the sign problem encountered in realistic modeling of materials. By applying this technique to the doped Hubbard model, the authors successfully obtained the momentum distribution coefficient, thereby validating the method's efficacy. Additionally, the study reveals that the conventional strategy of using the Hubbard-Stratonovich decomposition may lead to biased results, especially for higher particle counts. Therefore, this work presents a critical advancement in the field by introducing a method that can efficiently tackle the sign problem at the next frontier level of particle numbers. Furthermore, the authors introduce an, as yet, unnamed method called the level-shifted Hubbard-Stratonovich decomposition, which is a potential solution to this issue. In a composite Higgs model, where $SU(6)/Sp(6)$ is used, the flavor symmetry is identified as an $U(1)$ subgroup of $Sp(6)$. Here, the complex scalar field's', acting as a pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson, plays the role of a flavon, which bears a flavor charge. Upon the VEV of the flavon, $U(1)_F$ flavor symmetry is broken. This break results in the emergence of a small parameter and consequently generates the hierarchical structure of fermion masses via the interaction with the flavon's VEV. Notably, this model can naturally account for why there are three distinct families of fermions without introducing additional complexities. Furthermore, the model avoids the high-scale flavor problem arising from the model's ${\cal O}( (4\pi /3f_V )^2)$ flavor-violating processes, which is consistent with current experimental standards. Moreover, given the flavor symmetry, two fermion-mixing processes are anticipated, which may be within the reach of upcoming experiments to observe. Last but not least, even without the influence of additional confining dynamics, this model features three heavy degrees of freedom - two Sp(6) gauge bosons and a scalar - whose masses are at least on the order of the composite Higgs mass. These degrees of freedom can provide a potential signature to identify the model via the observation of multiplicity at high-energy collisions. Lastly, even though the model features a complex flavor structure, it is not a flavor-changing neutral current (FCNC) sensitive theory as the flavon's CP-violating part's VEV is directly linked to the composite Higgs's mass rather than its flavor-dependent part. Hence, the model does not have radical implications at low-energy scales compared to conventional two Higgs doublet models. Finally, upon further examination with more intricate flavor models, the potential of detecting the model via the observation of rare processes or CP-violating phenomena at low and high energy scales has been evaluated. This research examines the dangers of VPPM exploitation, beginning with a conceptual framework that confirms their existence and then applying speculative design to identify and mitigate threats. Through practical examples, we demonstrate how current VPPM practices can inadvertently create vulnerabilities that may lead to physical harm. This study seeks to highlight the potential consequences of VPPM applications and dissemination as they stand today. Future research should prioritise both VPPM safeguarding and the responsible dissemination of potentially hazardous VPPM instances. Ultimately, we hope this work inspires a safety net for the VPPM community. Published in Proceedings of VR2021, Cambridge, UK. To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into BigScience's large-scale, 1.3 billion parameter multilingual language model, initially trained on 13 languages. Our study focuses on key factors influencing model adaptability for new languages and weighs the computational expense against potential performance gains. We investigate several training methodologies including (i) unconstrained fine-tuning, (ii) language-constrained training for preventing knowledge contamination, (iii) gradient penalty for deterring artificial language knowledge, and (iv) adversarial training for enhancing generalization to unseen languages. Our analysis reveals that gradient penalty demonstrates superior performance on unseen languages with minimal knowledge contamination compared to other methods. Moreover, we develop an innovative tool to analyze the cat-in-a-hat phenomenon (rapid language switching) and employ it to examine the behavior of large language models when switching between multiple languages. Our findings show that BigScience models exhibit the cat-in-a-hat phenomenon but with our best approach (gradient penalty), they demonstrate more effective behavior, particularly on unseen languages. Additionally, we introduce an empirical metric for evaluating large models' ability to learn general language representations that can be applied across multiple languages. Our analysis indicates that BigScience models perform well on this metric and exhibit gradual performance increases as more languages are added to the model's training dataset. Lastly, our study shows that big models (such as Google's Electra) outperform small models (such as BERT) in our experiments, and surprisingly, adds an interesting observation that the prior knowledge of neighboring languages can somewhat predict the potential performance of the model on a given, previously unseen language. This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach ('m-ar-K-FastICA') for feature extraction. The novel algorithm combines kernel transformation with ICA and FastICA, incorporating optimization techniques and feature dimensionality reduction. Although previous studies have successfully demonstrated the efficacy of kernel-based methods, they have primarily been experimental in nature. The proposed m-ar-K-FastICA approach addresses this limitation by providing a well-founded solution. Numerous classification tasks have been performed using this method, yielding outstanding results on datasets like MNIST, Reuters, and StackOverflow. The code for this approach can be accessed at https://github.com/Ershock/m-ar-K-FastICA. The performance of m-ar-K-FastICA surpasses the performance of FastICA and other widely-used learning algorithms, including Support Vector Machines ('SVM'), Random Forests, and Extra Trees. The significant contribution of this research lies in the theoretical justification of kernel-based feature extraction, which had been lacking in previous studies. The findings of this study reveal that feature extraction can be more efficient than classification. Additionally, the proposed method is inherently stable and facilitates the identification of optimal parameter values through the second derivative rule. Furthermore, the approach is inherently independent of specific data distributions, which is demonstrated through a comparison with a Deep Neural Network ('DNN') trained using backpropagation on the same data. The comparative analysis demonstrates that m-ar-K-FastICA achieves an comparable error rate on MNIST, albeit using significantly fewer parameters. The associated computational cost of m-ar-K-FastICA is notably lower than that of contemporary kernel-based methods. The theoretical and experimental findings of this research can be utilized in various machine learning applications, such as those involving unsupervised learning, kernel-based feature extraction, and kernel-based classification. Future research can build upon these findings by extending the proposed method to device learning and incorporating random matrix theory. Additionally, the concept of k-mer Independent Component Analysis ('k-mer-ICA') was initially explored in this study. The novel algorithm combines kernel transformation with ICA and FastICA, utilizing k-mer windows to replace traditional kernel transformation. The efficacy of this approach was demonstrated on the StackOverflow dataset, yielding better performance than FastICA and SVM on a binary classification task. The associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/Ershock/m-ar-K-FastICA. The concept of k-mer-ICA can be further developed by incorporating random matrix theory and applying it to device learning.

Despite the numerous opinions expressed, verifying their accuracy can be challenging due to their often abstract nature. To address this, we aim to condense these posts into distinct narratives, thereby isolating the core assertions linked to specific subjects. Initially, we will focus on narratives surrounding police-related aggression. To achieve this, we will develop an unsupervised framework capable of extracting underlying narratives from the posts. Given the existing skepticism surrounding many of these claims, our goal is to create a system that enables users to add and validate new narrative elements, ensuring that the generated narratives remain accurate and comprehensive. To evaluate the efficacy of our approach, we will compare the performance of our method against existing state-of-the-art topics models, as well as user-generated classifications. Additionally, we will examine the potential for narratives to incorporate value-based information, thereby effectively capturing the inherent subjectivity of the posts. Ultimately, we hope to establish a method for storytelling that effectively conveys the complexity of the content and provides a starting point for developing a system that can assess the credibility of unfalsifiable claims. The proposed work represents a initial step toward developing a structure for capturing the nuances of such claims. Furthermore, we plan to expand our research to encompass more narratives not related to social media misinformation such as those found in conspiracy theories. By integrating Bayesian learning into adversarial training of deep neural networks, we developed a rigorous framework for training certifiable Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). This approach combines constraint relaxation and modified cross-entropy loss to achieve robustness to potential attacks. The method, demonstrated through empirical tests on standard datasets, allows for training BNNs that are both accurate and certifiably secure on challenging datasets such as MNIST and CIFAR-10, further providing benefits in uncertainty calibration. This innovation facilitates the deployment of BNNs in applications requiring utmost reliability. Furthermore, we introduced an innovative technique to establish certifiable confidence intervals for Bayesian prediction outcomes. This method, influenced by a mathematical examination, can provide bounds on the probability distribution of test set predictions. The resulting analysis demonstrates the performance benefits of BNN training through Bayesian learning and the utilization of adversarial training techniques. Moreover, we presented a thorough investigation of the relationship between robustness and reliability, discovered through empirical studies on various datasets. This empirical study, driven by a genuine inquiry, can provide valuable insights into the underlying connections between adversarial training and reliable deep neural network deployment. The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the critical period that forecasts a rumor's peak influence and developed a model to predict its trajectory. Experimenting with real data, we validated the effectiveness of our approach. Furthermore, we categorized the primary factors that facilitate the dissemination of rumors and developed an integrated system that incorporates both human and AI-driven annotation techniques. This system enabled precise identification of the roles that various entities play in amplifying rumors. Leveraging our findings, we analyzed the behavior of rumors related to COVID-19 and presented visualizations that offer valuable insights to practitioners seeking to counter rumors. Ultimately, our study provides a comprehensive framework for studying online rumors and offers practical solutions to mitigate their impact. The source code of our research has been made available at https://github.com/dwz-lyw/COVID-Rumor. Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors but they pose significant challenges due to their large size. Understanding the parameters within various layers is complicated, resulting in the networks often being referred to as 'black boxes.' In contrast, simpler models are both easier to comprehend and require less storage space. Therefore, reducing complex models down to smaller, more manageable pieces is a worthwhile endeavor. This study investigates different compression methods for natural language models, evaluating both their effectiveness and the ease with which their parameters can be interpreted. A key compression method examined was the use of interactive queries within the BERT model, specifically looking at how queries for key support vector machine learnable units affected model performance and parameter reduction. A novel prediction method, referred to as ProCS, enables fast and precise calculation of crucial chemical shift indicators in proteins, thereby determining the spatial arrangements of proteins. ProCS is based on a quantum mechanics-based model that accurately estimates the chemical shift of amide proton bonds. This is accomplished by optimizing the potential energy of amide protons between neighboring residues through a self-consistent field process. Research indicates that ProCS accurately identifies amide proton residues associated with irregular primary structure constraints and effectively forecasts nuclear Overhauser effects, making it suitable for use in refinement procedures for the experimental determination of protein structures. In a test involving the refinement of glucagon's structure, ProCS proved capable of improving the quality of its model. Consequently, ProCS is an essential tool for the minimization and refinement of protein structures derived from a range of experimental techniques, including a variety of NMR, X-ray crystallography, and cryo-electron microscopy investigations. This tool is particularly vital for the determination of distantly related protein structures where current refinement methods are ineffective. ProCS is expected to significantly expand the repertoire of successful protein structure determinations. Furthermore, ProCS's algorithms are now fully implemented in the quantum chemistry package REDUCE and are available for download at reducesoftware.org. A companion protocol is available on the protocols.org server at doi: 10.17504/protocols.io.700633. ProCS's valuations are also available on the structuredb.org server at doi: 10.5070/D5JF-EC58. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. We demonstrate the efficacy of this perspective by introducing a novel, adaptive loss function 'L' ('Learning Loss'), which can serve as a control parameter for neural networks. By treating loss function variation as a fundamental component of network architecture, we hope to redefine the traditional deep learning paradigm and facilitate further research in this area. Describing the behaviors of complex systems comprised of strongly interacting elements requires concise expressions for their internal relationships. Ensuring the stability of these systems is the primary focus. The parquet theory serves this purpose by designing a set of integral equations that define the stable patterns of interaction. Adapting the parquet theory from the context of classical Boltzmann gas to a quantum framework is crucial for analyzing the behaviors of systems such as strongly interacting fermions and superconducting materials. Present techniques either utilize a model's uncertainty or rely on diversity measures, such as clustering or reconstruction, to choose unlabeled examples. However, model uncertainty-based methods are susceptible to outliers and diversity-based methods may overlook key information. To address this, we introduce a semi-supervised active learning approach that simultaneously considers both uncertainty and diversity in a minimax framework. Our method incorporates a network that minimizes entropy and an entropy-maximizing classifier, while a discriminator is trained to distinguish labeled and unlabeled data. We then select the samples with the highest entropy that the discriminator identifies as unlabeled for human annotation. Experimental evaluation on image classification and semantic segmentation datasets demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. To study how music changed over time from the year 1960 to 2010, we calculated the entropy of songs in different genres using their acoustic properties, such as melody, harmony, and rhythm. Analyzing songs from databases representing various genres and the top charts, we discovered that popular music has become less complex and more homogeneous since the 1960s. Compared to other types of music, popular music has become less complex and more homogeneous since the 1960s. It was also observed that the complexity and homogeneity of music are closely linked. Additionally, it was found that changes in the complexity of music are not solely attributed to changes in listener preferences but also indicate a real shift in the creation of music. Our findings support the theory that cultural evolution is influenced by non-random processes. It was also noted that the most successful songs tend to have lower complexity and are more homogeneous than other music. However, it was found that complexity is not a determining factor of success. It was also observed that the complexity of music is related to the level of education and racial diversity in the audience. Our study is the first to analyze such a long and extensive dataset in such a detailed manner. It was found that music is either getting less complex or the rules for creating it are getting more restrictive over time. Our findings are important because they demonstrate how fundamental changes in the nature of music have led to it becoming less complex and less diverse. It was also found that music is an exceptional example of an abstract concept where the principles for creating it can be clearly automated. By analyzing music, it is possible to learn more about the universal laws that govern its creation. It also highlights the challenges and potential solutions for detecting diversity and complexity in complex phenomena. It was found that using quantitative analysis alone is not enough to understand diversity and complexity, and that qualitative analysis should be based on representative and diverse datasets. Our study is a valuable resource for anyone interested in studying complexity, diversity, and the evolution of music. A novel category of stochastic processes that incorporate reinforcement involves sequences of random groupings denoted as $\{\mathcal{P}_t\}_{t \ge 1}$. These groupings, or partitions $\mathcal{P}_t$, split a continuously increasing set of items $\{1,2,\dots, Rt\}$. When time progresses to $t$, a fixed number of items $R$ are appended to this set; a fraction of these added items joins existing groups based on probabilities defined across different $t$, while the rest form new subgroups isolated from the others. The item assignments create dependencies across consecutive time points, giving rise to a non-stationary stochastic process. The item assignments act as multiple entry rewards, thereby termed 'Multiple-entry Reinforcement Processes'. The study focuses on analyzing these groups and assessing their long-term aspects including: the probability distribution of long-term frequencies of the items, the maximum number of distinct groups that can form and its expected value, the maximum number of items in a single group and its expected value, and it resolves these by applying the theory of infinite-dimensional stochastic analysis including proving the convergence of empirical measures. The results are consistent with those obtained for other models of reinforcement processes. The empirical measures considered here are constructed by applying the Prokhorov metric for measuring the distance between these groupings. The study also delves into analyzing the item assignments from a statistical perspective by modeling the item groups as Markovian. The results are validated through numerical simulations and the findings are discussed. The research presents an analysis of various groups using clustering methods and the item assignments are compared with those obtained from other models including single-entry reinforcement processes. The study proposes an approach for visualizing the item assignments and the results are presented in the form of a movie that shows the evolution of the item assignments over time. The movie is available online under the reference number arXiv:2201.06743. The research presents an open source R package, called ClusterFrequence, that is available on CRAN for performing the analysis. Prawitz identified a key feature of Gentzen's intuitionistic natural deduction as the inversion principle, typically paired in proof-theoretic literature with the recovery principle. This paper presents an alternative, by reformulating both principles into a single requirement, referred to as the harmony condition, within the context of the Computational Ludics framework. This new framework illuminates the underlying notions: that the inversion principle embodies containment, while the recovery principle serves as its converse. Additionally, this paper derives and demonstrates the equivalence of the harmony condition with two further conditions defined in the Computational Ludics framework. Furthermore, this paper expands upon the harmony condition to accommodate multiple agents and incorporates a cut-elimination theorem. By accomplishing this, the proof retains its elegance and does not rely on any additional axioms. This way, the harmony condition serves as a unifying thread to prove equivalence and implications between key notions in the realm of proof theory. These computations can be applied to both sequent calculus and proof nets, resulting in a concise and simple cut-elimination theorem. This research thereby offers an alternative, and potentially deeper, understanding of the traditional proof-theoretic methods. Lastly, this paper showcases the Computational Ludics framework as a versatile tool for a proof-theoretic analysis. Its versatility results from the flexibility of the framework in defining notions like correctness and harmony, without relying on a specific structure for proofs as in the case of substructural logics. This is in addition to the framework's ability to handle multiple agents. This paper is a shortened version of the original research found in arXiv:2005.13655. It introduces the Computational Ludics framework as a proof-theoretic tool that offers a concise and elegant treatment of the subject. This research is centered on an alternative understanding of the notions of inversion, recovery, and cut-elimination within a single, harmonious principle. This principle is capable of capturing the essence of the proof-theoretic methods for both intuitionistic and classical logics, as well as for multiple agents, thereby providing a proof-theoretic explanation for their equivalence. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the cut-elimination theorem can be derived solely from the statement of the harmony condition. This research is conducted within the framework of the Computational Ludics. It begins with an examination of the structure of proofs in this framework. This leads to the concepts of correctness and harmony as well as the notions of inversions and recovery. A key finding is that the harmony condition encapsulates the essence of the inversion and recovery principles.

We show that a topological space's Smyth powerspace is core-compact if and only if the original space has local compactness. Consequently, this implies the Smyth powerspace does not uniformly preserve core-compact properties. Furthermore, this study incorporates examples to demonstrate the Smiley powerspace also fails to uniformly maintain continuity and the weakly developing property. Additionally, it proves the Smiley powerspace can preserve core-compactness in specific instances where the original space is compact. Moreover, this study examines the Smiley powerspace's behavior with respect to core-compactness when the original space contains points with distinct accessibility properties. Lastly, this study proves the Smiley powerspace can be core-compact despite the original space not possessing this property, provided certain conditions regarding the space's structures and the space's relationship with the Smyth upper powerdomain are met. Ultimately, this research concludes by saying the Smiley powerspace does not uniformly preserve core-compact properties, but rather, it depends on the specific conditions of the original space. The results show that a specific subgroup within these diffeomorphisms preserves the shape of the vortex loop itself, indicating the configuration space is comprised of loops confining a fixed area regardless of the vorticity distribution and any connected points. A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel approach to estimating the parameters of the Poisson process in a Bayesian framework, by transforming them using a tuning parameter'm'. This study develops a technique for selecting the optimal'm' value, which nearly orthogonalises the parameters, by minimising the correlation within their asymptotic posterior distributions. By choosing this optimal'm', the parameters converge faster and efficient sampling is possible using Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. Finally, parameter values are then extracted through a straightforward transformation. We present results from simulations involving models of both identical and non-identical extreme rainfall in Cumbria, UK. The novel parameterisation is shown to improve sampling efficiency and reduce dependence between parameters, resulting in a more efficient Markov Chain Monte Carlo performance and reliable posterior estimates via a straightforward transformation. The resulting parameter estimates exhibit convergence with sample size, as the frequency of weakly informative Markov Chain Monte Carlo samples increases. The approach presented solves one of the key challenges in extreme value analysis by providing reliable estimates of threshold excess probability distributions and parameters like the Quantile Regression Estimator's extreme value parameter. The parameters and associated results are available at https://github.com/jdhigham/extremes_pp_reparamisation. A corresponding R package 'poisson_reparameterisation' will be released shortly. In the field of offline reinforcement learning, we focus on adversarial robustness, a critical consideration in RL that deals with the challenge of learning a nearly optimal policy when a fraction of data in the training set has been compromised by an adversary. Our study begins by examining a worst-case scenario involving the linear Markov decision process and finding that even with the adversary only modifying the reward in each data tuple, a certain threshold of optimality gap cannot be avoided. Conversely, in contrast to robust supervised learning, which has seen significant breakthroughs with little dimension-related impact and similar lower bounds for the online RL with data corruption. Moreover, we introduce robust variants of Least-Square Value Iteration that are applicable both when the transition and reward data are available separately or jointly, with theoretical guarantees that show their performance gap is polynomially dependent on various problem parameters. Additionally, we present an algorithm that combines multiple existing policies and proves its robustness with optimal sample complexity. Lastly, we evaluate these methods extensively using synthetic data and find them to be highly effective in a variety of settings, particularly when the percentage of corrupted data is high. The code for our work, including both the theoretical analysis and the experimental findings, is openly available on GitHub at https://github.com/asharivrobert/robust_offline_reinforcement_learning. This repository also includes a tutorial that can be found at https://asharivrobert.github.io/roboffl/. This study demonstrates a logarithmic convexity linked to observability at a specific point in time for a one-dimensional heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions, leading to impulse approximate controllability in similar scenarios with dynamic boundaries. Additionally, we provide a detailed estimate for the cost of impulse control. Our research includes a step-by-step procedure for finding the impulsive control of minimal L^2-norm and supports these findings with numerical tests to verify the efficiency of the developed algorithm. This work represents a pioneering effort in the realm of impulse controllability for one-dimensional heat equations with dynamic boundaries, and it opens up new avenues for investigation in this domain. Specifically, the barriers to extending this research to two-dimensional models with or without boundaries will be discussed. Furthermore, this paper addresses impulse controllability for the three-dimensional heat equation under (more realistic) Robin boundary conditions, and it provides an estimated rate of convergence for the cost of impulse control as the number of impulsive instants increases. Finally, this study includes additional numerical tests to examine the behavior of the impulsive control as the number of impulsive instants grows, and it provides a minimum-norm impulse control for a three-dimensional heat equation with a very large number of impulsive instants. A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We identified distinct behaviors of two major detection methods - model calibration and density estimation - in response to background and semantic shifts in data, which were found across various language understanding datasets. In our evaluation, density estimation outperformed model calibration in background shift scenarios but struggled with semantic shifts, with both approaches underperforming when confronted with challenge data, underscoring a need for clearer definitions in method comparison. Furthermore, our findings suggest that natural language processing has yet to fully leverage out-of-distribution detection for practical use. We have contributed a comprehensive resource for the NLP community that includes a detailed methodology for detecting background and semantic shifts, as well as a comparative analysis of OOD detection methods in 12 language datasets with over 50 functional variations. This resource is expected to facilitate research and promote the inclusion of OOD detection in real-world NLP applications. The code for our research is available at https://github.com/epfml/ddDetector and the dataset can be downloaded from https://github.com/epfml/ood-resource. Additionally, our results are presented on the website ood-detectors.ml. We invite the research community to build upon our work and suggest improvements to our approach through interactive feedback on the website. We believe that a collaborative effort is needed to address the current vulnerabilities in language models and to develop more robust methods for handling out-of-distribution examples. In the spirit of transparency and collaboration, we have released our code, the dataset, and a public website to support this research. (From the introduction of the paper)

In recent years, artificial molecular motors utilizing electric currents have been explored, and like Brownian machines, they rely on random electron tunneling events to drive their operation. Even though their theoretical modeling has been considered, there has been a lack of a comprehensive dynamical model that accurately accounts for non-equilibrium tunneling rates. This work presents a dynamical model that addresses this gap by incorporating an uneven surface layer, and as a result, provides insight into the theoretical feasibility of designing molecular Brownian machine clocks that are accurate to a nanosecond range. Additionally, the model predicted a thermodynamically reversible efficiency maximum of 0.8 in the weak coupling limit for any given surface layer thickness. Nevertheless, the strong coupling scenario presented significant challenges due to numerical instability and required sophisticated analysis to identify potential limitations in designing efficient molecular machines. Ultimately, this study revealed the potential benefits and limitations of designing artificial molecular machines that operate on a nanosecond time scale. Interestingly, even with the most efficient strong coupling scenario, the calculated tunneling rates were much slower than those observed in real-world molecular clocks and were more comparable to those found in Brownian molecular motors. As a result, designing artificial molecular machines that operate on a microsecond time scale might be more feasible. Furthermore, there are potential applications and implications of these findings in terms of timing accuracy and what this could mean for future molecular nanotechnology development. Lastly, there are certain fundamental aspects of this study that are relevant to general Brownian machine research and provide valuable insights into their theoretical design. It is possible that future research will utilize this model to explore other forms of Brownian machines that operate at even longer time scales. There is also the possibility that further study will be required to confirm if the proposed time scales are within the reach of current advanced nanotechnology standards. Investigating these possibilities will be an important area of focus in future research and will likely yield the most beneficial insights for designing artificial molecular Brownian machines that can efficiently match theoretical models with real-world nanotechnology applications. In this study, we investigate the concept of general convolution by considering the set of all possible $n$-dimensional vectors from a finite domain $D$, where the elements of these vectors can take on values from $D$. A specific operation, denoted as $\oplus_f$, is defined as the application of function $f$ to pairs of elements from $D$ applied element-wise. This enables us to define a new convolution, known as the $f$-Convolution, for two given functions $g$ and $h$, each mapping $n$-dimensional vectors from $D$ to integers between $-M$ and $M$. By applying $\oplus_f$ to pairs of $n$-dimensional vectors, $g \otimes_f h$ is calculated as the sum of the products of the function values of $g$ and $h$ for each possible pair. This framework encompasses multiple other well-known convolutional problems. A major contribution of this research is to demonstrate that the $f$-Convolution, defined by $\oplus_f g \otimes_f h$, can be computed more efficiently than through brute force approaches, for certain low-degree functions $f$. Specifically, we provide an almost linear-time algorithm under certain conditions for such a computation. Furthermore, we propose a new framework for parallel processing, parallel-parallelism, wherein we define sets of accessible input data as "parallel universes" and assert that parallel computation is possible when accessing these universes independently. We assert that our new Smith-Zassenhaus algorithm is parallel-computable, thereby establishing new complexity bounds. Additionally, we introduce the concept of a free polynomial as an equivalence class of polynomials defined by polynomial $\oplus_f g \otimes_f h$. Finally, we outline several potential future research avenues, particularly focusing on a specific instance of the $f$-Convolution, the $L_2$-Convolution, for which we hypothesize that our proposed algorithm is both parallel-computable and efficient. However, we acknowledge that this may be impossible if the domain $D$ contains elements with unboundedly large values. Therefore, we suggest developing a new machine model capable of handling such infinite domains. If successful, this could yield a landmark discovery in the field of computational complexity theory. To search for the potential existence of the unique $0^{--}$ state, we created a systematic approach to designing tetraquark operators. In the process, we found that $0^{+-}$ tetraquark operators without derivatives are not possible. Due to the distinct Lorentz structure of the $0^{--}$ currents, it is prevented from incorporating corrections from four-quark terms into its spectral density, leading the gluon condensate to become the primary factor influencing the spectral density as power correction within the context of the finite energy sum rule. Our results from the sum rule analysis with the use of seven designed interpolating currents, however, indicate the lack of evidence to support a resonant signal related to the exotic $0^{--}$ state, leading us to conclude its absence below 2 GeV, in accordance with current experimental data. Furthermore, we discussed how quadrupole moments could be utilized in an alternative approach to the finite energy sum rule, enabling the extraction of the unique interquark potential energy for the $0^{--}$ state, in addition to examining the correlations between quadrupole moments and magnetic moments, with the latter potentially detectable through $e^+e^-$ collisions. Lastly, we explored the potential links between the exotic $0^{--}$ state and certain $1^{-+}$ and $2^{++}$ states, identifying possible underlying quark structures and exhibiting how the quadrupole moment of the exotic $0^{--}$ state bears a striking resemblance to that predicted for the exotic $1^{-+}$ state. In particular, we discovered that the quadratic correction to the spectral function of the $0^{--}$ state is equivalent to that predicted for the $1^{-+}$ state. Additionally, the central quadratic term in the correction factor of the $0^{--}$ state is analogous to that predicted for the $2^{++}$ state, with the respective corrections arising from the respective currents bearing similar structures. Lastly, the confinement decay mode was also discussed, with the unique $0^{--}$ state potentially decaying into two mesons through a confining string breaking process, in agreement with current experimental data. In this context, we also examined the potential confining structures of the $1^{-+}$ and $2^{++}$ states. Lastly, we proposed two possible future research directions - the exploration of novel tetraquark currents and the examination of exotic tetraquark potential within the context of quantum screening effects. Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in aerosol distribution were observed, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the work presented here lays the foundation for a refined modeling approach that incorporates specific human activities, thereby paving the way for more accurate epidemic prediction models. Such efforts could ultimately inform public health strategies for mitigating the spread of infectious diseases. Due to the diversity of airborne transmission scenarios (e.g. transportation, shopping, entertainment), we intend to apply our model to a variety of settings with the ultimate goal of informing public health policies. Specifically, we will investigate the effectiveness of various ventilation methods in public restrooms, which will be the subject of a forthcoming communication. Introduced in this study is a model that incorporates respiration, speaking, and writing activities to simulate aerosol transport and to quantify the likelihood of virus exposure given the duration and frequency of a person's presence. Furthermore, we demonstrate how our model can be used to estimate the efficacy of face masks and the influence of room air exchange on the spread of airborne infections. Although focused on epidemic preparedness, the work presented here is broadly applicable and could be adapted for other airborne disease scenarios. Ultimately, this research can be used to develop guidelines and policies for battling epidemic outbreaks and maintaining social continuity in the presence of transient airborne threats. In addition to epidemic scenarios, our model can also be used to investigate the broader implications of the complex transport of aerosols as they relate to society and public health. Double-sided auctions are commonly used in financial markets to facilitate matching of demand and supply. Our work builds on prior research, which mainly focused on handling a single quantity of trade requests. To expand this knowledge, we developed methods to support multiple goods and services, as well as multiple trade requests with diverse quantities. Furthermore, we created and tested a fully functional implementation of double-sided auctions that includes a range of features such as user interfaces, log management, and API integration, according to the ISOC CL standards. To ensure the accuracy of our work, we performed thorough verification of the auction's functionality. This verification process was aided by the use of the FOTML description language in conjunction with the Verifiable Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) tools. Ultimately, we achieved and documented proof of the correctness of our double-sided auction implementation. To validate our work, we conducted successful testing of our auction system through a demonstration, which also served as a training session for industry professionals. This demonstration served as a key event in an educational program focused on introducing the concepts and techniques of formal verification within the securities and derivatives trading community. To facilitate understanding and reuse of our work, we created a public repository that contains all the relevant materials, including the verified code, demonstration slides, and training program details. This repository serves as a valuable resource for anyone interested in double-sided auctions and verified software development for financial markets. The relevant information can be found at the following location: https://github.com/verified-derivatives/Double-Sided-Auctions. To address potential concerns regarding the performance of our approach, we carried out a comparative study of our methods, identifying significant benefits in processing speed and memory usage. This evaluation involved an analysis of our double-sided auction implementation, as well as a competing software system developed by Bloomberg for their LIPONT platform. The results of our comparison, based on a common set of trade requests, revealed that our approach and Bloomberg's LIPONT demonstrated equivalent levels of correctness. However, our double-sided auction emerged as the superior option due to its increased efficiency, achieved through a significant 5 orders of magnitude difference in processing speed and a 2.5 to 3 orders of magnitude difference in memory usage. The computational resources used for our comparison were chosen to reflect typical market conditions, Carefully selecting input parameters that included a high level of detail and multiple market data feeds. In modern research on data-driven systems, a primary focus lies on overcoming challenges presented by high-dimensional complexities, hidden system dynamics, and the presence of nonlinearity.  The dynamic mode decomposition technique has proven valuable in creating models from large data sets, yet the effectiveness of this method diminishes in cases where strong nonlinearity affects its accuracy. Conversely, sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics is able to learn comprehensive models, differentiating between linear and nonlinear interactions; however, it is limited in its application to lower dimensional systems. We introduce a kernel-based approach that utilizes sparse nonlinear dynamics to expand upon the limitations of dynamic mode decomposition in high-dimensional systems. Our method imbeds the idea of linear and sparse nonlinear dynamics into the dynamic mode decomposition framework through a kernel learning process, enabling the technique to function optimally in high-dimensional systems. We also devise an iterative optimization process, the linear and sparse dynamics optimization (lando), to deal with unknown pointwise nonlinearities that compromise dynamic mode decomposition's accuracy. The resulting model learned through this new approach provides a reliable and data-driven understanding of the system's behavior, thus allowing for accurate fault detection and dynamic performance assessment. We support our analysis with two practical examples: one relating to a turbine engine and another involving a twin-rotor gas turbine system. The work described here is an extension of the author's doctoral research. We advocate for the use of dynamic mode decomposition combined with sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics as a universally applicable tool for modeling dynamic systems in various domains. Results show that this approach is superior to previous dynamic mode decomposition results and rivals results from sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics. A reduction in errors of approximately 90% was achieved for the dynamic mode decomposition results and a reduction of approximately 97% was achieved for the dynamic mode decomposition results combined with sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics. We outperformed previous results obtaining a rise in the correlation coefficient of approximately 4% and achieved results near the baseline performance of sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics. A reduction in the computational time of approximately 99% was achieved by employing the dynamic mode decomposition combined with sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics method. The work described here is an extension of the author's doctoral research. We present a novel, the dynamic mode decomposition combined with sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics approach, that is demonstrated to be effective in various domains, the dynamics of which are partially linear and partially nonlinear. Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.
Previous methods often employ diverse memory mechanisms to track navigation history but fail to account for the fraction of relevant information in their memories.
We propose the MemoNav, a novel memory-based approach for image-based goal navigation that learns to selectively retain both short-term and long-term memories for efficient navigation.
The short-term memory in MemoNav dynamically updates and prioritizes new experiences based on environmental changes, effectively integrating new information and eliminating redundant information.
The long-term memory in MemoNet stores significant episodes and learns to categorize goals, leveraging both short-term and long-term memories to guide navigation decisions.
Through extensive experiments on a new benchmark of goal-based navigation with diverse types of objectives, MemoNav outperforms existing methods and significantly reduces the fraction of irrelevant information in their memories by up to four times.

This includes a finding that for channels with positive entropy output and input powers that have a maximum that can be achieved through limited power transmission, there exists an equivalent channel without feedback that utilizes directed directed reversible (DDR) machines. Additionally, we derive optimal transmission rates for specific channels, including the binary symmetric channel, binary erasure channel, and Znq channel, each under different conditions involving noiseless feedback and feedback that can be distorted. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between channel capacities with and without feedback, where feedback capacity is always greater than or equal to the non-feedback capacity in cases where non-feedback capacity is finite. This is accompanied by an example illustrating a situation where feedback capacity is infinite, yet non-feedback capacity is finite. Finally, we investigate the properties of feedback capacity functions and find that they are continuous, except in cases where the channel state depends on past inputs, resulting in discontinuities. However, we show that for channels with cross-talk, there exists a distance between feedback capacity and non-feedback capacity, where feedback capacity is greater than non-feedback capacity by a quantity that decreases as the channel cross-talk decreases. A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may be used to create fault-tolerable quantum computations via topologically non-Abelian states. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair-breaking when present. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance caused by the Zeeman field through mixing, thus restoring superconductivity. Additionally, we established that Rashba coupling's favorable impact on superconductivity originates from a spin-flip driven enhancement of the likelihood of a pair of electrons traveling in opposite directions with zero total spin. Our analysis also shows that under suitable conditions the normal state displays a non-trivial topological characteristics as per Schnyder's topological classification, with superconducting s-wave orders then establishing a one-to-one correspondence with two distinct topological insulator types. Our research provides tangible guidance for experimental investigations into topological superconducting Rashba Hubbard systems, offering potential avenues for realization via doping, chemical substitution, or applied surface proximities. Lastly, these findings present an interesting extension to earlier studies on attractive Hubbard models featuring spin-orbit coupling, broadening those outcomes and offering a flexible framework for future analyses involving additional perturbations and forms of superconductivity. This study focuses on scientific documents, presenting data in tabular form, to facilitate fact verification and support finding of supporting evidence. Researchers proposed two new subtasks related to tabular data: examining whether specific fact can be confirmed and locating all pieces of evidence that support a given claim. They introduced a dataset with nearly 10,000 annotated tables and five competing datasets from four participating teams. This work details the challenges, approaches, and evaluations of the subtasks, ultimately reporting that no team submitted entries for the "evidence-finding" subtask due to anticipated difficulties, but several teams participated in "fact verification." Notably, the team that submitted to the "fact verification" subtask also submitted to a related task at another seminar, while another team that encountered difficulties with "evidence-finding" achieved high rankings in "fact verification." Overall, the teams' performances indicated that automated methods for processing tabular data are still in the early stages of development. To address this, the researchers provided access to five pseudo-code-level benchmarks and two fully implemented baselines for "fact verification." They also made available the annotated dataset on GitHub, inviting researchers to continue exploring "SEM-TAB-FACTS" in the future.

This analysis explores the essential role of complex numbers in Quantum Mechanics, delving into common justifications for complex formalism and offering additional perspectives to support its necessity. By examining these factors, we hope to clarify the underlying reasoning for employing complex numbers in Quantum mechanics. Additionally, we consider how these insights might be applied to Statistical Mechanics, where complex numbers appear to be unnecessary. This discussion is primarily intended for undergraduate students or instructors seeking clarification on the origins of complex numbers in Quantum mechanics. 

We now understand that complex numbers are essential in Quantum mechanics but it is unclear if they are required for statistical mechanics. This raises the question if complex numbers are necessary for statistical mechanics as well. This question is particularly relevant because statistical mechanics has a similar mathematical framework, yet real numbers seem to suffice. This discussion examines the essential role of complex numbers in quantum mechanics, explaining the underlying justifications for their use and exploring their potential application to statistical mechanics. 

We consider the possibility that it may be possible to modify statistical mechanics to employ complex numbers, thus aligning it with quantum mechanics. This, in turn, could involve modifying the fundamental axioms of the theory, introducing complex numbers into probability distributions, or redefining states and operations as linear combinations of complex coefficients. However, developing a coherent theoretical framework using complex numbers for statistical mechanics remains a complex challenge. Consequently, it remains unclear if it is feasible to extend the real-number formalism successfully to describe the world around us. 

Ultimately, we acknowledge that the need for complex numbers in quantum mechanics remains a subjective interpretation, influenced by our choice of axioms. This choice may reflect our desire to conserve real-number properties, thereby necessitating the complex formalism, or we may view it as an independent set of axioms that happens to require complex numbers. Either perspective offers a plausible foundation for the theoretical framework of quantum mechanics and statistical mechanics.

These notes document my process of reviewing equations governing distant groundwater movement for a paper. By "distant," I'm referring to horizontal distances exceeding the thickness of the aquifer. They're based on assumptions discussed later on. These equations aren't an original contribution but rather a reference guide for those working on complex groundwater modeling with significant horizontal extent.

I began with Darcy's Law, revisiting the conservation equation for vertical averaging in groundwater flow. Following that, I explored approaches for numerically solving the flow equation. Then, I considered scenarios where the hydraulic conductivity varies solely with depth, simplifying the steady-state flow equation in these cases. Lastly, I used Sech3 as my boundary condition, exploring approaches for numerically solving the flow equation again. These equations apply specifically to unconfined aquifers with uniform vertical boundary conditions. Lastly, there's a brief discussion on solving the modied modied Holt and Parker equation. This being a review, I didn't compare the performance of dierent methods; rather, I hoped to provide a straightforward explanation of the underlying theory.

data, or offering a sole prediction outcome without considering various
probability outcomes.
  This study proposes the concept of Indecision Trees as a modification of the
existing Decision Trees model. These revised models are designed to learn under
conditions of uncertainty, draw conclusions in uncertain situations, produce
reliable probability distributions over potential labels, and be dissected into
clear, logical arguments that can be applied to other reasoning systems.

Trees, Bayesian networks and existing evidence-based learning methods, we show
that Indecision Trees achieve higher accuracy and provide more substantial
interpretation capabilities than the competing approaches while also outperforming
them in terms of efficiency. Furthermore, we demonstrate the potential of
Indecision Trees in real-world practical applications by analyzing medical test
results and drawing conclusions about a patient's health.

PrunedDTW enhances the efficiency of DTW by terminating its calculation once the local distance exceeds the global optimal. This optimization effectively reduces time complexity. Despite making calculations more efficient, PrunedDTW still performs all necessary calculations before declaring its early abandonment. In this research, we propose EAPA, an improved variation of PrunedDTW. EAPA brings two key innovations: it predicts the global optimal based on time series patterns and monitors the local distance alongside the optimal distance. Both advancements enable the early abandonment of unnecessary calculations.
