Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight instructor-defined test cases that a student has overlooked. While this feedback has some value, it can lead students to rely on guesswork rather than structured testing methods. Moreover, this feedback style does not educate students on the shortcomings of their test suites, potentially making them dependent on the tool's advice rather than relying on their own judgment. As a more effective approach, inquiry-based learning has the potential to promote student autonomy by reinforcing key testing concepts through feedback. We aim to improve this aspect by introducing Testing Tutor, a platform that offers various testing pedagogies and a customizable feedback engine. An empirical study comparing the impact of traditional and conceptual feedback on two groups of sophomore students was conducted. By using a mixed design with multiple dependent variables, it was demonstrated that conceptual feedback is more effective than traditional methods and further investigates how this style of feedback affects student behavior and test coverage. The study revealed that conceptual feedback leads to increased system coverage, fewer unrun-through test cases, and a deeper understanding of testing concepts among students. Consequently, incorporating inquiry-based conceptual feedback into educational tools may yield better learning outcomes and promote independent decision-making in software testing. For example, students can employ conceptual feedback to tackle "orphaned" test cases or explore specific testing methodologies like equivalence testing. The testing tutor's engine can even provide custom-made feedback with pre-defined testing concepts when no coverage insights are available, offering versatile options for instructors. Similarly, the engine can integrate with existing tools to offer a similar experience across different educational platforms. The source code of Testing Tutor is available at https://github.com/mostafa/sse-tt. The empirical investigation including the dataset can be accessed at https://doi.org/10.6084/m1.FA2E-1J68.1. In domains requiring reliability or transparency, explainable AI is increasingly becoming essential for handling the unpredictability of black-box machine learning methods, particularly in healthcare and data protection regulations. However, standard visualizations often fall short due to their inability to differentiate between subtle feature variations or accurately represent the interplay between absent and present features. This issue could be addressed by utilizing more advanced symbolic approaches but at the cost of reduced generalization capabilities. This paper proposes a breakthrough by integrating concept analysis and Inductive Logic Programming within a dataset to generate expressive feature-level explanations for DNN model predictions, overcoming previous limitations and achieving a higher success rate in accurately capturing feature relevance and subtle variations. Additionally, our method maintains the generalization capabilities of symbolic approaches, offering an optimal compromise between explanation quality and the generality of generated explanations. The proposed method shows promising outcomes in practical experiments, surpassing existing methods in explanation quality and achieving a notable 88% success rate, with an average of 70% of generated explanations accurately describing feature relevance, 62% describing absent features, and 42% describing subtle variations. The method also exhibits superior generality to previous methods, with a notable 97.5% of generated explanations applicable to other datasets or model variations. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy. This could lead to the growth of a wide array of materials on hexagonal materials, enabling novel devices with expanded functionality. Internet Service Providers have long requested that Content Providers contribute financially towards improving network infrastructure, with promises of better Quality of Service. This research examines profit-sharing agreements between a single Content Provider and multiple Internet Service Providers, with the Content Provider agreeing to split profits in exchange for enhanced service quality by the ISPs. To model these negotiations, we use a Stackelberg game, where the Content Provider decides the distribution of its profits and the ISPs determine their level of investment effort, while in another scenario, we look into how Content Providers and ISPs collaborate, with ISPs deciding on how to split the profits fairly through a general profit-sharing model, with one Content Provider allocating its profits equally among the ISPs. To solve these non-linear problems, we employ the Nash Equilibrium concept and Sufficient Descent Programming algorithm. Our findings reveal that under profit-sharing, the Content Provider's profit is lower than in a benchmark scenario, whereas in the collaborative model, the Content Provider's profit exhibits less variation. Furthermore, we explore how our results are affected by parameter changes. Additionally, we look into the effects of additional variables on the Nash Equilibrium and implement the SDP algorithm using MATLAB. This study offers novel approaches for solving profit-sharing problems in the content and service provider model and provides valuable insights into how changes in parameters influence the outcome. Furthermore, we examine the applicability of our framework to a broader profit-sharing model. Several interesting questions arise from our analysis, such as the impact of varying the number of ISPs and the content provider's risk preference on the equilibrium investment level. These queries, along with the related policy design issues, are left for future investigation. The study introduces a new framework known as the content and service provider sharing model. The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship. This abstract adjoint relationship holds due to a specific mathematical framework called 2-categorical architecture. This framework also allows for a second level of abstract interpretation where physical ideas related to symmetry and unitarity are implied. This implies that any physical transformation involving these concepts can be represented as a unitary operation within the resulting Hilbert space. Additionally, we propose an alternative approach to the GNS construction based on this framework, which we call the 'Hilbertisation' process. This new approach uses a mathematical concept called coends to achieve the same results as the GNS construction, which retains all the implicit physical meanings inherent to the original observables and states. This approach is applied to a range of physical systems including the SU(2) system and the Ising model in a specific limit. The coends employed in this model allow for a precise mathematical description of the implicit physical meanings related to symmetry and the volume of a system. These physical meanings are typically expressed using mathematical objects called integrals and these objects can be used to achieve exact results for key physical observables such as the partition function and the free energy. Moreover, we propose a new method to apply the GNS construction using a mathematical concept called ends. This approach allows for a precise control over the properties of the resulting algebra and the presence or absence of zero-point fluctuations. The main difficulty in applying this method is that it requires a pre-existing Hilbert space for a given C*-algebra, which may not always be the case. However, we demonstrate that this approach yields correct results for a range of physical systems including the SU(2) system and the Ising model in a specific limit. This latter example illustrates that the volume of the system can be accurately described using the tools of pure mathematics. Furthermore, we show that our Hilbert space is consistent with a pre-existing quantisation procedure known as the 'gauging' process, which has a physical interpretation in terms of a gauge field that couples to electric charge. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds that have been affected by both types of distortions.  After conducting mathematical analyses of noise effects on feature extraction techniques, the authors propose using a combination of linear and logarithmic spectral features to aid a deep learning-based classifier.  The proposed method, which utilizes linear and logarithmic features derived from three-component recordings, was tested on a noisy dataset obtained from multiple devices and comparison was made with models using traditional feature sets.  The results indicate that the proposed approach surpasses traditional methods in classification performance across various noise levels and device combinations.  Additionally, the authors provide support for using this method in real-world practice by demonstrating its applicability in a simulated clinic setting.  The simulated environment mimicked the classroom of a doctor's training by incorporating videos and case studies to test the effectiveness of the proposed approach.  The code and dataset used in this study are publicly available for public use.  The proposed method has been successfully implemented, and the source code can be accessed at https://github.com/ArashNoroozi/Heart-Sound-Classification.  The dataset used in this study can be obtained from https://doi.org/10.1201/EBK107197299-6/9780429288006.  The classification model, which yields a specific accuracy when tested on a particular dataset, has been submitted to ICASSP 2022 for evaluation.  The associated figures and results have been uploaded to the https://arashnoroozi.github.io/ project website for public reference.  The proposed method considers all possible distortion types, including device variability, to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds. This series' introduction highlights the significant impact of the pandemic on educational institutions and the growing need for flexibility in modern education, particularly in adapting to rapid technological advancements. The incorporation of AI and associated technologies can enhance educational outcomes by promoting collaborative learning environments, fostering innovative tasks, and making learning more accessible via engaging storytelling techniques. Furthermore, this series' contributions emphasize the importance of climate change awareness in educational curricula for AI and data sciences, as well as other fields, due to its far-reaching consequences on society and the rapid advancements being made in relevant technologies. By presenting a collection of guest papers, this introduction provides an overview of the pressing challenges addressed in these symposia and highlights their common threads of community, collaboration, and climate, serving as a starting point for future discussions and reflections within the broader AI community. Finally, this introduction includes a collection of insightful response papers that build upon the presentations in the winter series, offering additional perspectives and potential future research directions in the specified domain. Ultimately, these papers contribute to our mission of bridging the gap between artificial intelligence and real-world education by promoting more resilient, adaptable, and environmentally sustainable learning approaches for the AI and data science communities.

This study offers the first empirical evaluation of the influence of auction format integrity on bidding tactics and outcome profitability. Through a controlled lab experiment where human auction participants earn revenue, we assess whether a credible or uncredible auction environment impacts bidding. We discover that the majority of bids in an uncredible second-price auction occur within the revenue-maximizing range of both a credible second-price auction and a first-price auction. Sellers often deviate from the auction rules, but when participating in an uncredible auction, typically don't prioritize maximizing revenue. We explain the outcomes of our experiment using a theory that combines bidder misperception and a seller's reluctance to break auction rules, as confirmed by a test of actual preferences. Finally, we find that revenue is higher in uncredible auctions than in credible ones, particularly when compared to a first-price auction. Our research implies that the profitability of uncredible auctions can partially justify the prevalence of first-price auctions. Furthermore, we contribute to the existing literature on auctions by providing a real-world context for the results of Green and Heller (1981) on bidding theory. The explanation of accelerated cosmology is partially satisfactory but challenges to understanding the universe's early development persist. Our research focuses on the promising potential of a new symmetric teleparallel theory of gravity, denoted as $f(Q)$, where the non-metricity scalar $Q$ facilitates gravitational interactions and addresses some longstanding issues. To study the universe's initial phase, we establish a model based on a specific type of spacetime with both rotation and anisotropy and then derive equations governing the model's motion. By analyzing energy density, the relationship between energy and pressure, and spatial geometry characteristics, we find that this theoretical model exhibits spatial anisotropy during the universe's initial phase due to possible anisotropic fluid, which may however gradually diminish and allow the universe to achieve isotropy due to inflation and eventual fluid homogenization. Our findings indicate that $f(Q)$-gravity can be an effective theoretical tool to understand the universe's initial phase. Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between research findings. Unlike generic question-answering platforms, such as Wikipedia or Google, the required information often necessitates an in-depth understanding of the underlying research. The reasoning process is hindered by the absent context of research papers when using abstracts or input queries. To develop effective systems capable of finding requested information, a dataset consisting of 1,594 question-answer pairs was created within the biomedical domain. Each entry includes a research paper, a corresponding question, and an appropriate response as provided by domain-expert annotators. Additionally, we propose an initial assessment of the existing information retrieval and question-answering methodologies as a starting point for further exploration into developing an information retrieval system capable of complex semantic reasoning. The created dataset, referred to as SemQA, can be accessed at: https://github.com/dwamck/semqa. It is believed that SemQA will facilitate the development of an information retrieval system that can efficiently locate research-backed answers to naturally occurring questions. The research has the potential to significantly impact various tasks, including those involving quote identification, evidence extraction, and reasoning-based question-answering. By utilizing SemQA, developers can create and evaluate their own information retrieval systems capable of withstanding the scrutiny of semantic analysis. As such, the research can contribute to the advancement of research paper grounding, a phenomenon in which external knowledge is grounded in research findings for an in-depth understanding. In order to understand fast neutrino flavor instability in supernova events, two advanced simulations were conducted, one involving a massive 9 solar mass star explosion and the other, a 20 solar mass non-explosion. These studies revealed neutrino instabilities primarily occur within regions where neutrinos separate and near the shockwave barrier. Notably, only the explosive model exhibited instability behind the shockwave due to the interaction between particles and neutrinos. This could be attributed to the density of the matter which influences the direction and rate of neutrino distribution. Our results show that the success of a supernova explosion and properties of the collapsing star greatly affect neutrino instability. Therefore, it is essential to conduct more accurate and diverse stellar collapse simulations to predict the occurrence of flavor instability. Additionally, the possibility of instability behind the shockwave requires further examination in more supernova models. Since dense matter restricts the long-range axis of neutrinos, only neutrinos with a short-range axis may cross the shockwave, resulting in a significant increase in density and energy behind the shockwave that triggers instability. This condition is more commonly found in the explosive model conducted, emphasizing the connection between an successful explosion and flavor instability. Since neutrinos behind the shockwave drive the explosion, this relationship, observed in our model, suggests a direct link between flavor instability and core collapse events. Furthermore, our study indicates that the growth rate of instability is influenced by the density and neutrino axis length of the matter. This is consistent with past research findings for the non-explosive model and a few explosive models. Additionally, our results show that the growth rate behind the shockwave in the explosive model is faster than that in the non-explosive model due to the increased density and the neutrino axis length limitation. Past research concluded that the neutrino instabilities have a comparable influence on the model with a lower metallicity. However, our results indicate that the neutrino instabilities in the model with lower metallicity have a comparable effect on the core and the layer near the shockwave barrier. This is in contrast to the model with higher metallicity, where the focus of instability lies between these regions. Therefore, the effect of differences in metallicity on the occurrence and distribution of flavor instability is insignificant. Lastly, our results show that the growth rate behind the shockwave in the explosive model is not significantly influenced by the limited neutrino axis length. This is in contrast to the core and the layer near the shockwave barrier in the non-explosive model and a few explosive models.

ADHD is a widely prevalent psychiatric condition that has been challenging to diagnose accurately. The advancement in computational capabilities and machine learning methods has enabled researchers to investigate the use of resting-state fMRI imaging data for classifying ADHD. In contrast to prior studies, which often relied on the entire brain, this study focused on pinpointing the essential regions for utilizing a deep learning model. By using rsfMRI data from the ADHD 200 global competition, the researchers employed leave-one-site-out cross-validation to derive an integrated outcome. Notably, the study found that using merely 15 crucial regions of interest for training yielded a 70.6% accuracy rate, surpassing the existing benchmark of 68.6% achieved with all regions. Furthermore, the researchers developed and tested novel models, namely Separate Channel CNN RNN with Attention, Separate Channel dilate CNN RNN with Attention, and Separate Channel CNN slicing RNN with Attention, to identify the most effective structure. The ASSRNN model emerged as the top performer, attaining a 70.46% accuracy rate with only 13 essential regions. The study's findings demonstrate that concentrating on the critical brain regions for ADHD diagnosis via deep learning can yield superior outcomes compared to using the entire brain. Additionally, the researchers introduced three new state-of-the-art models that can serve as valuable tools for computational psychiatry research. The derived ADHD diagnosis model is potentially applicable in clinical settings to aid in diagnosing ADHD. In a discrete-time epidemic SISI model where population growth is constant and balanced, the per capita mortality and fertility rates are equivalent, and the model's evolution operator is a nonlinear function of seven parameters. When we reduce this operator to a quadratic stochastic one, we show that it has a unique interior fixed point and examine the long-term trajectory behavior under specific conditions regarding the model parameters. Specifically, we investigate the following questions: (1) For the unique fixed point to be globally stable in the vicinity of the parameter space's interior, what conditions must be met? (2) What kinds of conditions must be satisfied so that the model exhibits global attractivity on the boundary of the parameter space? (3) What kinds of relationships between the model parameters lead to bistability, and how does the unique fixed point and another stable fixed point that appears under these conditions relate to each other? Our study provides a comprehensive analysis of the model's attractors and their associated equilibrium patterns in the parameter space. Furthermore, we attribute the origin of these complex dynamics to the model's nonlinear evolution operator's interaction with the inherent structure of the state space, specifically to the intersection of the boundary of the state space and its singular points under specific critical values of the model parameters. Lastly, our findings also shed light on the model's applications in epidemiology, revealing that the model can exhibit diverse equilibrium patterns, including the coexistence of disease-free and endemic states, solely by modifying the model's parameter values in a controlled manner. These outcomes are contingent on specific theoretical models commonly employed in epidemiology. Ultimately, our simultaneous examination of the model's dynamic properties and its underlying structure allows us to offer insights on the critical factors contributing to the complex behavior exhibited by the model and how they relate to each other. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. In response, our project offers the first publicly accessible, web-based acronym identification and disambiguation platform capable of processing acronyms in scientific, biomedical, and general domains. This system can be accessed via the website http://iq.cs.uoregon.edu:5000 and supplemented with a demo video available at https://youtu.be/IkSh7LqI4Vw. Furthermore, the system's source code has been made available for further exploration at https://github.com/amirveyseh/MadDog. Additionally, our work includes presenting empirical findings from a broad user study conducted to assess the performance of our system in identifying acronym definitions and comparing it against human performance. The results indicate our system has achieved a success rate of 57% in acquiring accurate definitions, outperforming human expectations of 54%. The data collected from the study will be utilized to create a larger dataset for future research purposes. Lastly, our research provides an accurate measurement of the complexity of acronym comprehension, revealing that a thorough understanding of over 80% of acronyms is necessary for achieving satisfactory results. This finding may facilitate the development of more effective strategies in the future. In summary, our project offers a groundbreaking, comprehensive approach to identifying and interpreting acronyms, serving as a pioneering solution available for public use that can be applied across various domains. The system's source code has been made available for further exploration at https://github.com/amirveyseh/MadDog. Additionally, our research provides empirical insights into acronym comprehension and a dataset that may facilitate future research in this domain. Lastly, our finding on acronym comprehension has the potential to guide the design of future systems. Quantum interference, evident in low-dimensional systems, is one of the most notable manifestations of quantum physics. Historically, quantum interference has been observed in various contexts, but its influence on thermoelectric properties and heat transfer remains relatively unexploited. This study demonstrates that quantum interference can be harnessed to switch heat transfer and convert heat into an electric current in quantum Hall junctions. Furthermore, by achieving coherent interference across an entire heat current, our research illustrates the practical viability of heat rectification through the manipulation of phase and amplitude. We anticipate that this discovery will stimulate the development of cutting-edge heat management and energy harvesting technologies. Ultimately, our work is likely to be adapted for use in devices at the nanoscale. To achieve this, we developed an advanced analytical model, which was then validated through comparison with numerical simulations. Utilizing this framework, we were able to illustrate the intricate mechanisms underlying interference-induced thermoelectric properties and heat transfer. This includes the interference effects on charge current and heat flux, the phase-amplitude correlation, and the device performance metrics such as the thermoelectric figure of merit and efficiency. Our analysis also sheds light on the system's heat bath. We discovered that, under specific conditions, the system's heat bath can be characterized by an effective heat bath parameter that is tunable through interference. This finding presents a novel approach for controlling the effective heat bath parameter, thereby expanding our understanding of quantum systems coupled with environmental influences. To better understand our results, we also developed a physical interpretation of the analytical model. Using this model, we were able to estimate the impact of various physical properties on the thermoelectric properties and heat transfer. This includes the mean free path, electron g-factor, and g-factor, which are influenced by interference and system constraints. These estimates indicate that these parameters could be manipulated to achieve unprecedented levels of heat manipulation and efficient heat harvesting. Overall, our study showcases the sophisticated control of thermoelectric properties and heat transfer achieved through the interference in quantum Hall junctions, paving the way for the development of advanced thermoelectric devices and heat converters. Additionally, our work contributes to broader discussions on the application and expansion of quantum interference in thermoelectric research and leads to novel insights on the interpretation of interference-induced effects on thermoelectric properties and heat transfer. Lastly, our analysis lays the groundwork for investigating the time-dependent interference in quantum Hall junctions, opening doors for the exploration of associated phenomena and potential applications. It also brings to light the significance of interference in the interpretation of thermoelectric properties

Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal scope, resulting in the reduction of sequencing costs by up to 140x for the retrieval of smaller data objects. The combination of our hierarchical storage architecture and efficient data revision method has led to a significant reduction in sequencing expenses, with our current best achievement showing a 6.67x reduction for large data objects. Additionally, this architecture allows us to efficiently support updates to unmodified data, using a versatile compression algorithm based on suffix arrays to provide a high degree of flexibility in our DNA storage system. With the ability to extract full objects from any valid index, we've developed a method for performing efficient updates to unmodified data by converting the index to a compatible PCR format, retrieving the relevant object, and then applying the original index to enable accurate indexing once more. As an alternative to a full genome revision, our design allows for the efficient extraction of modified data objects, coupled with the reindexing of unmodified data for optimal storage performance. A significant advantage of our design over traditional approaches is evident in the handling of large data revisions. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter that have garnered interest from both theoretical and experimental communities. These materials are classified according to the characteristics of their topological invariants in momentum space - specifically, Zak's topological invariant and topological charges relevant to Weyl and topological insulator systems. These invariants serve as the foundation for classification, but the lack of explicit, readable content in existing research papers on these topics hinders the understanding of new researchers in the field. To address this knowledge gap, this paper aims to provide an in-depth review of the theoretical underpinnings and experimental implementations of nodal lines in momentum space, featuring recent realizations in photonic and other systems. These sections include discussions of quantum anomalous Hall, Weyl semiconductor, and topological insulator systems; a comprehensive exploration of zero-energy states and topological charges of Dirac/Weyl semimetals; and an examination of other types of momentum-space topological invariants. Additionally, this paper presents an overview of the other types of momentum-space topological invariants and a comprehensive review of the other types of momentum-space topological invariants. Finally, this paper concludes by analyzing the advancements in experimental implementations over the past five years and proposing potential avenues for future research in the field. These implementations include three-dimensional Dirac/Clinic points and lines as well as zero-dimensional and one-dimensional topological systems. As a result, this paper becomes a comprehensive knowledge base on momentum-space topological invariants and recent realizations in photonic and other systems. (Abstract edited for brevity)

These waves, typically triggered by pacemaker-generated activity, serve as a means of transmitting information and regulating behavior at the whole-system level. A common pattern observed in these systems is the utilization of spiral waves as a means of transmitting information and regulating behavior at the whole-system level. However, the high spatial redundancy and non-uniformities inherent in these systems render numerical simulations and experimental manipulations of their dynamics and wave propagation properties particularly challenging. In this work, we introduce and validate a pair of approximate analytical formulas that can accurately predict the speed at which pacemaker-generated waves in oscillatory media propagate at moderate and high spatial resolutions. Furthermore, our results provide a previously observed relationship in these systems, where the ratio of the pacemaker's oscillation frequency to the homogeneous medium's oscillation frequency is directly proportional to the ratio of their corresponding relaxation times. A fundamental concept in quantum theory, the entropy of a quantum state helps determine how probable a particular outcome might be in a quantum measurement. The overall entropy is split into two components by the Partial Entropy, a metric that measures how uncertain a part of a quantum system is about the whole. The Partial Entropy has numerous applications across quantum physics and computing. In this study, we provide two new algorithms for approximating the Partial Entropy between two subsets of a quantum system's registers. The first algorithm works with any number of registers and achieves an error rate of $\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}$, a rate that holds for any interpretation under randomness. The second algorithm, which is most useful when there are only two registers, achieves an error rate of $O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}})$. Both algorithms run in time that is proportional to $N^{1/3}$. The best previous algorithm, which also applied a reduction method, had an error rate of $O(\frac{1}{N})$. The two new algorithms are based on a technique called quantum conditional variance. The first algorithm applies the Wigner function to solve a nonlinear equation, thereby making a crucial assumption about the nature of the quantum state. The second algorithm approximates the entropy by dividing a single variable into two. The quality of the approximation for both algorithms depends on the quality of a quantum state's reduction. The reduced density operator, which describes how a part of a quantum system looks to the rest of it, measures how good the approximation is. We prove that the first algorithm can get as close as wanted to the entropy if the reduced density operator isn't too complicated. The second algorithm achieves the same result if the state isn't too entangled. The complexity of the induced map, which turns a particular form of a quantum state into another, measures how complicated the state is with respect to the rest of it. The induced map, which is tied to the partial entropy, is what the algorithms try to estimate. We show that the second algorithm is the best possible algorithm for its special case by one-sided simulating a quantum circuit that outlines the partial entropy. The simulation, which is based on a technique called quantum condensation, relies on the assumption that the partial entropy is small. Physicians' written assessments and interviews with patients, stored as unstructured clinical text notes (CTNs), have been analyzed using machine learning techniques to extract relevant information for further medical research and applications. Despite significant advancements, the task of accurately assigning International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes based on CTNs remains a complex problem due to its multi-class nature, extensive code list, and variability in CTN content. Researchers have proposed semi-supervised learning approaches that incorporate vast amounts of unlabeled CTN data to facilitate accurate ICD coding. These methods, primarily relying on language models, can efficiently process and condense unlabeled CTN data, producing concise summaries that provide minimal insights into patients' conditions. However, existing studies have not adequately explored the potential of semi-supervised learning in medical text summarization. Our study presents a novel semi-self-supervised text classification framework that combines a pre-trained language model and a fine-tuned transformer to effectively capture both local and global context in CTNs for ICD coding. The proposed framework was evaluated and compared with four established baselines on two datasets, demonstrating significant classification performance improvements, with classification accuracy boosting by up to 7.64%. Furthermore, our study provides thorough explanations for these outcomes and includes an in-depth analysis of the numerical values of the used datasets. The results show that the proposed method not only utilizes unlabeled CTN data through pre-trained language models but also enhances the model's generalization capability by reducing overfitting, ultimately yielding superior ICD coding outcomes. The code used in this study is available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/tjdcyou/SSSIKDCoding. Additionally, the developed model and associated data have been posted on arXiv as an article titled "Semi-self-supervised ICD coding". The associated data has also been deposited on MIMD share https://mimds-share.cs.msu.edu/projects/semselfsup-iqdcoding/. The models can also be accessed via PATE (https://pate.msu.edu/) with the specified details. The PATE project includes a full replication of the study's results, code, and models. Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, albeit limited by the rapid growth of computation time with dataset size. A shift towards quantum computing could potentially resolve this limitation, providing an alternative to current statistical models. We develop and test a quantum equivalent to the K-means clustering method on superconducting qubits, contrasting it to a previously implemented quantum support vector machine. Results indicate that our algorithm matches classical K-means performance in both clustering and classification tasks, achieving an impressive speedup due to a lower asymptotic complexity of $O(N^{3/2}K^{1/2}\log{P})$ with $N$, $K$, and $P$ representing the number of data points, clusters, and data dimensions, respectively. The significant advantage arises from the complementary strengths of quantum and classical algorithms. Additionally, we demonstrate the capability of our quantum K-means method to learn non-linear boundaries by utilizing an entangled two-qubit state as a feature map. Furthermore, using two-bit memory fidelities as features, we successfully trained a quantum support vector machine to classify breast cancer data from the Wisconsin Institute of Radiology. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited to simple sphere-based lighting models or overlook occlusion, resulting in inaccurate shadow calculations that can lead to inaccurate solutions in inverse problems. In response, we introduce an $O(NN^2)$ algorithm for computing shadows, where $N$ represents the number of triangles in a mesh, thus offering an efficient solution for complex models. By leveraging view-dependent surfaces and incorporating recursive clustering, our approach enables the efficient evaluation of complex geometric scenes, yielding faster shadow computation compared to existing mesh-based renderers. Ultimately, our method facilitates the accurate rendering of scenes comprising multiple animating objects, a capability absent in current state-of-the-art renderers. We also showcase its potential to improve model extraction in 3D video editing by outperforming both optimization- and learning-based methods, along with offering comparable results to state-of-the-art editing software. Lastly, we present a shadow-computing technique that can be integrated into prior work on differentiable renderers for an enhanced understanding of scene geometry. In particular, we find that analyzing shadow artifacts in deep learning-based 3DX-ray de novo CT reconstruction reveals partially broken occlusion, thus offering actionable insights for improving this technology. Specifically, our approach confirms the significance of model occlusion in 3DX-ray reconstruction, a key component in radiology, thereby potentially influencing future developments in this area. Building on long-term traffic data, this paper develops an innovative framework to estimate the average and statistical relationship of origin-destination demand while considering the day-to-day variability resulting from travelers' independent route selections. The framework also determines the probability distribution of link and path flow along with their associated costs, with variations stemming from origin-destination demand, route choice, and unforeseen errors. By applying statistical methods and iterative algorithms, the framework can refine its estimates and provide reliable results. Notably, the paper showcases two practical applications where the framework successfully estimates origin-destination demand and evaluates the reliability of network flow and link throughput. The methodology proposed in this paper can serve as a foundation for future studies on transportation network analysis. The study's major findings are as follows. The probability distribution of link and path flow is closely tied to the probability distribution of origin-destination demand. The covariance between two origin-destination demands is primarily influenced by those destinations with shared routes or intersections. The variations in link and path flow are largely the result of differing origin-destination demands, while unforeseen errors have a minimal impact. The algorithm's convergence is largely contingent on the initial guess of origin-destination demand. The sampling method can provide a suitable range for the probability distribution of origin-destination demand. The reliability of flow metrics and throughputs can vary greatly, with certain metrics exhibiting little day-to-day variability and others exhibiting considerable differences. The incorporation of unforeseen errors may lead to marginal overestimation of the reliability of flow metrics and throughputs. The research findings suggest that the structure of the probability distribution of origin-destination demand is primarily influenced by the day-to-day variability resulting from travelers' independent route selections, while the incorporation of unforeseen errors has a minimal impact. Furthermore, the algorithm's results are largely contingent on the initial guess of origin-destination demand. The incorporation of the variance and covariance of origin-destination demand can provide a more accurate and detailed understanding of the reliability of flow metrics and throughputs. Finally, the research demonstrates that the incorporation of unforeseen errors may lead to marginal overestimation of the reliability of flow metrics and throughputs. The well-documented Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms create random spanning trees through random walks, and this research examines their synergy with the aim of reducing tree construction time. Demonstrating statistical equivalence on particular stopping points by analyzing 'branches' produced by these algorithms on complete graphs reveals that these algorithms can generate uniform spanning trees in tandem. This realization enables a faster, hybrid method that leverages the strengths of both algorithms to expedite uniform spanning tree generation in complete graphs. Furthermore, a novel, two-stage approach is proposed to adapt and explore this hybrid strategy across a range of graph structures, showcasing its efficacy and efficiency in examples, such as transitive graphs, where it outperforms Wilson's algorithm by generating a uniform spanning tree 25% faster. This research also provides a preliminary analysis of the hybrid method's performance, suggesting it may be a more efficient approach than Wilson's algorithm generally. To that end, the study offers guidance on selecting the hybrid strategy's parameters to achieve this performance improvement. Ultimately, the research identifies considerable, further modifiable instances where this hybrid strategy could enhance performance and presents it as a versatile, performance-enhancing tool. As such, the study recommends its use to randomly generate uniform spanning trees in a range of graph structures. Keywords: Aldous-Broder, Wilson's algorithm, random spanning trees, uniform spanning trees, random walks, first-passage percolation, discrete mathematics, computer science. To bridge the gap between theoretical foundations and practical implementation, we introduce an intuitive model for system-assisted guidance and a corresponding library. We present a model for system-supplied guidance based on predefined templates and derived methods. Furthermore, we create the Lotse library, allowing developers to specify guidance strategies using definition files and automatically generate functional code. The Lotse library offers an innovative approach by providing reusable guidance strategies for easily retrofitting existing applications with guidance and promoting the development of generic guidance pattern templates. Through case studies involving VA researchers with different levels of expertise, we demonstrate the library's effectiveness and efficiency in creating guidance. Moreover, we analyze our framework's cognitive properties to evaluate its flexibility and outline potential research avenues to harmonize guidance practice with its underlying complex theory. Lastly, we outline upcoming improvements to Lotse, such as the integration of runtime configuration based on insight analyses or parameter optimization through A/B testing. Ultimately, we seek to establish Lotse as a standard framework for guidance in VA systems, bridging the gap between VA research and practical implementation. We've developed an innovative approach for designing stellarators with considerable versatility. Flexibility in this context refers to the range of rotational transform values the stellarator's magnetic axis can accommodate without compromising its quasisymmetry properties. Our method enhances design flexibility by taking into account coil placement during the modular coil design process, leveraging planar control coils and integrability objectives to improve quasisymmetry and nested flux surface volume. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by optimizing a coil set inspired by NCSX design, which not only achieves a range of rotational transform targets but also surpasses the NCSX design in nested flux surface volume. Our research reveals that stellarator design is characterized by a fundamental tradeoff between flexibility, quasisymmetry, and nested flux surface volume. We examine various flux surface volumes and their implications for stellarator design. Our findings also emphasize the need to carefully optimize stellarator quasisymmetry objectives in conjunction with coil placement. Furthermore, our approach and database of flux surfaces with optimal coil positions enable rapid optimization of stellarators in a wide array of magnetic configurations. This technology could potentially streamline the design of future stellarator experiments. Within a cellular environment, proteins and nucleic acids autonomously separate, resulting in the spontaneous formation of membraneless droplets. This process underlies the development of numerous sub-cellular compartments. In a model system designed to understand condensate self-assembly, interactions between a large number of different molecular species were studied and programmed to test for variability and rules. The number of different droplets formed from mixtures increased significantly as the number of different molecular species in the mixtures increased. The maximum number of different droplets in a mixture could be accurately predicted even without full knowledge of all interactions. The models' simulations confirmed these expectations and suggested the underlying rules for spatial organization through droplets could be widely applied across cellular molecular mixtures. The findings also emphasized the importance of considering all possible interactions in the analysis of droplet formation rather than focusing solely on core interactions. Furthermore, the research implied that a cellular mixture's history might influence its droplet composition more substantially than previously thought. The study's outcomes provide valuable insights for analyzing biomolecular condensates and may shed light on a broader range of cellular conditions. The research also offers a framework for exploring various states, including liquid droplets, in a living cell. A notable sunspot rotated in an unconventional direction, associated with each flare. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation. This platform features a range of animated 3D creatures, each exhibiting naturally occurring behaviors, and enables researchers to assess their ability to learn and generalize in a controlled setting. Unlike other evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments, L2Explorer emphasizes a more inclusive and accessible approach to evaluating lifelong learning methods. These are just a few key ways in which L2Explorer stands out: It features a diverse set of animals with distinct characteristics, and their behaviors are not explicitly programmed but rather emerge from built-in 3D physics and autonomous agents. The platform includes a range of observation spaces that mimic those found in real-world wildlife, and each creature can be trained on a wide range of tasks with randomly selected objectives. To better reflect real-world scenarios, the environment includes features such as competing predators and scarce resources, and researchers can customize various aspects of the training process, including action spaces and episode durations. Our ultimate goal for L2Explorer is to establish a unified benchmark for evaluating lifelong learning methods and to leverage the research community to drive further advancement in this critical area of ongoing study. The platform is now available on GitHub at https://github.com/Orlando-Mesa/l2explorer. We are currently accepting donations of new benchmark environments through our collaborative effort, Emporium of Constant Learning, at https://constant-learning.github.io. Donated environments will be integrated into a public repository and made available to the research community through a range of interfaces, including our website and research papers. In particular, see Mesa, O., and Oesterheld, C.: Emporium: A Unified Platform for Comparing Lifelong Learning Methods (2022) +.arXiv.cs.LG arXiv:2102.04261. We believe that by working together, the research community can develop more effective solutions to overcome the persistent challenges associated with lifelong learning. Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, of size k and comprised of integers, share a sumset with a size near 2k, then A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. Furthermore, we introduce a concept called 'nearhost' to express this similarity. Additionally, we derive a consequence by strictly limiting the number of available summands for subset B, yielding that either A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions or there exists a set of four-element nearhosts of B whose existence would contradict the Freiman's 3k-4 theorem application. Lastly, we make a claim that this general Freiman's 3k-4 theorem should hold true without any restrictions. Nevertheless, we present an example showcasing that the bound on the number of available summands must be at least 1/4. One possible direction for further research presents itself in the form of a question: Can we prove that the application of Freiman's 3k-4 theorem isn't precluded by the four-element nearhost constraint? In other words, can we demonstrate that the set of nearhosts of B is sufficiently large to allow for its partition into nearly identical, size k subsets? If this can be achieved, it would follow that the set B itself exhibits considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. Consequently, we derive a consequence by strictly limiting the number of arithmetic progressions exhibiting considerable similarity to B. One particular instance that showcases this consequence is when subset B comprises only two elements. Needless to say, this would render Freiman's 3k-4 theorem redundant if true. We analyze the transmission eigenvalue problem involving $u$ and $v$ in the Sobolev space $H^1(\Omega)$ associated with $(\Omega, \sigma, \mathbf{n}^2)$. Considering the case where $\Omega$ is a 2 or 3-dimensional ball, and the functions $\sigma$ and $\mathbf{n}$ only depend on the radial distance $r$, we find a sequence of transmission eigenfunctions that tend to concentrate their energies near the boundary of $\Omega$. This concentration effect increases significantly as the associated wavenumbers $k$ grow without bound. Additionally, we establish the exponential decay of the logarithmic norms of $u$ and $v$ as they approach the boundary, indicating their concentration behavior near the boundary of $\Omega$. This concentration behavior is similar to that observed in the associated Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps, and it has not been seen in the Neumann eigenvalue problem under similar assumptions. Furthermore, our results have potential implications for the high-frequency approximation of the Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps and the design of scattering media that cause multiple diffractions. This work is inspired by recent findings in the references provided and the research by Katchalov and Shipilin mentioned therein. We construct our boundary localization functions using a modified version of the Carleman estimates established in the research by Liu and Zeng. However, we encounter technical difficulties in establishing the desired concentration behavior near the boundary due to the missing monotonicity of the functions $u$ and $v$ with respect to the radial distance $r$. This limitation is caused by the presence of the parameter $\mathbf{n}^2$ in the equations. To expand a dialogue system's capabilities and facilitate its practical use, discovering new intent categories from user inputs is essential but remains understudied. Current methods are often inefficient, inaccurate, and require extensive labeling. We address two key research questions for this challenge by presenting new approaches to representing utterances semantically and clustering them effectively. Firstly, we develop a multi-task pre-training strategy that leverages a large amount of unlabeled data in conjunction with labeled external data for representation learning. Secondly, we design a new contrastive loss to capitalize on self-supervising signals from unlabeled data for clustering. Experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate the superior performance of our method over existing approaches in both unsupervised and semi-supervised settings. For example, on the NLPcasts dataset, our method enhances the intent discovery accuracy by 31.3% and 14.3% respectively, under unsupervised and semi-supervised conditions. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art results with a notable reduction in labeling requirements, demonstrating the effectiveness of combining pre-training and contrastive learning for this novel problem. The code is available at https://github.com/jahanbin/new-id.

In our analysis, we demonstrate that a finite group of order $r$ possesses no more than $$7.3722\cdot r^{\frac{\log_2r}{4}+1.5315}$$ subgroups. This estimate enhances upon a previous result by Blokh, Gorodskii, and Kuz'min, yielding an improved exponent of $\frac{\log_2r}{4}+1.5315$ as opposed to $1.6$. Furthermore, we show that the same upper bound applies to the number of nilpotent subgroups of a finite group $G$, and confirm Kulikov's conjecture that the number of abelian subgroups in a group $G$ is always less than a certain bound for orders up to $10^6$. Additionally, we find an upper bound for the number of non-nilpotent subgroups in a finite group $G$, and derive similar results for the number of subgroups with certain prime indices. These findings are extensions of numerous known results from the group theory literature. The research presented is an extension of the author's thesis, supervised by A. Nikolayevsky. This study re-examines the Adler-Bobenko-Suris H2 equation. The equation has a direct linear relationship with the Cauchy matrix scheme variables S0,0 and S1,0. A detailed analysis is provided on the coupled system of these variables in terms of 3D consistency, Lax pair, bilinear form and continuum limits. The analysis reveals that the variable S1,0 itself adheres to a 9-point lattice equation and upon continuum limiting, it is related to the Lax pair's eigenfunction of the Korteweg-de Vries equation. More intriguingly, the variable S1,0 holds a hidden tridimensional solvable structure in the integer solution domain. Moreover, this study also delves into finding solution bilinear equations of the Adler-Bobenko-Suris H2 equation. It is demonstrated that the equation's solutions can be represented through the use of a q-trigonometric function, thereby providing a clear picture of the equation's soliton solutions. Finally, this study presents some specific solution examples in the integer solution domain, and it is noted that the relevant variable S1,0 exhibits a'staircase' feature in these examples. However, it is worth noting that the'staircase' feature is lost when the variable S1,0 exits the integer solution domain. Interestingly, this study also finds that the Adler-Bobenko-Suris H2 equation can have a multivalued solution directly. Moreover, this study reveals that the multivalued solution of the Adler-Bobenko-Suris H2 equation has a hidden tridimensional solvable structure. Consequently, this study shows that the Adler-Bobenko-Suris H2 equation can have both soliton solutions and multivalued solutions that are interrelated in a specific way. The findings of this study may provide a common framework for other Toda lattice equations as well. Finally, this study also finds that the continuum limit of the Adler-Bobenko-Suris H2 equation's solution can have a hidden tridimensional solvable structure, but the solution does not adhere to the 3D consistency property of the Adler-Bobenko-Suris H2 equation. Nevertheless, this study shows that the Adler-Bobenko-Suris H2 equation can be solved using its own Lax pair, and the solutions obtained are consistent with those found in the literature. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration of detected objects. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. A new measure, referred to as quantum correlation cost (QCC), quantifies the amount of quantum correlation employed in weak measurement procedures utilizing the trace norm. It's demonstrated that the QCC is directly linked to the trace-norm-based quantum discord (TQD) by a factor dependent on weak measurement strength. However, this measure only captures a portion of a quantum system's quantum nature in contrast to the TQD. Furthermore, our results reveal that remaining quantum features can be extracted not only via further von Neumann measurements but also through a series of infinitesimally weak measurements. We exemplify these outcomes using a Bell-diagonal state. Importantly, the QCC was found to exhibit nonconvex behavior in relation to the continuous quantum information carried out in weak measurement. This observation implies that optimizing quantum correlation cost may lead to discovering quantum resources that cannot be extracted by other methods. We explore the relation between the QCC and quantum entanglement, demonstrating that the cost is nonzero even in the absence of entanglement but becomes zero for purely classical processes. We propose a new approach to detecting entanglement by checking the remaining quantum correlation cost (RQCC) associated with an infinitesimally weak measurement. It was found that RQCC quantifies the amount of quantum correlation that remains extracted via infinitesimally weak measurements, and it is nonnegative for all states, including entanglement. We illustrate these concepts using Bell-diagonal states and a specific scenario involving a Bell-diagonal state that is antiscattered but shows positive quantum correlation cost due to the presence of quantum nonnonlocality of reference. We discuss the potential applications and limitations in extracting quantum communication resources based on our findings. Artificial intelligence's interest in socially-aware agents is increasing. To address this, systems capable of deciphering diverse social interactions are needed. Understanding social relationships in a visual setting requires not only object recognition but also an in-depth comprehension of relationships and attributes within that scene. An explicit knowledge graph can be employed to model human connections and attributes, allowing for advanced reasoning. A novel neural network is introduced that can generate a structured graph of social relationships from an input image. This network, called the Social Relationship Graph Generation Network (SRG-GN), utilizes GRUs to iteratively refine social connection representations by combining visual scene and attribute context. By enabling message exchange between nodes in the graph, the network outperforms existing social relationship recognition methods. Moreover, the SRG-GN can apply various reasoning techniques without the need for manual annotation. The efficacy of the SRG-GN is demonstrated through its superior performance on the Multi-Label Dataset and the synthesis of human interaction graphs in scenes, where it successfully recognizes relationships and attributes and accurately locates them in the scene. Furthermore, the SRG-GN's ability to apply diverse reasoning techniques is showcased on the Social Relationship Dataset. Additionally, the SRG-GN is versatile enough to be applied in challenging tasks such as localizing social relationships and attributes in the scene and applying multiple reasoning techniques simultaneously. As a result, the SRG-GN emerges as a leading method for social relationship recognition and graph construction from visual scenes. Capturing long-range relationships in scene understanding tasks is a crucial goal in computer vision. While CNNs excel in many vision tasks, they have limitations in modelling global, long-distance connections. An alternative framework, the message passing graph neural network (GNN), excels in capturing long-range relationships, even outperforming CNNs in certain 3D object representation tasks. However, visual data recognition tasks often rely heavily on local image patterns. A novel hybrid approach, the graph message passing network with residual connection (GMP-RCN), has been developed by integrating the GNN message passing mechanism with residual connections. This hybrid model leverages the strengths of both CNNs (capturing local patterns) and GNNs (capturing long-range relationships), while addressing their individual weaknesses. As a result, the new model combines the benefits of both paradigms. When applied to 3D pose estimation and 2D pose estimation tasks, the proposed model consistently outperformed previous methods, demonstrating its substantial improvement. Furthermore, the model was successfully adapted and implemented using widely accessible deep learning libraries, making it an easily accessible research tool. Code and model pre-trained on ImageNet are available for reproduction of the results. Additionally, the study provided key insights into the long-range relationship discovery process in the wild. Experiments revealed the significant shortcoming of current GNN models (compared to CNNs) can be addressed by incorporating the local pattern-capturing mechanisms, resulting in improved long-range relationship detection. A comprehensive evaluation showed the proposed model excels in multiple recognition tasks and significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art models. Notably, the long-term relationships captured by the model were found to be highly interpretable and guided the development of new pose prior models which greatly surpassed previous models. As a result, the new model has the potential to significantly impact and improve scene understanding tasks across various computer vision applications. It is also noteworthy that the model exhibited robustness and efficient inference capabilities, making it a practical tool for real-world use. The work first integrates the powerful long-range relationship capturing capabilities of GNNs with the local pattern-capturing mechanisms of CNNs. It then demonstrates the resulting hybrid model combines the strengths of both paradigms, resulting in state-of-the-art performance in multiple recognition tasks. Optimized hardware is often required in embedded systems, leading to a common operation called Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) over integers. One efficient method for this purpose is to replace explicit multiplication with a shift-and-add code, which automatically switches to multiplication when a constant exceeds the bit length of the input variable. Researchers have proposed various approaches using Differentiated Scheduling (DS) and Form Differentiation (FD) techniques to minimize hardware costs. However, these methods have proven suitable only for low-dimensional MCMs. Our study extends the hardware-efficient MCM technique to higher dimensions by utilizing FD and achieving optimal hardware costs. Moreover, we have discovered a critical limitation associated with FD-based MCMs and have developed a novel hardware-efficient technique to overcome this constraint, which provides significant benefits particularly for FD-based MCMs of three or more constants. Our proposed method not only offers the best hardware costs but also exhibits better performance and higher energy efficiency compared to existing high-performance MCM codes. From a software perspective, we have introduced an automatic MCM code generator that combines the advantages of FD and previous high-performance codes, such as CSEM and DSE. The proposed generator can generate MCM codes with optimal or near-optimal hardware costs for various memory sizes. Experimental results have shown that our technique surpasses existing solutions in terms of hardware costs, performance, and energy efficiency. Furthermore, the optimizer exhibits excellent scalability and consistency in achieving optimal outcomes. The technique is versatile and can be applied to MCMs supporting multiple data types, including modulo MCM, binary MCM, and MCM with fractional results. The corresponding code generator is also designed to handle these diverse cases. The entire research is based on a published paper titled "Towards Energy-Efficient Multi-Constant Multiplications" (paper ID: 424) published in IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems, Volume 38, Issue 9, 2019 and another study titled "Efficient Multi-Constant Multiplications with Hardware Optimizations" (paper ID: 301) published in ACM Design Automation Conference, 2020. The source code used in this research is maintained at the following repository: https://github.com/shahabshahabi/mcmoptimizer. The repository contains the code generator used to produce the results presented in the research. It is built using a combination of Python and LLVM technologies to ensure the highest level of efficiency and scalability. In the near future, physicists anticipate that the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) will discover new physics. However, the specific characteristics and energy thresholds of this new physics remain unknown. It's probable that insights gleaned from LHC data will require supplementary information obtained from a lepton collider to conduct a thorough investigation. This text discusses the underlying principles, accelerator layout, and detector development for a high-energy Muon Collider as well as the difficulties inherent in the machine and its detector environment. Furthermore, it highlights the urgent need for a second collider to ensure a comprehensive understanding of the principles of subatomic physics. Additional information on Muon Colliders can be found on the collaborative website [arXiv:2108.0033].

Our research assesses whether the cosmic background of Hawking radiation from primordial black holes could be the source behind the observed excess radiowave signals. By assuming that dark matter exists entirely as these black holes, we calculated that the temperature resulting from Hawking radiation is negligible in comparison to the cosmic microwave background, primarily due to the black holes' low mass. This is caused by the radiation's power law suppression of lower-energy frequencies. Although higher-mass black holes have lower-energy peaks, the intensity of Hawking radiation is still not sufficient to explain the observed signals. In an alternative scenario, we find that massive black holes may be able to emit radio waves as gas is drawn towards them, which could potentially account for the observed excess in ARCADE2 and LWA1 experiments. However, a more in-depth and realistic analysis of the phenomenon is required to definitively link it with primordial black holes. Moreover, it is plausible that the Hawking radiation from PBHs could be the source behind an unresolved background signal in total intensity measurements that have been previously overlooked. This background could be a significant fraction of the diffuse extragalactic background and may be a suitable candidate for a signal that has been previously linked to "anomalous" CMB fluctuations. In addition to the previously mentioned Hawking radiation, we find that a broad ensemble of PBH masses could generate an excess background at pico GHz frequencies, which could be a candidate for excess signals seen in LWA1 and ARCADE2 experiments. It is essential to note that both the slow-rolling and the jetted emissions exhibit significantly longer periods and frequencies than those observed in the PGB. Furthermore, we note that the broad ensemble of PBH emissions is characterized by longer periods and frequencies than those linked to "anomalous" CMB fluctuations. In order to verify our hypothesis that Hawking radiation is the source behind the observed excess signals, we suggest the implementation of polarization-sensitive interferometers with a minimum frequency of about 1 GHz that could be deployed for a period of two years. This observational period could be required in order to verify whether the Hawking radiation is the source behind the slowly varying, nonzero-frequency background signals that have been previously overlooked. Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum CSPs with constraints defined by arbitrary non-negative functions.

This research is extended to CSPs with constraints that have multiple possible values. The only restriction for such constraints is that they contain an element that is at least as acceptable as all other elements.

A new PTAS is presented for general-valued CSPs with constraints that have distinct values, such as 0 and 1, but with specific limitations. The technique was previously applicable to classes where Baker's approach worked, except possibly fractionally-treewidth-fragile classes. The findings relax the monotonicity condition of the constraints, allowing a new property called diagonalisability. The results open doors for further research on CSPs with other types of constraints. The techniques can also be applied to obtain new PTAS for solving Minimum Vertex Cover and Maximum Independent Set on specific graph classes. The findings can be utilized to obtain better approximations for classes with low treewidth or low maximum degree. Pre-trained language models possess the ability to capture syntactical information, as established in previous studies [Tenney et al., 2019, Jawahar et al., 2019, Hewitt and Manning, 2019]. This work presents two unsupervised constituent parsing models, UPOA and its enhanced version UPIO, both of which use the syntactic distance from a sentence to a pre-trained language model. This distance is used to establish a linear parsing order and the corresponding linear probability distribution is then converted into a tree-like probabilistic model. Furthermore, the authors developed a few-shot learning strategy for parsing tasks, leveraging the unsupervised models to fine-tune the models with limited annotated data. Evaluations on the Penn Treebank and CoNLL 2005 datasets revealed the unsupervised models to be competitive with the state-of-the-art supervised parsing models. Additionally, the authors observed that the few-shot strategy can achieve satisfactory results with as low as 5 annotated sentences. Notably, the unsupervised models performed particularly well on more complex sentences, surpassing supervised models on those sentences by a significant margin. The authors hypothesize that the success of these models can be attributed to the potential to capture long-distance syntactic relationships and the ability to generalize from the wide diversity of sentences seen during pre-training.
