High-definition hyperspectral images possess the unique capability to distinguish between diverse objects within intricate environments by analyzing each pixel across various frequency ranges. Although HSI cameras are relatively inexpensive to produce, the associated computational demands for classifying each pixel into specific categories are significant. In this research, a groundbreaking approach is introduced that leverages newly developed hyperspectral images to streamline the semantic segmentation process. Initially, a well-known semantic segmentation network is trained on a vast road dataset. The resulting model is then fine-tuned using a minimal number of hyperspectral images collected simultaneously with standard RGB images. To mitigate the impact of reduced image volume resulting from 4-channel HSI images being reduced to 3 channels, we effectively utilize the acquired hyperspectral information. The experiment demonstrates that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques using standard RGB images by 3% and 6% on the Cityscapes and KITTI-360 datasets respectively, while also proving its robustness in handling sparse hyperspectral data. The source code is available at https://github.com/IMLAB-UoM/HSI-Cityscapes. Additionally, the hyperspectral images are made available at https://imsu.uom.edu.au/HSCI/.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and confirmed that the star exhibits no significant chemical abnormalities. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Lastly, we examined possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation profile, including the possibility of the star ingesting a giant planet or experiencing enhanced angular momentum redistribution through tidal inertial waves induced by a nearby substellar companion, and encouraged future observational and theoretical studies. Given the relatively high probability of our star having encountered a giant planet at an internal radius of approximately 2.15 R Sun based on evolutionary models, we suggested that this planetary body could be hosting in the star, causing the star to engulf the planet or vice versa. This study adds another entry to the growing list of unusual internal rotation profiles in stars, which might be attributed to unusual astrophysical events or our limited understanding of hydrodynamic processes. Future missions such as the Legacy Survey of Space and Time and the PLATO mission will be poised to expand our knowledge base significantly. Based on our analysis, we estimated that about 75% of all giant stars with masses less than 2.25 M Sun could host an alien planet within an internal radius of approximately 2.15 R Sun based on evolutionary models. This high estimate might be influenced by our limitations in predicting tidal evolution and the enduring uncertainty surrounding the fate of most low-mass stars as they evolve into giants. In algorithmic literature, the underlying computation model is typically implicit and assumed to be based on the RAM model. Despite being widely adopted, the RAM model lacks a solid theoretical foundation, characterized by inconsistent definitions and a lack of cohesive results. This research aims to rectify this issue by developing a new RAM model with desirable algorithmic properties and robust complexity classes, particularly linear-time computability for problems like LIN and CONST-DELAY-lin, an enumeration class of problems that can be computed after linear-time preprocessing. The proposed computation model has limited storage and processing capabilities - its registers can store $O(N)$ elements, where $N$ is the input size, and operations take unit time. The success of this foundation will be built upon demonstrating that a RAM with only basic addition operations can perform essential arithmetic operations efficiently after initial linear-time processing. Additionally, despite the limited storage capacity of individual registers ($O(N)$), it is feasible to handle larger integers by distributing them across a fixed number ($d$) of registers and leveraging surprising computational methods to execute a wide range of arithmetic operations on these 'polynomial' integers in constant time after initial linear preprocessing. The value of $d$ serves as the key input parameter that influences the complexity of these operations. Furthermore, a theoretical analysis will be conducted to determine the minimum value of $d$ required to efficiently perform a series of tasks, including division with the remainder, the computation of the greatest common divisor, and modulo arithmetic. The findings of this research will yield important guidelines for the efficient implementation of these operations in the RAM model with a limited number of addition operations and will have direct practical implications, enabling developers to determine the optimal storage capacity needed for effective computation. The proposed approach will be supported by a detailed mathematical analysis, and its correctness will be demonstrated through a substantial collection of meaningful examples. Interestingly, the RAM model with basic addition operations will be shown to possess an intriguing property, where the linear-time computability of a problem is equivalent to its const-delay-lin computability, an indication of its robustness and ease of implementation. The consistency of this result will be validated through a substantial collection of meaningful examples and will be further reinforced by a remarkable finding - it is generally computationally difficult to determine if a linearly computable problem also admits const-delay-lin computability. The proposed foundation will be a cornerstone for a broader theoretical framework that can provide a precise algorithmic understanding of contemporary software systems, enabling the identification of practical storage and processing requirements needed for efficient computation. To tackle the data sparsity problem affecting session-based recommendation models that predict the next item users will choose, researchers combined self-supervised learning with co-training. They proposed an enhanced framework by leveraging a session-based graph to create informative, not artificially sparse, data for these models. This new approach exploits internal and external session connections to produce contrastive learning, thereby preserving genuine data for superior session-based recommendation performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate the success of this innovative method in achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmark datasets. Moreover, the developers successfully avoided artificially inducing data sparsity, thereby preserving genuine data and showcasing the efficiency of this approach. Furthermore, they found that external session correlations could be leveraged to provide additional predictive insights beyond purely historical user behavior, thereby enhancing the predictive power of existing session-based recommendation models. Finally, since the proposed method only requires the session-based graph as input, it can be easily applied to various recomender algorithms without significant modification, thereby showcasing its potential real-world applicability. This research presents a novel method for generating LCD codes using group rings and a standard transformation that maps group ring components to a subring of $n \times n$ matrices, resulting in LCD codes that are also group codes due to being ideals in a group ring. Under specific conditions for the group ring element $v$, the proposed construction allows for the creation of non-trivial group LCD codes, with additional constraints enabling the development of reversible group LCD codes. A variety of binary group LCD codes are presented, including optimal and reversible group LCD codes with various parameters. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the existing lower bounds on the minimum distance of binary group codes can be achieved. The proposed construction also provides a framework for developing bipolar codes using group rings and offers a possible approach for generalizing LCD codes to higher character fields. Computational software, such as Macalane and Maggie, was utilized for the presented examples and performance comparisons. Specifically, the studies analyzed $Q$-extension of $Z_4$ and $Z_2 \times Z_2$ rings in connection with bipolar LCD codes. The presented results indicate that the constructed bipolar codes surpass the existing lower bounds on the minimum distance. A comparison of the present work with previously published research reveals that it offers superior performance. The standard approach failed to achieve the existing lower bounds on the minimum distance due to its limitations in developing bipolar codes using $Q$-extension of $Z_4$ and $Z_2 \times Z_2$ rings. However, further study is required to generalize the found results to higher character fields. A possible approach for doing so is presented. Moreover, the study offers a framework for studying bipolar codes using group rings and the results can be extended to generalizing LCD codes in $F_{2^m}^n$ character fields. We examine differential forms on an algebraic compactification of the metric graph moduli space, derived by mapping invariant differential forms from the tropical Torelli map. It's known that these invariant forms give rise to the stable real cohomology of the general linear group, a finding by Borel. We compute period integrals by integrating such forms across graph metrics and find them to be always finite and expressible as generalised Feynman integrals. Our integrals have further application in identifying non-zero homology classes in the graph complex, providing novel perspectives on the cohomology structure and forging links between graph theory, motivic Galois groups and quantum field theory. Specifically, our analysis implies the existence of non-trivial motivic multiple Zeta Value at arguments of degree two. Moreover, our work indicates the feasibility of computing motivic multiple Zeta Values of degree up to four through the evaluation of Feynman integrals. Ultimately, our analysis suggests the establishment of an algebraic and periodic Novikov-Polyakov feynman integral ring for the general linear group. Lastly, our integrals provide novel explanations for combinatorial phenomena, such as the symmetry between tree and non-tree graphs and the occurrence of rational weights in the feynman integral evaluation. Additionally, our analysis suggests the establishment of an encoding system, where every feynman integral is represented through a combination of trees, roots and numerical coefficients. Such encoding system, when applied to period integrals, yields an innovative and straightforward algorithm for computing motivic multiple Zeta Values. This algorithm exploits the algebraic and periodic feynman integral ring structure. Our work has further implications in the context of the motivic fundamental group of the general linear group. By combining period integrals with the feynman integral ring structure, we can compute a key element of the motivic Abel-Jacobi map. This, in turn, allows us to study the image of the tropical Torelli map and its feynman integral related properties at a algebraic level. Moreover, our analysis indicates the feasibility of expressing feynman integrals through the metric graph moduli space using a system of roots and numerical coefficients, where the metric graph moduli space is shown to be topologically non-trivial and homogeneous. Our integrals also provide novel explanations for the occurrence of numerically independent periods in the graph complex and the feasibility of expressing feynman integrals through a combination of trees, roots and numerical coefficients. In various object categorization tasks, particularly in visually complex conditions, it has been demonstrated that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can outperform feedforward models.  This research aimed to uncover the specific role of RNN recurrence in aiding object categorization.  We trained RNNs on an object categorization task and discovered through linear diagnostic analysis that auxiliary variables such as object position, orientation, and size are communicated through recurrence and contribute significantly to performance improvement.  This evidence confirms our hypothesis that auxiliary variables are utilized to optimize object categorization in cluttered environments.  Additionally, our results suggest that intermediate representations within RNNs comprise a combination of primary object features and auxiliary variables, with recurrence primarily utilized for detecting objects' spatial relationships.  This finding validates our proposed hypothesis and provides a systematic explanation for the recurrent neural networks' superiority over feedforward models in object categorization.  Our study also offers an adaptable method for diagnosing and interpreting the role of recurrence in various deep learning architectures. Despite numerous studies on non-Hermitian topology, the influence of correlations remains a significant unresolved issue. We conducted an in-depth analysis of correlated non-Hermitian systems, with a particular focus on the topological characteristics of one-dimensional systems. Our results reveal that correlations cause a significant reduction in the topological classification from $\mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ for one-dimensional systems with a single synthetic dimension, along with $\mathrm{U(1)}$ symmetry and spin-parity symmetry. We also investigated the properties of an extended Hatano-Nelson chain, which demonstrates substantial correlation effects; interactions abolish the skin effect that exists in the non-interacting system. The findings of this study underscore the instability of the skin effect against correlations, which is consistent with the reduced point-gap topology in one spatial dimension. The discoveries presented here provide novel insights into the topological characteristics of correlated systems, thereby initiating new areas of research within the field of non-Hermitian topological physics. We also introduce a new class of insulators, which can be characterized by a single integer called the correlation number, serving as a theoretical indicator of correlations that cannot be eliminated by any unitary transformation. The correlation number serves as a precise measure of the correlations in systems possessing $\mathrm{U(1)}$ symmetry and spin-parity symmetry. We conducted an exhaustive classification of extended Hatano-Nelson chain based on the correlation number, revealing diverse possible values for the correlation number, which can serve as a criterion for categorizing different classes of extended Hatano-Nelson chain. The correlation number also possesses a pivotal property where two connected systems have the same correlation number if, and only if, they are similarly filled; this is similar to the same principle that governs the filling number in topological physics. We also studied the eigenvalue distributions of the three-banded Hamiltonians under the influence of correlations. The findings of this study reveal that correlations bring about significant modifications in the eigenvalue distributions; this is evident from the central mode, which becomes broader upon the presence of interactions, along with a significant shift in the edge modes that arise from the synthetic dimension. The shift in the edge modes indicates that correlations can either enhance or decrease the sensitivity of the edge modes in detecting the topological characteristics of the systems. The discoveries presented here provide novel insights into the topological characteristics of correlated systems, thereby initiating new areas of research within the field of non-Hermitian topological physics. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, but a specific one is constructively demonstrated. It is hypothesized that there exist no finite GCM quadruples in spaces of four or more dimensions. Furthermore, a theoretical upper limit is proposed for possible sizes in multi-dimensional GCM quadruples. It is conjectured that this upper limit is accurately represented by the sequence $d_{\mathbf{m}}(4)$, where $\mathbf{m}$ represents a multi-dimensional vector. Existing evidence for this conjecture has been found in one-dimensional and two-dimensional cases. The findings from four-lepton final state analysis provide joint constraints on Higgs boson width and its interaction with electroweak vector bosons. By applying matrix element techniques, production and decay mechanisms of Higgs boson are identified, and its sensitivity is enhanced. The constraints on non-standard interactions with electroweak vector bosons align with the standard model predictions in on-shell and off-shell regions. Assuming the standard model coupling structure, the Higgs boson width is constrained between 0.4 and 5.4 MeV, while the simulated expected range is between -8 and 12 MeV. The constraints on the Higgs boson width remain comparable with the consideration of tested non-standard interactions. The constraints on the non-standard interactions with electroweak vector bosons show significant improvement over previous analyses using four lepton final states. The observed and expected limits on the non-standard couplings are set at 0.30, 0.47, and 0.42 for CP-even couplings, and 0.45, 0.60, and 0.52 for CP-odd couplings with the photon, W and Z bosons respectively. The results provide the most precise constraints on the Higgs boson width and its interaction with electewek vector bosons to date. Given an algebraic variety X that has a transitive action from the group Aut(X), the highest degree of transitivity of this action is called the transitivity degree. This degree is denoted by the maximum value of m for which Aut(X) acts transitively m times on X. In cases where Aut(X) is m-transitive for any positive value of m, we define the transitivity degree to be infinite. This study involves determining the transitivity degree for specific varieties, such as quasi-affine toric varieties, and homogeneous spaces, while exploring related open problems and conjectures. Specifically, we found the transitivity degree for each projective space to be infinite, determined the degree for some Grassmannians and Lagrangian Grassmannians, and established constraints for the degree in the case of Lagrangian quadrics. Moreover, we showed that certain groups act transitively in a specific, well-defined manner on projective spaces, and proposed a conjectured upper bound for the transitivity degree in various spaces. Additionally, we retrieved and extended known results in favor of a theorem stating that a particular group action is transitively infinite if a specific condition is met. This study also delves into the relationship between the transitivity degree and algebraic cycle classes. Specifically, we demonstrated that such degree classes can be generated by a specific set of classes based on a particular space for each positive value of m. Furthermore, we showed that a particular class is linearly independent for each m. Lastly, we studied degree maps between specific spaces and homogeneous varieties, while examining the rationality of their field extensions. Specifically, we found the rationality condition for a particular space based on a given group for its first few degrees, and proposed a conjectured condition based on a group property. This study also explores similar problems for projective spaces, Grassmannians, and Lagrangian quadrics. Additionally, we derived and extended existing work in favor of a theorem stating that a particular space is rationalally independent for its first few degrees, and examined its relationship with a group property. Lastly, we studied the action of a group on rational points in a projective space for its first few degrees, while examining the transitivity degree and rationality of its function field. Social media platforms are facing significant problems due to the presence of toxic content like hate speech, off-color language, and misogyny. These difficulties have caught the attention of the Natural Language Processing (NLP) community, driving innovative research in the field. In this study, we report on the performance of our models in the inaugural Arabic Misogyny Identification challenge, where we evaluate three models that can learn multiple tasks simultaneously, alongside their individual-task counterparts. Our approach relies on the pre-trained MARBERT language model to analyze text inputs. Our results indicate that the proposed models achieved top-tier outcomes, securing first, second, and third place in both the misogyny identification and classification tasks. Additionally, we found that the multi-task models consistently delivered better performance than their single-task counterparts, demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach. Our source code is publicly available on GitHub for the sake of reproducibility. Furthermore, the proposed models have been implemented using the popular Hugging Face Transformers library to facilitate widespread adoption. Our aim is to eventually expand the scope to encompass other toxic content types, such as hate speech, to provide a more comprehensive system that can accurately identify and mitigate a broader range of toxic content on Arabic social media platforms. Our model predictions have been uploaded to the designated competition website for validation purposes.

Several key network communication challenges such as caching and computation are interconnected. A centralized caching approach seeks to mitigate network strain during peak wireless network times, whereas distributed computation explores the balance between computation and communication within a distributed system. This paper, drawing inspiration from a study of arithmetic sequences, introduces a comprehensive framework for creating caching schemes. This framework enables connections between caching schemes and numerous combinatorial objects, offering versatility in scheme design. We show that schemes built using a placement delivery array can be expressed through a new approach, and other known schemes can also be accommodated within this framework. Furthermore, we propose a new caching scheme featuring linear subpacketization and near constant transmission rates using a specific type of arithmetic sequence. Additionally, we modify this framework to be applicable to the distributed computation problem. A novel transmission method in the shuffle network, derived from a specific type of arithmetic sequence, is also introduced. Comparatively, our framework exhibits reduced communication load and lower-degree network structures compared to existing solutions. However, the examples constructed using this framework often have high computation loads; hence, strategies to reduce them are needed. We offer a method for reducing the computation load in caching schemes by leveraging tools from data compression. Similarly, for distributed computation, we develop a method involving data transmission from multiple nodes to reduce the load on a specific node. These approaches are versatile and can be applied to various schemes within our framework without explicit redesign. However, designed schemes with reduced computation and communication loads do exist, such as distributing the computation in a multi-node setup and using direct transmission from nodes in a single-node setup. These examples illustrate the potential for our framework to be refined further. Lastly, we investigate the potential for transmitting compressed data in caching schemes and propose a compressed caching scheme featuring linear subpacketization and reduced computation load. Nevertheless, the existing compressed caching schemes have limited success in reducing both the computation and communication loads simultaneously. We observe that various established compression methods can be applied to the shuffled data in a specific situation, resulting in reduced communication load and a balanced load between computation and communication. This approach, while not universally applicable, indicates that existing compression methods may not be suitable for the distributed computation problem. Consequently, new compression methods tailored to the specific data patterns in a shuffled computation setup may be necessary to achieve improved performance. We propose such a method, providing a scheme with reduced computation and communication loads for a specific and widely applicable data type. However, developing general, sequence-independent schemes remains challenging due to the diverse data patterns. Therefore, our framework is primarily suitable for sequences with defined cycle

We establish a formalization of the Scott model in univalent type theory, adopting a constructive and predicative framework. To capture the essence of domains in PCF, we design a sequence of increasing universes, whereas the top universe serves as the domain domain. Furthermore, we employ a novel technique for generating a universal lifting domain, along with a fundamental theorem demonstrating that the lifting domain can form a strict order. Our work also involves an innovative application of a technique for generating a product of universes, as well as a novel interpretation of the $\mathsf{UNIT}$ type in PCF. Leveraging these elements, we construct a sound and adequate proof of a PCF interpretation within univalent type theory, wherein the domain domain employs a countable sequence of universines. Consequently, this provides a proof that the fundamental theorems of PCF - including Scott's correction theorem and the finite development theorem - can be constructively established without relying on choice. To confirm that our domain construction aligns with the intended Scott model, we demonstrate that it is possible to generate an interpretation in which the domain domain uses a single infinite universe, along with an infinite recursive sequence. Moreover, in an alternative construction, we showcase an interpretation where the domain domain uses a single infinite universe without requiring recursion, achieved through a distinct analytical interpretation. Finally, we note that the key insights underlying the second construction can be employed to create an even more sophisticated non-recursion-free interpretation in a type theory without universes, albeit with some compromises on the domain's expressiveness. Throughout the paper, we also present a range of other fundamental results on domain construction in univalent type theory, including new proofs of several previously established results. Researchers have suggested the application of quantum interferometry and information processing in Bose-Einstein condensates. However, the current understanding of BECs relies on complex descriptions, often through quantum field theory or nonlinear differential equations. These descriptions sometimes conflict with key principles in quantum mechanics. Nevertheless, it is possible to develop a consistent quantum mechanics for interferometry and information processing in BECs. We propose a method to create nonlinear quantum gates, which can handle multiple particles in a controlled manner, and provide an implementation in a system of two coupled optical fibers. These gates can generate useful states for interferometry and information processing despite the nonlinear interactions. Specifically, we examine the generation of entangled McGuire states and explain an interesting property of these states. Furthermore, we suggest a quantum algorithm, analogous to the black-box search in quantum computing, for utilizing the nonlinear interactions in BECs. To obtain a solution set devoid of degeneration, which end-users seek to avoid, the nondegenerate locus of a polynomial system needs to be computed. The nondegenerate locus comprises points where the codimension of the solution set matches the number of equations in the system. Historically, the nondegenerate locus has been obtained using ideal-theoretic techniques like saturation ideals and equidimensional decompositions. We propose an algorithm leveraging signature-based features of Gröbner basis algorithms to directly calculate the Gröbner basis for the nondegenerate locus closure without initially solving the entire polynomial system through Gröbner basis computation. The proposed method exploits the structure of the nondegenerate locus through its closure already being defined by the given polynomial system, thereby dispensing with the need for an ideal-theoretic approach. The algorithm has been successfully tested with several benchmark problems from various fields, including geometry, codimension-one degeneration, and algebraic stacks, along with some end-user applications in geometry. The Turan tetrahedron problem seeks to calculate the Turan density of the tetrahedron graph K4^3 by finding the maximum l1-norm of a K4^3-free n-vertex 3-uniform hypergraph's codegree vector. We develop a new method for determining hypergraph extremality and apply it to calculate the asymptotic extremal function of the tetrahedron graph under our novel framework. The codegree squared sum, or co2(G), is introduced to measure codegree magnitude in a 3-uniform hypergraph, with exco2(n,H) representing the maximal codegree squared sum among n-vertex H-free hypergraphs. Utilizing flag algebra computations, we determine the codegree squared extremal numbers for K4^3 and K5^3 and demonstrate associated stability properties, revealing the structural resemblance of K4^3-free hypergraphs to certain 3-partite 4-uniform hypergraphs and showing that the codegree squared extremal number achieves its minimum value for K4^3. Additionally, we identify key algebraic properties required for successful application of our method and determine the asymptotic extremal number for the tetrahedron graph via flag algebra calculation. The found extremal number validates the conjectured value of 1/2 for the Turan density of K4^3. Furthermore, our analysis is generalizable to hypergraphs resembling the tetrahedron graph K4^3 and our method may be applied to calculate the extremal number of various hypergraphs. Specifically, we calculate the extremal number of the homogeneous K5-toothpick graph as well as other hypergraphs. Lastly, we hypothesize an even broader application of our method, conjecturing that it could be utilized to calculate the extremal number of any hypergraph. The proposed method boasts significant computational efficiency, specifically for hypergraphs exhibiting local weak Turan density. As such, we foresee its potential to resolve numerous challenging problems in the field of extremal combinatorics. The code for our flag algebra-based computations is available at https://github.com/yoelbirchwood/Tetrahedron-ExtremalCombinatorics. Yoel Staveley Birchwood and David R. Wehlau contributed equally. The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy. Furthermore, we successfully applied this new interpolation scheme to solve two nonlinear partial differential equations – the heat and wave equations. The resulting solutions not only preserve the monotonicity of the initial function but also provide more accurate approximations compared to existing methods, with a convergence rate of O(h^2) for the numerical solution of the first equation, and O(h^3) for the second equation. In addition, the solutions have been successfully extended to free boundary problems in both one and two dimensions. The results have been compared with the B-spline least squares method, showing that our approach often yields more accurate solutions. Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results using multiple Convolutional Neural Network configurations. Evaluations across multiple locations using this dataset are also explored. Furthermore, we analyze the performance of different network configurations using multiple loss functions and evaluate the effectiveness of data augmentation techniques. Lastly, we evaluate our model's accuracy across different locations and environments, and demonstrate its reliability using test images depicting various sizes of road scenes. The code for this work is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/etehani/RoadWeatherClassification. The RFS dataset is also openly available at https://github.com/etehani/RoadWeatherFieldDataset. Additionally, the model pre-trained on ImageNet was used as the initial model for our Convolutional Neural Network configurations. The weighted class averaging technique was used for model evaluation and training. The proposed data augmentation approach utilized the SimpleLine segmentor to segment the road into areas before applying the mask during training. The count of super-pixel masks was set at 20, and the size of these masks was 50x50 pixels. The road color was defined as the range 140-220 in the HSV color model, and the threshold for pixel color was set at 0.05. The size of the region of interest in our images was approximately 300x200 pixels. The Convolutional Neural Network configuration comprising three convolutional layers with max pooling and two fully connected layers with dropout performed well on our dataset. A total of six models were trained and evaluated using this configuration, and the results were subsequently combined using class averaging to obtain the final result. The time taken to collect and annotate our dataset was approximately two months, and the time taken by our model to converge was around 12 hours on an NVIDIA 1080Ti graphics card. Our analysis examines how climate change interest shifts among diverse groups and how their individual interests interconnect. Initially, we track the individual trends, followed by developing a cross-influence model that we then validate using a VAR model. Our results indicate significant fluctuations in the general public's climate change interest, as evident from our creation of a Climate Change Index for Europe and the US based on media mentions, whereas economists show relatively little interest as measured by prominent journal publications. Interestingly, science journals and policymakers display a more stable interest in the subject, albeit with policymakers typically becoming interested somewhat later. Interestingly, the general public's interest peaks during contentious congressional hearings, whereas policymakers' interest peaks shortly before, suggesting a disconnect between the public and policymakers. Furthermore, we find that science journals and economists are influenced by the former, but not vice versa. Additionally, we develop an interactive model depicting the complex dynamics among these groups and identify key climate change-related periods, such as the publication of the IPCC first assessment report and the introduction of carbon pricing mechanisms, which are marked by significant shifts in group interests. Our analysis suggests that public interest is sparked by visible, high-profile events, while policymakers tend to become interested in climate change after such incidents. Conversely, scientists continue to pursue their established research lines, only later (if at all) adapting their focus in line with the prevailing societal expectations. Lastly, policymakers appear to require external triggers, such as international cooperation or financial incentives, to develop a sustained interest in climate change governance. Ultimately, our findings provide insights into how to effectively communicate climate change science to policymakers and the broader public, underscoring the significance of timing in shaping policy through a well-crafted strategic climate change science and policy strategy. Additionally, our results imply that policy initiatives, such as carbon pricing, are more likely to succeed if accompanied by concurrent public engagement efforts. Finally, our analysis suggests that a greater focus on climate change science, coupled with enhanced public engagement and a more dynamic approach to policymaking, could boost the overall priority afforded to climate change issues. It remains to be seen whether our findings are universally indicative of continued inter-group dynamics or if they represent an enduring state. Nonetheless, our model can readily be adapted to analyze future group interactions and identify potential long-term patterns. Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their versatility and flexibility, yet accurately modeling and controlling them to grasp objects efficiently remains challenging. Soft grippers' infinite-dimensionality and non-linearity make traditional control approaches difficult to implement. In response, researchers have turned to data-driven methods. However, these methods typically require extensive model learning through simulations or offline processes, which often fails to adapt to novel scenarios or real-time physical robot control requirements. In this research, we propose an innovative online algorithm that uses the spectral analysis of the Koopman operator to approximate the dynamics of soft grippers. Spectral decompositions can provide insights into controllability and observability properties. By applying these insights, we demonstrate that a single spectral decomposition-based model can effectively control and track various trajectories of multi-fingered soft grippers, even in the presence of significant model errors. Through physical robot experiments, we also validate the efficacy of our data-driven approach, demonstrating precise trajectory tracking and grasping of diverse objects using the proposed algorithm. This work is pioneering in utilizing the Koopman operator theory for online model reduction in the control of soft robotic systems. Furthermore, it opens up new avenues for soft robotic control to tackle the inherent complexities in modeling and control processes. This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients, which, despite significant progress in recent years, still lacks effective solutions. Current methods, both traditional and deep learning-based, primarily rely on single-textual sources such as patient demographics and clinical history. Unlike existing approaches, this study explores the potential of combining multiple data types like text-based clinical information and visual medical scans to inform survival time predictions, simulating the decision-making process of a medical professional. Building upon this insight, this work introduces the Lite-ProSENet model, which integrates multiple data modalities within a prognostic survival time learning framework and exhibits superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods, showcasing 3-4 fold improvements in accuracy, 2-4 fold improvements in regression metrics, and 1.5-2.5 fold improvements in model generalizability. Furthermore, the findings highlight the model's medical validity, showcasing a high correlation between predicted survival times and actual observed durations. Moreover, the study illustrates the model's practical value in identifying crucial clinical and visual features that contribute to patient survival, which can guide clinicians in making more informed decisions. Finally, the work introduces a publicly available lung cancer dataset, Clin-ProSE, featuring 1,112 lung cancer patients with associated medical scan data, making it accessible for research purposes. The proposed model, along with the associated code and dataset, can be accessed at https://github.com/alaidyprose/Lite-ProSENet. Additionally, the prognostic survival time models have been deployed on an interactive website at https://prose-cid.github.io/. Experimental findings can also be found on the prognostic survival time analysis platform, PSG-A at https://psg-a.github.io/. This work was supported by P30CA016536 from the NCI. Researchers have addressed this issue through various techniques, combining either syntactic or semantic analysis in the past. However, individually, these methods often fail to yield practical results in real-world applications. For instance, latent semantic analysis can capture semantic text characteristics, yet it disregards syntactic constraints when generating word suggestions. In contrast, more advanced models like Deep Learning integrate both approaches to achieve impressive outcomes. While these models can be computationally demanding, hindering their feasibility in certain scenarios, continuous advancements in technology and mathematical modeling enable the development of faster, more accurate systems. Additionally, this model can be applied in other domains as a knowledge retrieval model. The proposed model was evaluated and compared with other models in the same challenge. The results indicate that this model, although relatively simple in design, can offer better performance and more efficient computation compared to more sophisticated Deep Learning models. Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to be an authoritative reference on various topics.  However, due to a limited number of editors and a vast amount of articles, only 0.6% are considered of high quality according to their established criteria. To enhance article quality through machine learning, we must first label individual sentences as high or low quality, yet this process relies on human annotations that are time-consuming and often yield inaccuracies. To resolve this, we developed an automated system that examines semantic modifications in Wikipedia edits to create labels, considering the pre-edit version as an example requiring improvement, and high-quality sentences as instances that need no improvement. By employing our labels in machine learning models, we found that performance improves over relying on existing, manually created labels. Furthermore, we discovered that Wikipedia editors' behavior provides more accurate labels compared to crowdworkers who lack the same level of contextual understanding and agreement as Wikipedia editors. The proposed solution has the potential to significantly reduce the costs associated with labeling data and, using a trained model, provide an alternative to manual labeling that is both effective and efficient. To facilitate the reuse of our findings and the development of similar methods, we make our code, data, and results publicly available. We also introduce "WikiLQ", a publicly accessible web interface for generating high-quality labels based on our algorithm. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, a novel approach that trains a model to accurately replicate another network's decisions without accessing its training information, simply requiring input-output responses. Notably, our proposed method can achieve performance comparable to traditional knowledge distillation methods in certain scenarios, and even surpass them in certain high-risk scenarios. The associated code can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/hjdw2/DB3KD. Additionally, an IPython notebook for generating the supplementary figures is located at https://github.com/hjdw2/DB3KD/blob/5c4f8f3c/extra.ipynb. Lastly, the associated data can be found at https://doi.org/10.6086/M114-22-1.1.

The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces encompassing torus bundles, nilmanifolds, and other examples from string theory. This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. The proposed metric leverages polarization properties and accurately determines the minimum number of bits needed to determine the start of a binary path on a trellis diagram with high confidence. As a result, it enables average computation reductions of more than two orders of magnitude for some polarization-adjusted convolutional codes under tight target error rates. Furthermore, the proposed metric allows for average computation reductions of more than one order of magnitude in successive cancellation decoding for some polar codes under a specific polarization transform. Importantly, the proposed metric does not rely on pre-computed polarization profiles and can be easily extended for multi-dimensional paths. Moreover, it maintains a low non-zero error rate in case paths are heavily imbalanced. Experimental results confirm its excellent performance compared to existing methods. An open-source implementation is also provided to verify its efficacy. Moreover, a novel technique is proposed to generate PAC codes based on the polarization transform approach. Some PAC codes generated through this approach match or exceed the performance of leading codes in their respective rate-and-length regimes. The proposed PAC codes, along with associated profiles and implementation details, are publicly available on a GitHub repository. Moreover, the proposed metric is compatible with existing polar code tools and can be used to enhance their performance. Experimental results confirm its exceptional performance compared to standard tools. Lastly, the proposed PAC codes exhibit superior performance when combined with existing techniques in the literature. Some PAC codes even match or exceed the performance of the best known codes in their respective regimes when combined with existing techniques. However, combining the proposed PAC codes with existing techniques does not significantly affect their already superior performance. Finally, the proposed metric can potentially be extended to other code types due to its generalizability. Some code types, such as LC-LNGC codes, naturally benefit from the proposed metric with high performance gains in decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance. Moreover, the proposed metric can potentially be applied to other code types after some modifications. Furthermore, the LC-LNDC code type, which is related to LC-LNGC codes, also benefits from the proposed metric with high computation reductions and superior error-correction performance. This project tackles the complex problem of simultaneously monitoring the positions and shapes of hands and objects in a sequence of depth point cloud data, starting from the known poses in the initial frame. To achieve this, we introduce a network called HandTrackNet, the first point cloud-based hand joint tracking system, to calculate hand joint movement between frames. Furthermore, we develop a module called HandShapeNet to forecast hand shape based on the movement of hand joints. Since actual ground truth point cloud sequences for training are scarce, we create synthetic point cloud sequences through a proposed generation method, called SEM Generation, which applies a physical-based hand and object renderer using Spherical Trigonometry. Additionally, we release a new benchmark, called HOHI-Benchmark, consisting of a large dataset of real-hand pose annotations, making it accessible for research. Through extensive experiments on a challenging real-hand and real-object sequence dataset, our method demonstrates superior performance over current state-of-the-art hand pose and shape prediction methods, showcasing its ability to handle various hand and object poses, as well as complex hand shapes and poses. The proposed framework achieves a high overall Mean Absolute Three-Dimensional Error (MATDE) of 3.97, outperforming the best alternative method with a 0.48 error margin. As a result, our method successfully predicts both hand movement (with a Small Motion Error rate of 2.81) and hand shape (with a Shape Error rate of 13.14%). Crucially, our method successfully forecasts both hand movement and hand shape for a wide range of hand and object interaction scenarios, including various hand shapes, as well as object movements and hand oxide interactions. We've observed the appearance of field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a weakly coupled, spin-1/2 Heisenberg material called [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2. Due to its moderate exchange coupling of about 6.8 Kelvin, the application of laboratory magnetic fields produces a noticeable anisotropy of the spin correlations in an XY plane. This significant BKT regime develops because of a weak interlayer exchange of about one millikelvin that causes 3D correlations as the critical temperature is approached, resulting in an exponential increase in spin-correlation length. Nuclear magnetic resonance, muon spin resonance measurements and quantum Monte Carlo simulations using the experimentally determined parameters are employed to determine the critical temperatures associated with BKT transitions as well as long-range order. Finite-size scaling of the spin stiffness shows that the long-range order has not yet been fully achieved even near the critical temperature of long-range order which is about 0.83 Tesla. This study optimizes the execution time of established algorithms for classically simulating quantum circuits comprising Clifford and T gates. The efficiency improvement stems from deriving a novel upper limit for the number of stabilizer states required to express $m$ copies of the magic state, $|T\rangle$. The findings reveal that a superposition of no more than $O(2^{\alpha m})$ stabilizer states can accurately represent $|T\rangle^{\otimes m}$, where $\alpha\leq 0.3963$, surpassing the previous best-known estimate of $\alpha\leq 0.463$. This advancement allows for the development of a classical algorithm for simulating $n$-qubit Clifford + T circuits using a binary decision tree of depth $O(m\log(n)/\log(\alpha))$, thereby leading to a linear reduction in time complexity compared to the best-known previous approach, which had a time complexity of $O(m\log(n)/\log(1/\alpha))$. Furthermore, the generated stabilizer programs are also utilized in the construction of quantum algorithms for maximum matching and independent set problems in graphs, which exhibit a best-known $O(\sqrt{N}\log(N))$ running time rather than the $O(N\log N)$ of prior methods. The proposed method is built upon a recently proposed approach for converting stabilizer programs to linear programs, with substantial modifications to optimize its upper bound on the stabilizer rank. Additionally, a detailed analysis is provided to establish a lower bound on the efficient complexity of the magic state, demonstrating that its simulation using $n$ qubits and $poly(\log n)$ gates is beyond the capabilities of current known quantum technology. Lastly, the findings are supplemented by presenting a recently designed efficient quantum algorithm for solving circuit satisfiability, a problem which is believed to be insoluble with $n\geq 167$ qubits, but can be solved efficiently with the proposed method using a reduced number of qubits. The paper concludes by outlining future research avenues to explore the previously mentioned lower bound on the efficient complexity of the magic state. The work presents two novel concepts: the entanglement entropy of a quantum state as a measure of its computational efficiency and the entanglement asymmetry, a statistic that effectively differentiates between useful and useless quantum states for solving specific computational problems. These ideas originate from the connection between the quantum entropy and asymmetry and various information-theoretic concepts, such as mutual information and Kolmogorov complexity.

As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-based TRNGs suffer from reduced throughput, elevated energy expenditure, prolonged latency, and a limitation to generating random numbers continuously. In order to overcome these shortcomings, this paper presents an SRAM-based TRNG that can sustain long periods of operation. The proposed TuRaN approach utilizes a lower supply voltage than recommended to cause SRAM access failures, which are then used to generate random numbers. TuRaN achieves its high throughput of 4 bytes per cycle, coupled with a competitive energy consumption of 20 pJ/byte and a latency of 0.2 microseconds, at the expense of a reduced confidence level in randomness compared to prior SRAM-based TRNGs. TuRaN is implemented on both an FPGA and a mobile processor using 28nm SD SoC technology. Furthermore, the experimental results of evaluating TuRaN's properties have demonstrated its capability to pass standard statistical tests for randomness, including the NIST SRD v1.0.3 tests and the DieHard3.2 tests. In summary, the proposed TuRaN approach provides the highest throughput of any SRAM-based TRNG design to date. A comparison of TuRaN's performance characteristics with previously proposed SRAM-based TRNGs is presented in Table I. As a result, TuRaN is well-suited for applications requiring a high throughput of random numbers. However, due to its relatively low confidence level in randomness, TuRaN may not be suitable for the most critical security-critical applications. A preliminary design and simulation of a single-electron resistive switch has been developed, incorporating two linear molecules that interact electrostatically: one molecule is a single-electron transistor and the other is a single-electron trap. To confirm our design's validity, a theoretical analysis was performed using ab-initio path-integral molecular dynamics and electronic structure calculations, revealing that these molecules can exhibit significant charge redistribution at the molecular level in response to an external electric field. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the trap molecule can activate the transistor molecule to switch from a high-resistance to a low-resistance state. Additionally, our simulations indicate that both the trap and transistor molecules can act as a nonvolatile memory element with a stable high-resistance state and a low-resistance state that can be triggered by the trap molecule. Our study also suggests that these molecules can be integrated into a nanowire or thin-film device for an efficient nonvolatile memory operation. Considering the promising results from our theoretical analysis, it is anticipated that these single-electron resistive switches can serve as a foundation for developing next-generation nanoscale nonvolatile memory devices. Firstly, large-scale experimental verification of our theoretical predictions is necessary to confirm the underlying physical mechanisms governing the behavior of these molecular single-electron resistive switches. Secondly, various simulations, such as the multiple-time scale rate equation model, can be conducted to provide a more detailed insight into the dynamics of these molecular single-electron resistive switches and potentially identify potential pathways for further optimization. Given the significant advantages of these molecular single-electron resistive switches over existing flash and spin-transfer torque magnetic tunnel junction-based nonvolatile memory technologies in terms of scalability, our work is expected to contribute positively to the development of future nanoscale memory devices. Finally, it is noted that even though these single-electron resistive switches have the potential to be developed and become a reality, they may not be suitable for widespread commercial applications due to their single-electron-based mechanism, which implies a limited number of charge tunings (typically less than 256), which may not be sufficient for many practical nonvolatile memory requirements. However, they can serve as an efficient building block for developing single-electron-based resistive switch-based hybrid CMOS/nMOS integrated circuits where a small number of charge tunings are sufficient. Our study suggests that these single-electron resistive switches can provide a fundamental mechanism for developing efficient single-electron-based resistive switch-based integrated circuits with a high scalability, high data retention, high read-out reliability, high programming endurance

A multi-loop Feynman integral can be numerically evaluated using a random momentum configuration, however the numerical stability largely depends on the choice of momentum. 

In this thesis, a theoretical framework for analysing multi-loop Feynman integrals is established using a causal representation which is known for its numerical stability. 

The evaluation is achieved through the combination of two methods: an extension of the standard integration technique using a d-dimensional space and the causal representation, and a loop-tree duality approach.

Two numerical implementations have been developed which demonstrate the numerical stability of the causal representation. 

Furthermore, this thesis delves into the connection between the causal representation and anti-causal representation and explores design elements that can enhance the numerical stability of integral evaluation methods. 

A detailed analysis has been conducted to evaluate the numerical stability of several Feynman integral examples using various techniques including topological expansion and differential reduction. 

The results have also been compared with the well-established Lee-Pomerancik framework. 

Two numerical codes incorporating the causal representation and anti-causal representation have been written and released under an open-source license. 

These codes, known as Celestial and Stellar, have been used to evaluate a range of Feynman integrals to high precision. 

The thesis concludes by examining future development possibilities for both algorithms and suggests several potential research areas including the application of Feynman integral evaluation to particle physics problems, the integration of Feynman integral results into publicly available software packages and the exploration of new techniques to improve numerical stability.

This study investigates the effects of information dissemination on cryptocurrency markets. Firstly, a cryptocurrency trading network is defined by employing cryptocurrencies as nodes and weekly log returns linked via Granger causality. The analysis traces its development over time, focusing on years 2020 and 2021. The logarithmic US dollar price returns of this network are examined using Granger causality and O-information to quantify both pairwise and high-order statistical relationships. The Granger causality results indicate significant events during 2020 and 2021, including the 'Memorial Coin' event in April 2020, and various other episodes, that boosted cryptocurrency values. The event-related analysis reveals a high correlation (0.9146) between the strength of events and their financial impact, implying a strong information dissemination effect on cryptocurrency markets. The focus then shifts to high-order relationships in the network. By calculating O-information for all possible paths of up to four nodes, the analysis reveals a high degree of non-pairwise information dissemination among cryptocurrencies, suggesting a high level of complexity in the cryptocurrency trading market. The central node analysis identifies Ethereum as the most influential cryptocurrency in the network. Finally, an event-related study on entropy in the cryptocurrency trading network shows a significant (p-value < 0.001) relationship between entropy and financial performance, indicating that an information-based approach can provide valuable insights into cryptocurrency market dynamics. The findings of this study offer novel perspectives on the non-pairwise information dissemination effect and the practical applications of Granger causality and O-information analyses in cryptocurrency trading markets. The results can be useful to cryptocurrency exchange operators, market analysts, and investors seeking to gain valuable insights into the logical connections among cryptocurrencies and their subsequent financial impact. The formation of particles from trace gases is a crucial source of cloud condensation nuclei that facilitate the creation of clouds due to their role in overcoming extremely high supersaturated conditions needed for homogeneous water droplet formation. The application of quantum chemistry in modeling this process has improved the prediction accuracy for specific systems, particularly those involving the dimerization of sulphuric acid and water. The current study analyzes the impact of incorporating the zero-point motion energy into the classical potential energy surface. The results indicate that incorporating the zero-point motion energy leads to an approximately 15% decrease in the critical supersaturated condition for water dimerization and a 30% decrease for sulphuric acid dimers. Furthermore, the quantum-based approach is found to be more accurate in modeling the growth rates of sulphuric acid clusters up to a size of six. The findings suggest that the utilization of quantum-based structures in modeling the growth of small clusters is essential and the incorporation of zero-point energies has a significant effect on determining the energetic requirements for these systems. The results have been published in a research paper that also delves into the systematic development of a potential energy surface for sulphuric acid and water systems through the comprehensive calculation of quantum potential energy surfaces. The study also explores the significance of utilizing an ab initio-based Hamiltonian for modeling the dynamics of small sulphuric acid and water clusters. The way solids respond to temperature gradients can be understood by likening it to gravity's effect in space. In studying this, researchers investigate whether this analogy accurately describes the collective behavior of quantum Hall states and other chiral topological systems. By analyzing the Haldane model, which simulates different environmental conditions, they examine the consequences of two scenarios: one with variable gravity and electrostatic forces, and another with variable temperature and chemical potential resulting from interactions with surrounding electrons and phonons. The study reveals that this thermal analogy does not hold; while an uneven gravitational force induces specific energy flows, a comparable uneven temperature has little to no effect in systems that exchange energy with their surroundings weakly. Additionally, the similarity between an external electric charge and the system's internal energy is not valid under these circumstances. However, the similarity between an external magnetic field and the system's internal chemical potential is not fully invalidated, yet is significantly altered by the system's interaction with its surroundings. Furthermore, the similarity between a temperature gradient and an external force, which was thought to be a fundamental property, is not present in all situations. Based on these findings, the assumption that a system in partial filling will always be in thermal equilibrium with its surrounding electrons and phonons is invalid when the system's interaction with its surroundings is weak. The resulting flow of heat in chiral topological systems is more complex and dependent on various factors than previously thought. The violation of this thermal analogy could lead to discoveries of new effects that can be observed in quantum Hall systems, which could serve as a gateway to understanding unusual phenomena in more complex systems that exhibit a high degree of interaction with their surroundings. The study also proposes an approach that can be used to study the collective behavior of quantum Hall states and other chiral topological systems by comparing their behavior to well-studied systems in space. The Haldane model, which was used in the study, represents a highly isolated electron system in a specific two-dimensional material that is in close contact with electron and phonon reservoirs that can interact with it. The violation of this thermal analogy could be observed in other scenarios, such as weakly coupled graphene or pormanganite, by studying their response to temperature gradients. The resulting heat flow could be measured using local heat transfer or a scanning thermal microscope. For deep learning models, understanding how complexity is controlled has been a challenging task, given that many conventional methods are unsuitable for their inherent complexity. Our research introduces a concept called geometric complexity, quantifying the variability of model functions using a discrete Dirichlet energy metric. A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel method outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination techniques, particularly in the case of $q^2$-dependent Wilson coefficient $C_7$. It also enables simultaneous extraction of the Wilson coefficients of the $b\to s\mu^+\mu^-$ effective operator, previously studied by the BABAR and BELLE collaborations, within a likelihood analysis. Based on this method, the sensitivity of the $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays to $C_7(q^2)$ can be increased by about 30% through the use of the Wilson coefficient $R_6$ provided by QCD factorization. This improved approach is applicable to various $B$ meson decays into a vector and two leptons. Furthermore, it is feasible at the upcoming Belle II experiment to achieve a precision of $\sigma[2\times10^{-9},0\times10^{-9}]$ for the $C_7(q^2)$ Wilson coefficient with $4000$ $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays. With $5000$ $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ events and $4000$ $B^+\to K^{*+}\mu^+\mu^-$ events, the Belle II experiment can even achieve a precision of $\sigma[2.3\times10^{-9},0.4\times10^{-9}]$ for the $C_7(q^2)$ Wilson coefficient. This could serve as a crucial standard for measuring heavy quark masses, particularly for the bottom quark, as well as testing its mass dependence within the standard model at a precision of $0.8\mathrm{\,MeV}$ ($0.3\mathrm{\,MeV}$) for the bottom (top) quark. Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  A key strategy for enhancing the accuracy of automated essay grading has been the application of machine learning techniques to automated essay grading.  However, due to the limitations in essay datasets, deep learning methods are often hindered by data shortages.  Consequently, researchers have been exploring various techniques to improve model performance through data augmentation.  Inspired by success in the same field with NLP tasks such as language modeling and sentiment analysis, we have employed a more sophisticated neural network, the Transformer, to explore its potential in automated essay grading and text classification tasks.  We have applied a range of data augmentation techniques including the simplification of existing approaches and the introduction of two never-before-seen methods.  Through our experiments on two datasets, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of our data augmentation techniques led to an enhancement of the state-of-the-art performance in both tasks.  Additionally, we have introduced and made available two new data augmentation techniques along with the accompanying code at this link https://github.com/Orion-7/AEAST.  We expect these augmentations to be useful to the NLP community in similar applications.  Furthermore, we have shown the correctness of our augmentation techniques through both human and automated evaluations.  We have also successfully applied our model to a real-world dataset of essays from the SAT subject test.  The results from this application further underscore the effectiveness of our data augmentation techniques.  Lastly, we have conducted an ablation study to analyze the contribution of each technique, further validating the validity of our data augmentation techniques.  The outcome of our research has led to a notable enhancement in the performance of automated essay grading in two areas and the introduction of two new data augmentation techniques that can be utilized by the NLP community.  We have also successfully applied our model to a real-world dataset of essays from the SAT subject test.  The results from this application further validate the effectiveness of our data augmentation techniques.  Additionally, we have conducted an ablation study to analyze the contribution of each technique, further validating the validity of our data augmentation techniques.  The results from these experiments have shown that our data augmentation techniques are generalizable and can be effectively utilized in a range of tasks.  We have also successfully applied our model to a real-world dataset of essays from the SAT subject test. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to particle exchange statistics in this context. Consequently, the conclusion that bosonic particles have integer spin and fermionic particles have half-integer spin follows naturally. This approach also yields a method for calculating spin based on parity for fermions, which can be used to estimate their spin. Ultimately, a historical review of spin and permutation calculations is provided, culminating in the conclusion that relativistic wave equations do not genuinely capture the connection between spin and permutation, which is apparent in the non-relativistic formalism. Rather, relativistic theories are consistent with this non-relativistic perception. Lastly, the implications of relativistic quantization methods that disregard parity and angular momentum entirely suggest that the distinction between fermions and bosons is solely a non-relativistic concept. As a result, the bosonic/fermionic classification may become obsolete in a fully relativistic theory, and the distinction between particle wavefunctions may lose its significance when relativistic effects are considered. Nevertheless, both relativistic and non-relativistic frameworks are compatible in this context. Lastly, the possibilities and challenges of experimenting on fermions with unknown spin are explored. We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through benchmarking analysis.
While Delegated RingCT may not possess the same level of anonymity compared to other RingCT implementations, we propose that its ability to be compatible with DPoS consensus mechanisms provides a reasonable trade-off for enabling a more efficient and scalable decentralised cryptocurrency with preserved anonymity capabilities. 
In contrast to previous RingCT-compatible DPoS schemes, Delegated RingCT effectively addresses privacy-related issues inherent in linkable ring signature protocols by preventing OP_CHECKDELEGATEPROP, a proposed Bitcoin opcode, from potentially compromising users' anonymity when employed in a DPoS setting. 
Ultimately, Delegated RingCT provides a practical solution for supporting DPoS-based decentralised cryptocurrencies with integrated transaction anonymity capabilities. 
Furthermore, we outline a strategy for the widespread adoption of Delegated RingCT, starting with its integration into a research-oriented cryptocurrency known as BCN and encouraging its further distribution among the cryptocurrency community. 
Finally, we suggest Delegated RingCT as a fundamental framework for supporting DPoS-based decentralised cryptocurrencies with integrated transaction anonymity capabilities, paving the way for its potential adoption in prominent cryptocurrencies such as Neo and BCN. 
In particular, we propose Delegated RingCT as a suitable replacement for Neo DCT, potentially facilitating its integration into this widely-used cryptocurrency. 
A comparative study between Delegated RingCT and previously proposed RingCT-compatible DPoS schemes is presented, showcasing the anonymity and computational efficiency capabilities of each scheme for a sample set of delegates.

Our findings build on work by Kyng and Zhang who previously made similar discoveries in terms of time complexity, utilizing reductions between approximate solvers; our own proof demonstrates that these reductions can be implemented using threshold circuits with specific characteristics. Furthermore, our research shows that if solving linear systems in R^d can be done in near-logarithmic space, this capability can also be leveraged to solve approximate linear programming problems within a similar space complexity. These solutions rely on a concept we call "structured linear systems," which include work by Tardos and are also explored in the study of approximate fixed-point theorems by Feige, Vazirani, and Vazirani. Our research further reveals that if near-logarithmic space complexity solvers for linear systems exist, this capability can also be utilized to design a feasible and efficient approximate fixed-point theorem, addressing a challenge posed by Feige, Vazirani, and Vazirani. Our findings can be applied to space-bounded XAP (generalized assignment problem) with key parameters including the geometric growth rate of costs and the reciprocal of the demand's maximum multiplicity. Lastly, our research exhibits the direct relationship between solving certain linear systems and applying reduction methods, showing that a previously established time complexity bound can be translated into a space complexity bound, and finally, our research reveals an approximate fixed-point theorem for a specific instance of space-bounded XAP with limited geometric growth rate constraints.

Previous Hebrew NLP initiatives focused primarily on Modern Hebrew, disregarding its rich history and cultural significance. This research introduces the Hebrew Treebank (HTB), creating the first-ever UD-annotated collection of traditional Hebrew texts, spanning from the 12th century to the present day. HTB incorporates an innovative approach to identifying sentence boundaries, utilizing a lexically-driven method that enhances traditional syntactic analysis. This new approach is crucial for enhancing the understanding of Hebrew texts. The project's benefits extend to Hebrew NLP, enabling the inclusion of Hebrew in the UD framework and paving the way for advanced linguistic studies, such as corpus-based linguistic research, and facilitating comparisons with other languages, including Arabic and Yiddish. This work also evaluates state-of-the-art parsing models using various training and testing sets, including HTB. The results demonstrate that with sufficient data, current parsing models can effectively analyze Hebrew texts. Unfortunately, due to funding constraints, the HTB project has come to a halt, threatening the future of Hebrew NLP and UD-annotated Hebrew text analysis. This study serves as a model for future initiatives focused on traditional Hebrew and other underrepresented languages, emphasizing the significance of combining cutting-edge NLP technology and UD-based linguistic studies. The LST toolkit is designed to be versatile, applicable to a wide range of languages and UD frameworks. The website also features a comprehensive guide to the LST toolkit, as well as the HTB data set, which includes annotated texts, instruction manuals, and programming code (available under the CC-BY license). The site includes a section dedicated to LST-based parsing in other languages, including Arabic and Yiddish. These resources are intended to facilitate the creation of additional UD-annotated Hebrew text analysis initiatives.
