Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. Our analysis compares the proposed model to existing hierarchical models and highlights its superior performance and efficiency. In particular, HDTM exhibits a significant enhancement of 84.5% and 94.4% in its retrieved topics and subtopics accuracy, respectively, over the current state-of-the-art model, while simultaneously requiring only 5.9% of the previous model's computational resources. Our model is designed with scalability in mind and is suitable for a variety of application domains, including information retrieval, search engines, and content navigation platforms. In addition, we have also developed a set of tools to facilitate the utilization of our model in web-based applications, comprising a package to automatically extract and map topics and subtopics from large networks, as well as a visualization interface that allows users to navigate the retrieved hierarchies and configure them according to their specific needs. The proposed model, tools, and relevant data are made available under a free, open-license model to facilitate the replication and advancement of our research findings. In particular, the model consists of three datasets: (1) regular hierarchical models, modeling topics and subtopics as distinct components of the underlying network, (2) flat models, combining topics and subtopics into a single layer, and (3) topic-cooccurrence models, (all formerly known as "Document Topic Model" or "DTM"). The model consists of three variants: HDTM-R, HDTM-T, and HDTM-S, which differ in their network regularization, time-based topic evolution, and sample-size selection strategies, respectively. The proposed model offers a notable improvement over the traditional models in both regular hierarchical and flat configurations. We conducted an exhaustive examination comparing the statistical properties of non-hierarchical three-body systems with corresponding theoretical models. By running and analyzing one million simulations for diverse initial conditions, both with and without equal masses in three-body systems, we were able to achieve precise statistical accuracy. Four distinct measures were used to characterize the distribution of ergodic disintegrations: the probability of escape for individual bodies, the exponent representing narrow escapes, the predicted absorption as a function of binary energy and angular momentum, and the distribution of lifetimes. Our results showed that escape probabilities matched theoretical predictions with high precision, marking a significant improvement over previous statistical theories. Furthermore, the measured values of the exponent near marginally unbound escape thresholds agreed well with an independent, flux-based prediction. Both findings support the flux-based three-body statistical framework, and our measurements of absorptivity and lifetime distributions provide valuable resources for further testing and validation of statistical models. Ultimately, these findings open the door for a similar statistical approach to more complex n-body systems. The fully documented code used for these simulations is publicly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/AleksandarRuzelika/ThreeBodyStatisticalTools. Additionally, the binary parameters' absorption surface was also made available in an open-access database https://3bs.statisticaltools.top. This database can be accessed at https://github.com/AleksandarRuzelika/ThreeBodyStatisticalTools/blob/main/db.js. It is planned to be replaced with a more scalable database interface in the near future. Mature versions of this research will be published on the arXiv platform. Specifically, a paper detailing the measurement of escape probabilities will be published at https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.12557 and a paper on the fully developed statistical model will be published at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.07812. We propose an arrangement of predicates in continuous logic such that the
logical framework's meaning can be structured within a hyperdoctrine framework.
This hyperdoctrine can be incorporated into a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects within a suitable category of topological structures. 
To achieve this incorporation, we first simplify the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic and establish an equivalence between its category of equivalence relations and that of complete metric spaces under uniform mappings. 
Next, we define a suitable category of topological structures, incorporating the simplified hyperdoctrine framework's properties, and structure it such that the subobjects in this category form a hyperdoctrine equivalent to the one representing continuous logic. 
Consequently, we can determine a topological meaning for continuous logic sentences by examining their relation to subobjects in this category. 
Moreover, we define a subcategory comprising topological structures with continuous uniform structures and demonstrate that its subobjects form a hyperdoctrine framework that can be used to assign a topological meaning to sentences in continuous logic. 
Finally, we describe a topological structure on the space of continuous functions between two metric spaces, showing that its subobjects form a hyperdoctrine framework that can be used to topologically interpret continuous logic sentences. 
In particular, we find that the topological structure on the space of continuous functions between two metric spaces is equivalent to the one comprising closed subsets, where equivalence is understood as a 1-category morphism that is fully faithful and conservatively interprets. 
This result is accompanied by a proof that the topological structure on the space of continuous functions between two metric spaces does not have a geometric representation. 
Lastly, we propose an abstract approach to assigning a topological meaning to sentences in continuous logic, incorporating feedback from the Frege-Büchi collapse and the Priestley valuation theorem. 
This approach can be applied to various other logics, as illustrated by its application to continuous first-order logic. 
Finally, we outline a possible research path to establish a topological structure for categorical logic. 
Caveats and potential issues with our logic framework are also addressed. 
In particular, we monitor the overlap between the space of continuous functions and the space of measurable functions. 
This note is accompanied by a series of lectures on the topological structure of continuous logic.

A new technique is proposed to forecast suicidal ideation based on the integration of Electronic Health Records and Ecological Momentary Assessment data utilizing advanced deep sequential models. These datasets consist of asynchronous, variable-length, randomly sampled sequences which are modelled separately using Recurrent Neural Networks and combined through the alignment of hidden states, along with attention and pre-training schemes to capture temporal patterns in EHR data and account for varying sequence lengths. We examined over 8,000 massive, edge-on disk galaxies from the SDSS dataset, focusing on two types: S and U galaxies. U galaxies, particularly those with more extreme warping, exhibited higher star formation rates. Contrary to expectations, U galaxies in groups and clusters do not show a correlation with the tidal force exerted by their nearest neighbor. However, U galaxies are more common in groups and clusters and share similarities with 'jellyfish' galaxies formed through ram-pressure stripping (RPS). This led us to suggest that RPS could be a potential mechanism explaining the presence of U galaxies in groups and clusters. Additionally, we found that U galaxies are more common in groups dominated by a large elliptical galaxy, and observed U galaxies tend to have brighter wings and higher surface brightness compared to isolated galaxies. Our study also found that U galaxies have a higher fraction of HII regions and brighter star formation lanes in their disks. Further investigation is needed to elucidate the exact causes behind the unique features of U galaxies. Conclusion stability is calculated as the number of consistent conclusions among a set of labels divided by the total number of labels, considering both the original labels and those derived through transformation. This metric accounts for potential biases in the original labels and their variations. Conclusion stability is initially demonstrated on a dataset of mining design discussions, after which it is applied to a dataset of online mining discussion comments. The results show that using transformation to generate new labels can increase the consistency of those labels and make them more stable. When conclusion stability was applied to a dataset of mining design discussions, it yielded a consistent outcome. Conversely, the results were inconsistent when it was applied to a dataset of online mining discussion comments. Ultimately, the proposed conclusion stability metric provides a reliable method for evaluating the consistency of design-related discussions, as well as their interactions. It also sheds light on the characteristics of online discussion comments, revealing that their conversations are a double-edged sword, offering both beneficial and detrimental design conclusions. Consequently, the proposed stability metric can serve as a useful evaluation method for human-robot interaction discussions, as they appear to be a mixed bag. Moreover, the proposed stability metric can facilitate the creation of automated mining tools for code, as well as natural language, by providing a reliable means of evaluating their conclusions. Finally, the proposed stability metric can assist in building automated mining tools for design, as well as natural language, by offering a trustworthy means of evaluating their conclusions. Proximal methods can efficiently uncover the underlying pattern in nonsmooth optimization problems, and, in many cases, identifying this structure is a free byproduct, also enhancing the convergence rate once aligned with that of the problem's optimal solution. Nonetheless, pinpointing the exact structure is not possible without adaptation. By assuming a proximal gradient method is able to recognize the differentiability manifolds in a nonsmooth objective, we show that incorporating Riemannian Newton-like techniques alongside the proximal gradient steps results in a significantly improved convergence rate for specific nondegenerated nonsmooth nonconvex optimization problems. Moreover, our algorithm is accompanied by a numerical study that includes optimizations regulated by $\ell_1$-norm and trace-norm. Despite the theoretical restrictions to nondegenerated problems, our numerical results indicate the efficacy of this hybrid approach for various problems involving degenerate objectives. Furthermore, the introduction of an adaptive procedure for estimating the nondegeneracy of a problem allows for the application of our developed method to a wide range of objectives. The presented methodology is further exemplified through its application to key problems in machine learning, including sparse PCA, NMF, and model order selection in system identification. The associated code is available under the MIT License at https://github.com/pfuster/proximal-manifolds. This work was initially presented at the 22nd International Conference on Artificial Neural Networks (ICANN 2022).

A prime ideal $I$ in a ring $R$ is said to be weakly $1$-absorbing if for every three non-unit elements $a,b,$ and $c$ in $R$ where their product is non-zero and within $I$, it follows that either the product of $a$ and $b$ is in $I$, or $c$ is in $I$. Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing a photonic device with an inherent frequency-dependent delay, replacing the conventional dispersion solution. As a result, our device can handle high signal inputs without the need for intense lasers, making it an innovative solution for spectroscopic tasks. Additionally, we improved the technique known as Massive Spectral Mapping, making it possible to conduct high-resolution spectroscopy on vast stellar databases within a shorter time frame. This was accomplished by utilizing our astophotonic device and combining it with techniques like spectral image inversion and machine learning. Utilizing a 16-element photonic device, we successfully mapped the spectral lines of over 70,000 stars within a few hours, showcasing the impressive capabilities of our innovative photonic design. This technology has immense potential for integrating photonic devices with cutting-edge data analysis methods to accelerate various scientific applications. It is an extensively multipurpose tool that may find numerous applications across diverse fields, ultimately facilitating groundbreaking discoveries in astronomy and beyond. This technological advancement may also pave the way for incorporating photonic devices in fields such as medicine, defense, and environmental studies to address critical challenges in those domains. Specifically, we believe that astophotonic devices can be utilized for observing extremely distant supernovae, conducting global CO2 gas analysis, and developing an automatic pandemic surveillance system by detecting the chromatic properties of certain species. By harnessing the power of photonic research, we can accelerate various applications and achieve groundbreaking outcomes that benefit society in meaningful ways. This novel approach can also spur the development of new, innovative photonic designs that require minimal costly infrastructure and can be customized to address a wide range of unique applications and research domains. Those seeking to explore the vast potential of photonic research can follow our lead and leverage advanced photonic technology, incorporating it with cutting-edge data analysis methods like machine learning and image processing, to tackle complex problems and accelerate various scientific tasks. This collaborative approach can yield novel solutions that facilitate groundbreaking outcomes in astronomy and other fields and enable the rapid deployment of photonic technology for real-world applications. Ultimately, we can expedite the global transition to astophotonic technology, empowering scientists to make data-driven decisions and initiate innovative projects that harness the advanced capabilities of photonic research. This way, we can leverage the capabilities of 21st-century technology to address fundamental problems in astronomy and other fields and promote the development of new, innovative photonic designs that foster rapid scientific progress

Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of creating optimal reward functions for agent training by utilizing expert behavior instead.  The challenge lies in environments that are modeled as Markov Decision Processes, and current imitation algorithms often rely on access to expert demonstrations within the exact same environment in which the imitation policy is to be learned.  However, when discrepancies arise between expert and agent domains due to varying dynamics, perspectives, or morphologies, imitation tasks become increasingly difficult.  This paper proposes a new framework that establishes correspondences across disparate domains using only unaligned trajectories containing states from the expert domain.  The framework leverages cycle-consistency constraints in both the state space and a domain-agnostic latent space to facilitate this correspondence.  Additionally, it ensures temporal alignment using a normalized position estimator.  Once the correspondence is established, the learned demonstrations can be directly transferred and applied to the target domain, empowering imitation.  The approach is validated through experiments across a diverse range of complex domains.  Notably, it achieves successful imitation in multiple domains without requiring any explicit access to the target domain.  It also surpasses state-of-the-art performance in both fully-observable and partially-observable domains, including those with high-dimensional observations.  The results can be found at https://mimil-epg.github.io/CIDO/.  The code can be found at https://github.com/mimil-epg/CIDO.  The videos can be found at https://mimil-epg.github.io/CIDO/videos.

A major uncertainty in determining the initial mass function of the first (Population III) stars hinges on the ultimate fate of secondary protostars that form in the accretion disk - whether they will merge or remain separate. We concentrate on how the initial star formation was established by employing a two-phase picture: initially, fragmentation of the protostar's disk generates multiple nascent stars with small masses, and subsequently, due to magnetic field amplification, the disk becomes unfragrant to small-mass objects. We derived an equation for the critical amplification level of the magnetic field that transitions from fragile to unfragrant and observed this critical level in our model based on the accretion disk's structure. We based our analysis on a two-dimensional simulation that combined both magnetohydrodynamics and mass accumulation processes. We discovered that the amplification of the magnetic field by mean-free-path processes or due to turbulence's assistance breaks the cycle of fragmentation, effectively ending it. Additionally, we found out that the initial protostar's mass is directly related to the initial binary separation in accordance with the white-dwarf cooling model, suggesting a binary initial mass function that conforms with the standard $d\mu/m_{\rm initial} \propto m_{\rm initial}^{-0.6}$ pattern in the 1-5 M$_{\odot}$ range, thus resolving the "mass-gap" issue, but possibly generating a "metallicity-gap" at higher Pop II stages. This research offers a valuable explanation for the effectiveness of the electron-conduction mechanism in the initial fragmentation stage due to its high coefficient that surpasses other processes. Moreover, we observed that the initial binary separation is directly related to the mean-free-path amplified magnetic field and note its universality across various initial mass ranges. Finally, although our model is grounded in a detailed simulation of a spatially three-dimensional, protostar accretion disk, our findings are applicable to a broader range of scenarios - even those that incorporate gravitational spreading and disk contraction. However, our model does not account for the pre-protostar cloud's magnetic field, which may significantly impact the initial binary separation in a contrasting manner. Consequently, our analysis suggests that a Pop III initial mass function with distinct components in the 1-2 M$_{\odot}$ and 2-100 M$_{\odot}$ ranges is necessary to resolve the metallicity anomaly between these objects and the subsequent Pop II stars. Ultimately, a comprehensive theoretical framework of the subsequent star formation process is required

Radio maps are being explored as a promising approach to equip advanced wireless networks with situational awareness. They will likely serve a pivotal function in enabling UAV communications by allowing the assessment of signal strength and interference levels at unknown locations. Different from conventional radio map estimation techniques, which depend on uncontrolled sensor measurements, a new method proposes that a UAV collect data at designated locations along a carefully planned route to quickly obtain a reliable map. This route is optimized using a measure that identifies the most informative locations to collect data from. A novel real-time Bayesian algorithm has been created to constantly update the map estimate and suggest the next data collection site. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of this approach, revealing that the proposed algorithm can achieve a reliable map estimate after collecting data from as few as 20% of the total grid points in a 2D environment. Moreover, it outperforms existing methods in terms of computational efficiency, uncertainty reduction, and time required to achieve a reliable map estimate. This research presents a thorough mathematical analysis of the proposed algorithm and validates its performance with extensive numerical simulations using a deep learning-based model of radio map formation. Additionally, the findings obtained from simulating a real-world urban outdoor scenario are presented. This research is expected to facilitate the development of rapidly obtainable, reliable maps using a single UAV. A demonstration video of the proposed approach is available at https://youtu.be/AAL_C1C1TmM. This paper outlines a novel approach, GLA, for identifying unusual patterns in discrete time series by leveraging Hidden Markov Models and clustering. The method generates significant outcomes under both artificial and real-world conditions, as demonstrated in the provided case studies. Additionally, we offer an open-source implementation of GLA via a Python package called anodidae. 

Key Considerations for Implementing GLA:

The choice of Hidden Markov Model type and its parameters significantly impact the performance of GLA. To aid in selecting these parameters, we provide an analytical method and numerous test cases within anodidae. 

In real-world settings, particularly when dealing with large datasets, processing GLA becomes computationally intensive. Anodidae includes an optimized version, called Hierarchical Gaussian Mixture Model, that addresses this performance issue and yields notable results under both artificial and real-world conditions. 

Ultimately, the effectiveness of GLA depends on a thorough understanding of the time series data, the underlying processes, and the desired outcomes. anodidae encompasses various techniques and algorithms to facilitate this comprehension, including the application of HMMs and GLA through an intuitive API. 

Case Studies:

We conducted two main investigations to validate anodidae's performance in identifying unusual patterns. 

  1. Artificial data: This study compared anodidae's Hierarchical Gaussian Mixture Model against alternative anomaly detection methods including AutoARMA, Local Outlier Factor, and One-Class SVM. The results showed that the cluster-based approach in anodidae outperformed these methods in accurately grouping artificial data and detecting anomalies.
  2. Real-world GPS data: The method successfully identified unusual patterns in a set of real GPS data provided by Fluke Transport, effectively clustering the data into logical groups and detecting unusual behavior. 

The anodidae package provides an open-source implementation of GLA, including the code for the method and the data used in the case studies.

This research delves into a multi-aspect approach to person verification incorporating auditory, visual, and thermal modalities. Given the efficacy of auditory and visual modality combination, this investigation extends to exploring the effect of incorporating thermal images on verification robustness. Specifically, state-of-the-art deep learning architectures were applied to establish unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal verification systems which were compared under optimal and impaired conditions. Moreover, a comparison of fusion methods using simple score aggregation and soft attention techniques was also conducted. Experimental results obtained on the SpeakingFaces dataset showed that a multi-aspect verification system outperforms unimodal and bimodal approaches by significant margins, both in noise-free and noise-present scenarios. To promote research in the area and guarantee replicability of this research, our source code, pre-trained models, and dataset preprocessed for analysis were made freely accessible on our GitHub repository. Additionally, an open-source demo for person verification has been uploaded to our IPython Notebook repository. It is hoped that these shared resources will contribute to the growth of research in multi-aspect person verification and enable researchers to build upon this work in novel ways. Currently, this research is limited by the scarcity of multi-modal person verification datasets, and a proposed fix involves developing extended versions of existing datasets. This work is expected to be updated with the latest research developments in the near future. A pre-print of this research has been published on arXiv, and we look forward to presenting the full research paper at an upcoming IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing (ICASSP). Lastly, this research would not have been possible without the support of our funding agency, the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council (NSERC) [grant number R250A3467045]. Additionally, we express our gratitude to SpeakingFaces dataset creators Dr. Massaoud Abdalla and Dr. Daniel Gatica-Pinot for their invaluable time in annotating the dataset, and SpeakingFaces students who assisted in data collection. One-sided differential privacy has become the standard for generating private databases, especially when dealing with channels. However, research has shown that depending on how the private database is created, significant privacy losses can occur, especially when there is a relationship among the attributes. In this study, we explored one-sided differential privacy's vulnerability to information leakage in cases where there are dependencies among attributes. Our results revealed that releasing a private database under the one-sided differential privacy framework can result in nearly complete information retrieval when there are dependencies among attributes. Based on this finding, we developed a new model called the dependent one-sided differential privacy model. It was discovered that any release of a database under this new model has at most $\log_2 (m+1)$ extra entropy loss compared to a release without any privacy constraints when there are $m$ possible values. Furthermore, we provided a method for creating private databases under this new model and demonstrated its tightness. Additionally, we explored the relationship between our model and existing ones such as the one-sided differential privacy model. Our results showed that there is a trade-off between the one-sided differential privacy model and our new model, with the latter offering tighter bounds when there are dependencies among attributes. The study also provided empirical evaluations of the tightness of our model and compared it with other existing models such as the state-of-the-art $q$-wise dependent one-sided differential privacy model. It was discovered that our model is more suitable when there are dependencies among attributes, while the $q$-wise dependent one-sided differential privacy model becomes more suitable when there are no dependencies among attributes. The study also provided a novel conversion protocol that allows a private database created under the one-sided differential privacy model to be transformed into a private database created under the dependent one-sided differential privacy model. In protoplanetary disks, it is not unusual to come across gas and dust emission substructures.
These substructures may have connections to the formation of planets themselves.
Our investigation into the AS 209 gas substructures employed thermochemical modeling using RAC2D and precise observations from the Molecules with ALMA at Planet-forming Scales project.
Our observations within the CO 1-0 line revealed a distinct double-peaked profile with separated emission features.
To replicate this observation, we needed to combine multiple gas species and their radial and vertical velocity distributions.
Our model showed that CO is largely concentrated in two areas--a ring with inner and outer boundaries--and CO depletion played a minor role in shaping this pattern.
For dust, we saw agreement between our model and observations for the outer ring, but some deviations occurred for the inner ring.
Our findings show that complex chemical structures and altered physical conditions can equally explain the formation of CO emission gaps and rings.
Additionally, our model predicted a perfect fit to C18O emission if we assumed a 0.1 mm snow line and 10 micron photodissociation region surface temperature.
Our observations and modeling support the idea of a planet with a mass less than 0.2 M_J at AS 209's gas substructures. For future research, we recommend examining substructures within other protoplanetary disks to see if they too exhibit double-peaked CO profiles.

We prove the existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving first-order controls with a constraint requiring state and control trajectories remain within a closed, bounded Euclidean space area. This outcome builds upon Cannarsa and Capuani's research, adapting it to apply to mean field games of controls with velocities as controls. The existence of an equilibrium in this context is challenged by requiring the necessary regularity of controls, a requirement we overcome by imposing a small Lipschitz constraint on the dependence of the Lagrangian function on the joint measure of states and controls, and showing that under these constraints regular paths can be closely approximated. This allows for the derivation of an equilibrium in the mean field game through a process involving a von Neumann type algorithm. The regularity of obtained trajectories is ensured by applying a maximum principle for reachable sets. The result is further generalized to controls with a more general form, although the generality comes at additional cost to notation and readability. Two such structures were found utilizing the Wavelet Domain Block Independent Bayesian Estimation (WDBIBE) method, which employs an algorithm to identify patterns in the galaxy's star distribution without making any assumptions about their shape. However, further investigation into these structures reveals they exhibit some irregularities that necessitate a reevaluation of their classification as stellar "strings". Two key aspects necessitate a reassessment: the level of tension among their constituent stars and their distance from the galaxy's center. Furthermore, it is suggested that these structures might be comprised of multiple distinct groups of stars that are not connected to each other. Utilizing the cross-correlation method, it is calculated that the stellar structure GaiaDr2-SS1 is comprised of multiple clusters at a high statistical confidence of 99.99%. Similarly, another structure GaiaDr2-SS5 comprised of multiple clusters at a statistical confidence of 99.97%. Additionally, it is discovered that these structures, specifically GaiaDr2-SS1 and GaiaDr2-SS5, exhibit radial age distributions, contradicting earlier assumptions that stellar "strings" form from in-placesupergiant star formation which would generally exhibit uniform ages. Due to these irregularities and contradictions, it is proposed that these structures be reclassified as stellar groups in need of further study to uncover their true nature. It is acknowledged that further research on these structures could shed more light on their origins but for now it is not justified to draw such a conclusion solely based on these findings. For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like style, type, and color. Current studies view visual compatibility as a straightforward'match' or'mismatch' classification problem, where each garment item is labeled as entirely compatible or incompatible. Yet, this simplistic approach is impractical for real-world Outfit Maker apps where users must identify which specific items might clash with their created outfits. To address this limitation, we introduce the Visual InCompatibility TransfORmer (VICTOR) that's tailored to tackle two distinct challenges: quantifying an outfit's overall compatibility and pinpointing individual mismatched items. Leveraging a fashion-oriented language-image contrastive pre-training framework, we fine-tune VICTOR on a wide range of fashion visuals, followed by pose-based feature extraction and matching. Experimental results show that our proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art performance on the FashionISTA dataset not only in overall compatibility assessment but also in local mismatch detection, thus providing a more comprehensive understanding of visual compatibility. The proposed method's success is showcased through its effective identification of incompatible outfits and individual mismatched items on the FashionISTA dataset. The source code for this work can be accessed at https://github.com/stevejpang/VICTOR. We have also released the backbones of our model and the pre-trained image features for public use at https://github.com/stevejpang/VICTOR_public. Additionally, the demo video can be viewed at https://stevejpang.com/victor_demo. (From https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07338)

Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface of support, we see that its breaking pattern changes constantly based on the rate at which we are stretching it. This effect is caused by the ongoing competition between two speed factors: the rate at which the particles reassemble, which is influenced by forces like viscosity and surface tension, and the rate at which neighboring particles move apart due to the expansion of the surrounding fluid. This balance of forces ultimately decides the length of clusters within the raft. A theoretical model that takes this competition into account successfully predicts the breakdown patterns we see in our experiments. The main challenge hindering the advancement of integrated gallium nitride electronics lies in its low hole mobility. In our investigation, we consider whether the mobility can be enhanced through epitaxial matching of GaN to certain II-IV nitride materials. We performed detailed computations utilizing the ab initio Boltzmann transport equation to calculate the hole mobility of GaN, revealing that aligning GaN under uniaxial compressive strain by matching it to ZnGeN$_2$ or MgSiN$_2$ inorganic materials flips the order of the heavy and light hole bands, resulting in a reduced hole mass along the compression axis. Consequently, our calculations indicate that matching GaN to ZnGeN$_2$ or MgSiN$_2$ boosts its room temperature hole mobility by 50% and 260%, respectively, when compared to strain-free GaN. Furthermore, our study on the strain-mobility trends discloses a nonlinear correlation. Moreover, our model suggests that matching GaN to an imaginary solid solution composed of Zn$_{0.75}$Ge$_{0.75}$Mg$_{0.25}$Si$_{0.25}$N$_2$ could increase its room temperature hole mobility by up to 150%. Ultimately, our theoretical findings provide a foundation for the experimental development of GaN-based electronic substrates with enhanced hole mobility by utilizing advanced nano-architecture techniques. We examine isothermic surfaces with a Hopf differential that decomposes into a real function and a specific quadratic differential with a singular point. However, this differential is nonzero and holomorphic throughout the rest of the surface except at this singular point. By focusing on a patch excluding the singular point, we find new isothermic surfaces applying the Darboux and Calapso transformations. Furthermore, we investigate how the transformed patches behave as they approach the singular point and check for continuity in that region. Additionally, we identify a condition under which the transformed patches will be geometrically equivalent to the original patch. Lastly, we provide examples of isothermic surfaces with this particular quadratic differential to illustrate our findings and offer insights into further research possibilities. These examples cover a range of surfaces, including compact noneellipic surfaces, as well as surfaces containing a circle, a scherk calibration, and a specialized combination of these elements. The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance for enhanced performance in resultant models. Despite this opportunity, past approaches have failed to thoroughly explore the incorporation of temporal information. In an effort to close this disparity, this research investigates how static models, initially developed without regard to time, can be applied to temporal knowledge graphs. Specifically, two novel techniques are introduced to achieve this end. The first method utilizes a measure of similarity between time-based vectors to gauge the temporal relationships between entities. When a significant discrepancy is detected, the corresponding entity embeddings are modified to'shift' them into greater agreement. The second technique frames the task as a link prediction challenge and utilizes a bidirectional Gramian Optimization for robust performance. Experiments have demonstrated the efficacy of the proposed methods, with our models attaining a median performance of 113.89 for the TKG-BERT dataset and 109.39 for the TIGRA-20174 dataset in terms of the mean rank metric. Furthermore, the proposed methods have been found to be resilient to false positives and our work has been influenced by recent studies on temporal knowledge graphs. The proposed models, along with the relevant code and datasets, have been made publicly available for reproduction of the presented results. Additionally, an analysis of the efficacy of various temporal modeling approaches has been provided. The results of this investigation suggest that static graph models can offer a more straightforward and effective solution for the handling of temporal knowledge graphs. The integrations of the developed techniques into existing graph embedding models have been explored and it has been observed that the proposed methods can be effectively applied to a wide range of embedding models, including but not limited to, QuATERNION and TQL2. The research has been focused on the space of temporal modeling and our methods can be utilized to enhance the performance of models based on QuATERNION and TQL2 as well as other similar models. The underlying code for this research has been made publicly available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/krishanranju/TOE. Furthermore, the employed datasets can be obtained from the following link: https://github.com/David-Schwieger/AirlineGraphs. The used knowledge graphs can be accessed via KBP35 and KBP40. Additionally, the used knowledge graphs for TIGRA-20174 can be obtained from Schmiech et al. (2018) under the label 'IGRA14'. The used knowledge graphs for TKG-BERT can be obtained from Jithendra et al.

Detecting complex multifrequency microwave (MW) electric fields is difficult 
due to interference from overlapping frequencies. Research using Rydberg 
atoms shows promise in MW radar and communications systems. Yet, the atoms are 
susceptible not only to desired signals, but also to interference from 
atomic interactions and environmental noise. To resolve these challenges, we've 
successfully integrated Rydberg atoms with deep learning algorithms, allowing the 
model to leverage the atoms' sensitivity while minimizing the impact of noise 
without requiring the resolution of complex mathematical equations. In a key 
test, our Rydberg-deep learning system has enabled the direct extraction of 
encoded information from frequency-division multiplexed (FDM) signals, marking 
an important breakthrough in this field, and holding the potential to 
revolutionize the sensing and communication capabilities of Rydberg-based MW 
technology. Furthermore, this innovation has expanded the potential uses 
of Rydberg atoms in various quantum applications. Additionally, the integration 
of deep learning algorithms has opened up new avenues for the widespread 
adoption of Rydberg-based MW technology beyond conventional atomic physics 
experiments. With its potential for real-world applications, this innovation 
has introduced a new era for Rydberg-based MW research. Lastly, although this 
research focused solely on Rydberg atoms, the integrated approach here can 
be applied to other sensitive atomic systems as well. Finally, we have 
successfully demonstrated the direct extraction of encoded information from 
multifrequency microwave signals using Rydberg atoms and deep learning, 
enabling the widespread utilization of Rydberg-based microwave research.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system. This interaction may have created a massive, extended halo around UGC 8839 and led to its extraordinary spiral arm geometry and the peculiar distribution of the HII regions. Additionally, the unusual features of UGC 8839 suggest its interaction with a nearby galaxy, NGC 2604. A possible future merger with NGC 2604 could provide the galaxy with enough energy to drive dynamic bar development in UGC 8839. Furthermore, the unique characteristics of UGC 8839 make it a potential host for a Ultra-Low Surface Brightness (ULSBD) galaxy, a type of galaxy with extremely low surface brightness that requires further research to understand its unique properties. Finally, the exceptional stability of the disk in UGC 8839 may indicate the presence of a massive, previously undetected black hole with a mass similar to that in M87. To confirm this hypothesis, high-resolution observations of the galaxy are needed. High-resolution imaging and spectroscopy could also confirm whether UGC 8839 possesses a massive, isolated bulge and a massive, extended halo similar to those of Malin 1. Additionally, the unique properties of UGC 8839 make it a candidate for a Stack-ranked Galaxy, where the HII region in UGC 8839 could be a massive, extended structure similar to a galactic disk, possibly formed through gravitational shearing by a distant foreground galaxy, NGC 2604. This phenomenon could lead to unique, symmetrical galactic features in UGC 8839 and potentially a massive, balanced galactic disk in NGC 2604.

Our approach presents a unified model that generates either sampling-based or mode-based high-fidelity audio. It combines visually triggered sound sampling with neural audio generation, leveraging the strengths of both while addressing their weaknesses. The model learns to decide the best approach for each given visual and audio prompt through a novel training technique. Results over surpass sampling-based quality in visual-based sound generation, underscoring the significance of developing unsupervised visual-based methods in this domain. The model's performance outshines cutting-edge unsupervised neural audio generation methods in both quality and audio length. It's fascinating to note that the model often generates novel, unexpected sound elements that weren't present in the training data. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy or model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. The undulator pulse triggers pulse generation by breaking up the energy modulations within the electron bunch, and the subsequent undulator section can increase the pulse's coherence and peak power through a series of microbunching and defocusing processes. The availability of a pulse injector with high average charge has been a crucial factor for implementing this concept in practice. The proposed modification has been successfully tested and demonstrated the production of pulses with a duration of approximately 160 fs within a 6 nm bandwidth centered at 6.5 eV, with a potential for extending the technique to generate even shorter pulse durations in the soft and hard X-ray ranges. By combining both vertical and horizontal viscosity factors, a fourth-order Taylor-Goldstein differential equation arises to describe vertical velocity perturbations, reducing to a modified equation when only the latter factor is considered under inviscid conditions. Assuming that key parameters are slowly changing, geometrical and physical approximations are explored for this modified equation using the WKB method near critical levels and singularities, including turning points. Additionally, the physical approximation exhibits a remarkable resemblance to the geometrical one but lacks the ability to describe large-scale turbulent flows as effectively as its geometrical counterpart. This physical approximation shows promising potential for modeling shear flows, including laminar and turbulent cases within a specific range. However, it fails to account for shear flow developments away from critical levels and cannot model certain turbulent phenomena. Consequently, this physical approximation is better suited for a low-to-moderate shear range and specific conditions. It is also intriguing to note that this approximation can be utilized in a regime characterized by a lack of net shear, exhibiting a substantial similarity to geometrical approximations in such contexts. Furthermore, the derived physical approximation displays a substantial similarity to the geometrical approximation in certain contexts, particularly where there is a lack of net shear, and even shows a comparable level of accuracy to the geometrical approximation in a range of moderate shear values. Nevertheless, the physical approximation is likely to experience difficulties in accurately modeling certain turbulent phenomena and shear flow developments away from critical levels. Ultimately, this paper demonstrates that the physical approximation can effectively tackle a particular class of shear flows and possesses a substantial similarity to geometrical approximations in certain contexts, but it is susceptible to limitations in modeling certain turbulent phenomena and shear flow developments. It is hoped that the results presented here can contribute to a greater understanding of the dynamics of a particular class of shear flows. A thorough discussion on the implications and potential applications of these findings to both marine engineering and geophysical flows is presented. It is anticipated that the results obtained could also be informative with respect to the modeling and description of a broad range of turbulent shear flows. method combining Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Simulated Annealing to quantify the

and assigns candidates to districts using a fair representation metric that maximizes
like-minded voters and minimizes opposing voters. Through the application to Texas,
our results reveal a high degree of unfairness associated with actual districting
plans, further supported by the identification of inherently fair districting options. 
These findings strongly suggest the presence of election manipulation in Texas.

We provide a characterization of smooth quadrics based on the existence of full exceptional collections with a specific property, generalizing a previous result obtained by C. Vial for projective spaces. Additionally, we identify a key condition necessary for the establishment of such collections in quadrics. Furthermore, by employing reflection functors, we demonstrate that any rational scroll can be expressed as a tensor product of a quadric and another smooth projective variety equipped with a full exceptional collection satisfying a particular condition. This discovery has an application in the study of numerical invariants, as we derive formulas for the Euler characteristic and Cox rings in terms of the invariants of the involved quadric. These formulas exhibit a resemblance to previously established results concerning projective spaces and reveal a previously unseen symmetry. Moreover, the approach allows for the development of a categorical interpretation of the established relationships between invariants. Considering an arbitrary full exceptional collection in a quadric, we prove that its extension to the tensor product is a full exceptional collection in the quadric's tensor product with another smooth projective variety. Based on this extension principle, we propose a method for the categorical generation of quadrics and investigate the conditions under which the generation is faithful. This approach also enables us to establish a connection between the behavior of full exceptional collections in a quadric under the tensor product and the birational geometry of the variety. Specifically, we show that certain types of generation in a quadric correspond to non-confining or confining behavior in its mirror, which has applications in studying symmetries and transformations between full exceptional collections in smooth projective varieties. Utilizing an established relationship between full exceptional collections and semistable vector bundles, we prove that tensor products of quadrics can be equipped with a full exceptional collection whose components have specific mutual relations and exhibit numerous signs of completeness. This discovery raises the question about the completeness of such collections and brings it closer to resolution. Combining abelian generations of projective spaces and quadrics, we propose a full exceptional collection in the tensor product of two specific smooth projective varieties, which we conjecture to be complete. This collection is expected to be the first instance of a full exceptional collection in a smooth projective variety of dimension five that is complete in the strongest sense. The approach can also be applied to the construction of complete full exceptional collections in line and Hermitian forms. Moreover, the method allows for the development of a categorical interpretation of the established relationships between invariants and provides a potential tool for the generation of full exceptional collections in smooth projective varieties

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
The solution involves a combination of sophisticated technologies including program compilation, specialized hardware, and advanced algorithms to eliminate unnecessary computations.
The performance gains enable thorough research on agent cognition by conducting hundreds of experiments in a remarkably shorter time.
Our empirical study indicates that diverse cognitive approaches outperform a strong baseline in various challenging game scenarios. 
Interestingly, some agents excel in specific general game strategies, underlining the need for further tailored agents that can effectively apply intuitive strategies in these games. 
The text-based games, along with their high-performance versions, and simulation results are freely available for anyone to repeat our experiments and build upon our research. 
The code has been released at https://github.com/baekmoosis/textworldexpress and the web interface at https://tixy.textworld.gym. 
The text-based games used in our research can also be played interactively through a web interface at https://textworld.ai. Additionally, the research data, including results and agent definitions, have been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/baekmoosis/textworld-experiments. 
Finally, the source code of TextWorldExpress has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/baekmoosis/textworldexpress. 
The research presents a new standard for text-based game processing speed and sets the stage for future research to build upon these optimized games, conducting more extensive studies. 
The surprising performance disparity between basic text-based games and the highly optimized text-based games may hold significant practical implications in various computer science domains including AI, highlighting the need for similar performance enhancements in real-world AI systems. 
The research also sheds light on current cognitive approaches in AI and suggests potential areas of improvement to develop more effective AI agents in text-based games and potentially other domains.

In robotics literature, there has been a recent shift towards transfer learning between robots. However, the transfer of this information from human to robot systems has been overlooked. This research proposes a new method for transferring manipulability information from one robot to another with a different kinematic structure. Since these ellipsoids are based on symmetric positive-definite matrices, they can be treated as points on a specific geometric manifold. This work provides the first approach to transfer manipulability by leveraging the technique of point cloud registration. It employs the ITSKAP solver for optimizing correspondences between ellipsoidal regions on two distinct robots and allows the efficient transfer of multiple manipulability tasks. To achieve this, it is necessary to define a suitable distance metric that preserves the geometric properties of the manipulability ellipsoids. Based on a specific mathematical framework, a new distance metric is introduced and shown to be more beneficial than others. Additionally, it employs certain advanced techniques to improve its results. These techniques include: using the parallel transport algorithm to ignore task dependencies that are not relevant to the target robot; employing manifolds that adapt to the scatter plot of the manipulability tasks to disregard task dependencies that are not essential; and employing an efficient registration method to handle multiple manipulability tasks. The proposed approach is evaluated by comparing it against existing methods that transfer manipulability. It shows that this approach can successfully transfer complex human-like manipulability trajectories to a PUMA robot and a KUKFX150 SR300 robot. These are robots with very different kinematic structures. Furthermore, it demonstrates the transfer of manipulability information between two industrial robots and a humanoid robot with a different kinematic structure. These results are presented in a public video. The research proposed a new method for transferring manipulability. A novel method for training a single neural network to determine the three-dimensional orientation of any object is proposed. Unlike existing top-down approaches, this method doesn't require pre-built 3D models for each object. Instead, two common image datasets and a collection of physically simulated objects are used to generate vast numbers of 2D sketches and their corresponding three-dimensional poses. A generative model separates these into two parts: a shape-agnostic component, and a component specific to each object. The shape-agnostic component is then trained and used to predict the three-dimensional pose from any 2D sketch. This method is proven more effective with our benchmark of over 150K images across 188 objects, and outperforms other top-down approaches in both generalization to novel views and novel objects. Additionally, it is shown that the learned shape-agnostic component can be applied to novel, unseen objects, and that its predictions are resilient to both out-of-distribution testing and image processing perturbations. Misinformation spread online does not necessarily lead to the adoption of false information; in fact, a proposed novel framework can discern one's attitude toward this misinformation. This new framework leverages neural networks and attitude consistency to classify stances toward COVID-19 vaccine-related misinformation. A novel neural framework, utilizing knowledge graphs to organize stances, successfully identifies attitudes toward this misinformation with outstanding results. Comparisons with current state-of-the-art systems document the superior performance of the developed approach. This new system aims to contribute to the minimization of COVID-19 vaccine misinformation spread on social media platforms. Moreover, the developed framework bears potential for generalization to address various other misinformation concerns. Experimental findings indicate that the novel framework achieves superior performance with high consistency. Eclipse predictions for binary stars can be significantly improved by revising older data that is no longer accurate. This involves accounting for potential companions that can create recurring periods in time shifts. A study discovered a low probability (0.00005%) of detecting new companions using eclipse time shifts. Researchers analyzed data on Algol ($\beta$ Persei) and found tentative signs of up to five additional companion candidates, which are believed to have orbital periods ranging from 1.863 to 219 years. These signals are consistent across 236 years of data and also matched the first 226.2 years of the data, accurately predicting eclipses for the following 9.2 years. The companion candidates' orbital planes are thought to be aligned due to the stable and unchanging eclipses of Algol since the early observations of Goodricke (1783). The new findings are an encouraging sign for detecting other binary companion candidates. The most promising candidate has an estimated mass of 0.046 $M_{\odot}$ (for an inclination of 40 degrees) or 0.032 $M_{\odot}$ (for an inclination of 80 degrees). The detection of this companion is currently the longest to be found using the eclipse time shift method. The study also discussed how astrophysical processes could stabilize the eclipses of Algol and described its bright state and historical observations. Furthermore, the researchers provided an in-depth analysis of the statistical errors associated with detecting new companions and the systematic effects that need to be further investigated. The errors considered included the Zone Age Model, the stellar active elements, and the time-averaged dispersion. The study explored these aspects in more detail and presented alternative methods for confirming the companion candidates in the future. This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with a limited energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found in earlier research conducted by Li and Zhang, which has also been generalized to non-convex domains in previous work by the same authors. This approach is primarily grounded in a well-known result from Hardy, a mathematical relationship describing the relationship between the distance from a point to a compact set and the potential energy of a solution in a specific region. We apply a divide-and-conquer strategy in order to derive this relationship and, subsequently, the main theorem. The core of our work involves creating an approximate model that separates key components – a model that is both energy-dependent and location-sensitive – which ultimately enables us to utilize a critical compactness criterion in conjunction with a scale transformation. The critical compactness criterion itself relies on a critical frequency, the definition of which is heavily influenced by the obstacle's shape and size. The most challenging aspect of our proof involves verifying that the frequency remains bounded for a certain class of solutions characterized by both minimal energy and a roughly homogeneous distribution in all directions. This verification involves establishing that the energy associated while moving far away from the obstacle does not decrease too quickly. The key to this finding lies in a mathematical inequality which connects the distance from any point to the compact set and its influence on the potential energy of solutions in similar areas. This general inequality encompasses a range of related specialized inequalities that can analyze specific shapes of the compact set, including when the shape is concave or singly-convex. However, for a potentially infinite number of other compact shapes, our approach involves developing a mathematical relationship which calculates the effect of the distance from any point to the compact set on the potential energy of solutions in similar areas. This general approach extends our initial consideration of a specific non-convex polyhedron, which was found to provide a satisfactory approximation for any compact set that has a relatively small size and a relatively high symmetry. We utilize a feed-forward network to predict residuals at unseen points and select nodes with maximum residual magnitude as new training points. This work provides a comprehensive examination and a thorough modeling of multi-domain ferroelectric FETs, focusing on the significant role played by domain wall dynamics within the ferroelectric material. It's demonstrated that periodical domain structures can be stabilized through control of the boundary tensions, and further reinforced by the presence of an external electric field. Consequently, a switch from a normal to a negative capacitance response in the device can be achieved. We develop a detailed model, incorporating both electrostatic and mechanical effects, to illustrate the memory function and the negative capacitance behavior exhibited by the device. Our simulations reveal that the periodical domain structures can facilitate the transfer of information between the device nodes, while also enabling the retention of data in response to surrounding fluctuations. Moreover, it is shown that the negative capacitance regime can be operational for extended periods of time and at relatively moderate temperatures. Our findings also suggest that the size of the memory capacity, stored in the domain-period, significantly influences the negative capacitance duration. Lastly, it is shown that the retention time can be significantly prolonged if the period of the memory bit falls within the quasi-quiet regime of the thermally-activated domain nucleation rates. Our model provides predictions that align with the results of numerical simulations, and ultimately, suggest an feasible pathway for the realization of stable CMOS-compatible ferroelectric nanoscale memory elements. Moreover, the work presents an analysis of the probability distributions of domain wall positions, captured through real-kappa microscopical model, and shows that the distribution of the membrane potential can be characterized by an equilibrium Gaussian distribution, while the non-equilibrium dynamics can be explained by the domain period and the domain wall location. Our study presents a novel understanding of the ferroelectric wall dynamics, captured through the negative capacitance behavior in multi-domain ferroelectric systems, and provides predictions that are potentially relevant to ferroelectric technology and ferroelectric biosensors. Finally, it is shown that the ferroelectric wall dynamics can be explored within a simple model based on the temporal evolution of the wall average position, and this position can be controlled by adjusting the boundary tensions and the elastic constant of the domain wall. Our study provides a fundamental understanding of the ferroelectric wall dynamics through a negative capacitance response in ferroelectric FETs, and illustrates how ferroelectric domain wall dynamics can be utilized to develop stable CMOS-compatible ferroelectric nanoscale memory elements. A significant knowledge gap exists in understanding the Cargo ecosystem's architecture and how vulnerability dissemination occurs within it. Existing studies that generalize security management approaches across multiple ecosystems often overlook the unique technical characteristics of individual ecosystems, hindering direct applicability of security governance strategies to Cargo. To address this disparity, this research employs knowledge graph techniques to construct a dependency vulnerability graph for Cargo and presents an innovative algorithm to identify vulnerability dissemination paths and scope. By conducting a comprehensive empirical study on Cargo's ecosystem, this research investigates vulnerability characteristics, propagation extent, and factors influencing vulnerability dissemination, revealing that Cargo's security vulnerabilities primarily stem from memory-related issues and are largely enabled by existing vulnerabilities in popular libraries such as Go Standard Library and golang.org/x/tools. The findings also show that Cargo's ecosystem-wide vulnerability propagation could be significantly alleviated by addressing security vulnerabilities in a small subset of critical dependencies. The outcome of this study can guide the governance of Cargo ecosystem security and inform future research on vulnerability management. The proposed approach and generated knowledge graph, represented by a knowledge graph model and accompanying graph nodes and edges, are available on GitHub for public access. The empirical study's source code, comprising three key algorithms, is also available on GitHub for reproducibility. The results of the study, including graph node properties, vulnerability characteristics, and propagation metrics, are available on GitHub in the form of two indexes for public access. The study demonstrates the constructiveness of the proposed approach, yielding valuable insights into Cargo ecosystem vulnerability management. The utility of the knowledge graph model is validated through qualitative analysis, confirming its applicability to Cargo security governance. The empirical study provides a quantitative evaluation of the proposed approach, offering an accurate benchmark for future research on Cargo ecosystem security vulnerability management. The contribution of this research can guide the development of vulnerability management strategies, informing the security governance of Cargo ecosystem developers, and providing valuable insights for future research on securing the Cargo ecosystem. The source code of the study has been made available on GitHub for public access. The generated knowledge graph and source code can facilitate reproducibility and enable the development of customized services to enhance Cargo ecosystem security governance. The study's findings can guide the security governance of Cargo ecosystem developers, informing future research on securing the Cargo ecosystem. The proposed knowledge graph model and accompanying graph nodes and edges can be applied to address other challenge problems in the Cargo ecosystem by modeling the interdependencies between package versions. The study provides novel vulnerability propagation patterns and vulnerability characteristic patterns that can be utilized by developers to create security-aware documentation for promoting secure coding practices among developers. For analyzing ergodic properties in stochastic dynamical systems, it's essential to demonstrate irreducibility. This paper confirms the irreducibility of stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations subjected to discrete jump noises and shows these results apply universally, imposing minimal restrictions on noise conditions. A critical factor in this study is the authors' and T. Zhang's previously established criteria for irreducibility in stochastic equations with jump noises. This proof is then utilized to demonstrate ergodic behavior in stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations and includes scenarios of weak dissipation with jump degenerate noise. Additionally, the researchers provide two counterexample cases highlighting the necessity of two primary conditions for irreducibility to be valid. These conditions are also expanded upon for their broader generality in the context of one-dimensional stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations. Lastly, the researchers propose future research directions in this area. Due to the inclusive environment and diverse perspectives presented during the school, the researchers were motivated to explore the irreducibility of stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations under discrete jump noises, ultimately yielding the presented findings. For a finite noncyclic nilpotent group G, we're analyzing the minimal vertex degree in its power graph. This power graph connects vertices based on one being a positive power of the other. By examining the group's prime divisors and Sylow subgroups, we've pinpointed vertices related to its cyclic subgroups. This allows us to establish a connection between the group's properties and its minimal vertex degree in the power graph. This study provides degree calculations for specific types of noncyclic abelian groups. Additionally, we've found a lower bound for the minimal vertex degree in the power graph of any noncyclic nilpotent group. This lower bound is expressed relatively simply in terms of the group's properties. Nevertheless, this lower bound does not yield an exact minimum vertex degree in the power graph for every noncyclic nilpotent group. I explore a feasible method to investigate this at the Large Hadron Collider operating at sqrt(s) = 13 TeV, an equivalent increase in fixed-target energy of 40,000 times, with crucial implications for understanding the characteristics of cosmic ray showers. Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations but are limited when dealing with orientation transformations. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel model, Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), based on Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), which can learn representations that are less sensitive to orientation changes. By combining LGFs with standard DCNNs, our OCNs can leverage the benefits of existing deep learning frameworks while improving their robustness to orientation changes. Our proposed LGFs are constructed by selecting key Gabor filters and expressing them as sparse linear combinations of these markers, utilizing a matrix factorization-based method to improve computational efficiency. Our experimental results show the advantages of the proposed OCNs over state-of-the-art models on Digits37, Vehicle91, and Airplane datasets. Additionally, our model achieves superior performance compared to the current best methods for orientation-specific representation learning, while also demonstrating greater flexibility in various applications. Furthermore, our OccuBonns algorithm is presented as a method to obtain orientation-related benchmarks using LGFs. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Saurav-31/Orientation-Convolutional-Networks. Experimental findings suggesting the potential for generalization to other domain adaptation tasks are also presented. It has been discovered that retraining the LGFs on target domain data yields notable improvements in performance, which could be valuable for researchers in the domain adaptation field. Our findings provide support for the idea that the proposed LGFs can serve as effective target domain-specific benchmarks. Additionally, it has been observed that the proposed LGFs can be employed as an effective data augmentation technique to yield notable performance improvements, particularly cross-domain domain adaptation tasks. Our work offers a novel approach to the challenge of orientation transformations via the development of LGFs, which are constructed by combining key Gabor filters and their linear combinations to represent complex images. Additionally, it has been discovered that the proposed LGFs can be utilized to obtain sparse linear combinations of these markers and that their efficiency can be improved using matrix factorization-based methods. Our model provides a flexible framework for the generation of orientation-related benchmarks, as well as generalization to domain adaptation tasks. This study seeks to enhance the computational efficiency of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) in point cloud learning. We critically examine the conventional graph convolution, comprising a KNN search and a multilayer perceptron. By dissecting its underlying mathematical operations, we arrive at two key insights for GCN optimization. Firstly, the 3D point cloud representation's geometric structure is efficiently propagated across the GCN through KNN search. This insight drives the simplification of consecutive KNN searches. Secondly, the activation function's unique properties allow the overlap of adjacent feature aggregation operations. Based on these findings, we develop a novel and highly efficient GCN framework, E-GCN. Comparative evaluations on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate the computational efficiency and superior performance of E-GCN over traditional methods. Furthermore, the efficient GCN framework facilitates the deployment of the model on resource-constrained hardware, such as the NVIDIA Jetson TX2. Comprehensive experiments validate the efficacy of the insights and efficiency of the proposed E-GCN framework. The code is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/hellokun779/EFGCN. Additionally, the model demos can be found on our website at https://hellokun779.github.io/EFGCN.

We introduce a groundbreaking type of Trojan attack, which can launch successful infiltration without relying on specific model hosts. Traditional Trojan attacks require knowledge of the target model architecture and work best with similar networks, but our proposed attack surpasses these limitations by focusing solely on the data. Our method utilizes semantic segmentation to create unsuspecting users of malicious models, without needing target model information or awareness of domain boundaries. As evidence of its effectiveness, our semantic Trojan attack successfully infiltrates various CNN models across multiple domains and demonstrates superior generalizability across diverse datasets and architectures by a significant margin over traditional backdooring techniques. Our attack's legitimacy is verified through thorough human validation, and to ensure its long-term sustainability, we have also developed a framework for regularly updating and maintaining its efficacy. Ultimately, our findings reveal the existence of a distinct Trojan attack strategy, which can successfully compromise a wide range of models in domain adaptation scenarios. In this paper, the carbon-carbon fusion research is revisited to incorporate the latest developments. Specifically, key experimental and theoretical findings from a recent analysis by Beck {\it et al.} (Eur. Phys. J. A {\bf 56}, 97 (2020)) are considered to outline the pathway for enhancing low-energy astrophysical $S$-factor determinations via new Threshold Hand Mirror (THM) measurements. These determinations can be accurately obtained by conducting experiments at lower-energy ranges using a mirrored geometry. This approach can potentially resolve the ongoing fusion puzzle and is expected to yield reliable values for the astrophysical $S$-factor. Furthermore, a novel measurement technique is proposed that utilizes a dual-beam setup with a very low energy range (approximately 15-40 keV) and a high geometrical detection sensitivity. This should result in a highly precise $S$-factor value, and the proposed method is recommended for implementation in the future. In addition, a general THM measurement strategy is provided, along with relevant technical considerations for obtaining high-precision results. It is noted that existing high-precision THM data are remarkably consistent with recent refined theoretical calculations by Beck {\it et al.} (Eur. Phys. J. A {\bf 56}, 97 (2020)) and are significantly superior to other experimental and theoretical findings. Consequently, future Trojan horse experiments are urged to concentrate on even lower energy ranges (approximately $\sim$10-50 keV) for enhancing existing $S$-factor values.
