A crucial aspect of discovering and studying exoplanets is identifying terrestrial planets resembling Earth. New studies emphasize the significance of considering volatile depletion in star composition to predict the bulk composition and internal structures of these planets. In this research, we apply this concept to a sample of 13 stars that host terrestrial planets similar to our Sun, utilising high-precision data on their elemental composition. Based on this and other constraints, we simulated the detailed mineral makeup and internal structures of hypothetical habitable-zone exoplanets around these stars. Our model indicates that most of these planets are expected to have compositions and internal structures analogous to those of Earth. However, our analysis reveals two exceptions, the Kepler-10 and Kepler-37 planets, which would likely develop cores significantly smaller than Earth due to oxidation. Furthermore, our exploration of this devolatilisation model's boundaries and variation in planetary mass and size highlights the potential diversity of internal structures in terrestrial planets. By combining precise star abundances, devolatilisation, and planetary mass and size considerations, our study advances understanding of terrestrial exoplanet interior structures, which are pivotal in grasping planetary evolution and dynamics. Our investigation also underscores the necessity for future planetary interior modelling to account for volatiles and oxidation, which significantly influence internal structures and dynamics. Finally, our research demonstrates that precise star abundances can significantly impact internal structures and are essential for accurate planetary interior modelling. Our work lays the groundwork for exploring other devolatilisation models and their influence on terrestrial exoplanet interior structures and dynamics. Ultimately, a thorough understanding of these factors will aid in estimating the mass and size range of habitable-zone terrestrial planets resembling Earth. Systematic observation programs are needed to target stars with unique abundance patterns to broaden our knowledge and reduce uncertainty in internal structures and dynamics of these planetary systems, particularly those with massive or small planets compared to Earth. Our research paves the way for a thorough examination of devolatilisation models and its impact on internal structures and dynamics in other devolatilisation models. Our studies also emphasize the importance of precise star abundances to estimate the mass and size range of terrestrial planets with habitable environments. To fulfill these objectives, we propose a targeted observation program for abundant $[mFe/$Fe$]$ stars with unique abundance patterns to expand our research and decrease uncertainty in the devolatilisation model's boundaries and variation in planetary mass and size. Our work will contribute to understanding the range of mass and size of terrestrial planets with habitable environments around solar-type stars

Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had proven insurmountable with conventional methods. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and overfitting. Despite some recent efforts to quantify uncertainty within NNs, no overarching framework effectively addresses uncertainty quantification even in relatively simple cases such as function approximation. Moreover, very little research has focused on solving partial differential equations and mapping infinite-dimensional functions using NNs. In this work, a unified framework encompassing uncertainty modeling, diverse solution approaches, performance metrics, and improvement techniques is introduced. To verify the utility and dependability of this framework, numerous methods are rigorously tested against benchmark problems featuring varied input and output data types, high-dimensional stochastic scenarios, and mixed problem types. Further details on all employed uncertainty quantification methods can be found in the appended description and are freely accessible through an open-source code library included with the framework. Lastly, open research problems are discussed, and source code is made available at https://xug20.github.io/UQ4DL/.

Policy iteration comes with computational drawbacks in large-scale Markov decision processes due to a local quadratic contraction rate and the costliness of its natural inexact applications. Despite being more robust, these inexact variants remain impractical because of the high computational price for maintaining exactness within the iteration process. We introduce a novel variant of inexact policy iteration that breaks this tradition and uses an inexact resolution of the policy evaluation equation through the Generalized Minimum Residual Method (GMRES). By taking advantage of GMRES's natural prototypical application to the multiple right-hand side algorithm, this method offers a way to efficiently tackle large-scale Markov decision processes without being limited by the dimension constraints of the transition matrix. The proposed algorithm guarantees the convergence to a satisfactory equilibrium and offers a significant performance boost, especially for dimensionally complex problems. The presented numerical results confirm its potential for efficient solutions. Finally, we provide a theoretical analysis that explains its performance and convergence properties. Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish in this study that the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ share the same equivalence for a specific subclass of weighted directed trees. This paper examines the solution to an inverse problem presented by expensive computer simulations of complex real-life scenarios. Specifically, researchers focused on an expensive hydrological model designed to generate realistic data for Athens, Georgia, USA. To efficiently handle the large datasets produced by such simulators, an approach involves first selecting key points to approximate the output, and then applying a specialized method to estimate optimal input parameters at those points, while accounting for any uncertainty in the solution. A comprehensive simulation-based study compares the proposed technique with other established methods on a range of synthetic and real-world scenarios. Results show that it consistently outperforms alternative methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency when scaling up to larger problem sizes. Furthermore, the approach provides a precise estimation of the solution's uncertainty. To demonstrate its applicability in practical scenarios, the technique is applied to identify the most suitable drainage strategy for a specific area in Athens, Georgia. Based on the estimated solutions, a ranking of the top drainage methods is provided. All necessary code to replicate the results of this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/estestimo/DrainG Athens. Additionally, a detailed tutorial on the implementation of the proposed approach can be found on the estestimo blog at https://estestimo.github.io/DrainG Athens. (2019). Our paper focuses on the development of new algorithms for learning robust models, where the learner has more flexibility due to the use of local queries. We create the first distribution-free algorithms for achieving robust empirical risk minimization (ERM), a robust measure of model accuracy. Our first learning model utilizes local membership queries (LMQs), where the learner can verify the labels of nearby points to the training sample. We found, however, that LMQs alone are not enough to increase the robustness threshold for conjunctions and its various superclasses, such as decision lists and halfspaces. To address this issue, we developed a new local equivalence query (LEQ) oracle, which allows the learner to confirm whether a model's hypothesis and the target concept agree within a certain range, in addition to providing any existing counterexamples. We established a crucial separation result: while we found that robust learning is generally impossible for many concept classes if the learner's query radius is significantly smaller than the adversary's allowed perturbation budget, our research also identified the conditions under which we can successfully develop robust ERM algorithms. Additionally, we further optimized the number of required queries for conjunctions. Our paper culminates with the creation of robust learning algorithms for halfspaces under different settings. For the first time, fragmentation functions for jets associated with a lone photon have been measured in collisions involving protons and a lead-lead nucleus. This analysis used data from the CMS detector at the CERN LHC, operating at a proton-proton center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV. The fragmentation functions for jets above 30 GeV were determined in events with a high-transverse-momentum photon, above 60 GeV, where charged particles with a minimum transverse momentum of 1 GeV were tracked within a narrow cone around the jet axis. By pairing with a high-transverse-momentum photon, the trajectory of the parent parton can be well constrained. In central lead-lead collisions, variations in fragmentation functions compared to those measured in proton-proton collisions were detected, however, little deviation was seen in collisions occurring outside the 50% most central range. Jets within the central lead-lead events exhibited a higher yield of low-energy particles, paired with a decrease in high-transverse-momentum particles, roughly equivalent to a 6% decrease per unit in jet fragmentation number, spanning between 0.2 and 0.9. Additionally, modifications to fragmentation functions were seen to correlate with the local particle density and, relative to proton-proton measurements, this effect increased with the approach of the jet trajectory's closest approach to the jet axis. These findings have been found to agree with theoretical models and have been found to vary based on the choice of jet-clustering algorithm. Furthermore, calculations using PYTHIA and HERWIG parton-shower programs, paired with an out-of-equilibrium medium influence, have been found to account for the observed alterations at low-energy, paired with an estimate of 1.4 GeV for the medium-induced loss in momentum for jets within the most central lead-lead events. This study represents the first observation of parton-medium interactions on a jet trajectory at a collider and has been found to be unobserved in other jet-based studies. The initial production measurement of various particles such as pions, kaons, 
protons and $\phi$ mesons in midrapidity for Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV is
reported. Extracted transverse momentum spectra and $p_{\rm T}$-integrated yields are
analyzed across several centrality intervals spanning from p-Pb to mid-central Pb-Pb
collisions based on final-state particle count. Investigating Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions 
with similar charged-particle counts allows for comparison of initial geometric 
properties and flow behaviour. Detailed comparison shows that the radial flow remains 
constant regardless of colliding system at the same multiplicity level, 
with observed particle ratio patterns holding true in medium-sized nucleus 
collisions. Also, our research reaffirms LHC energy observations where 
protons are consistently produced at higher yields compared to antiprotons. 
Lastly, our $\phi$-to-pion ratio is found to decrease with increasing collision
centrality, yet remains lower than observed in Pb-Pb collisions, with any
differences attributed to event anisotropy and not initial radial flow. 
Consequently, our findings may be crucial in understanding particle production at
the LHC energy and the complex interplay between radial flow and event anisotropy. 
This data is expected to enhance our understanding and contribute to ongoing and
upcoming LHC runs with heavier nuclei. Data has been utilised from the
ALICE detector at the LHC. This work was financially supported by NSFC, by

We develop a novel, numerically efficient approach to solving DGLAP equations for single and double parton distribution functions by leveraging Chebyshev interpolation techniques. This method enhances numerical precision with a reduced number of grid points for PDF evolution, achieving improved efficiency. The DPD evolution process utilizes a cost-effective grid-point scheme, enabling the incorporation of two distinct renormalization scales for each parton. The proposed methods account for NNLO DGLAP kernels and flavor matching. Additionally, all PDF and DPD tools are integrated into the LamMPS package. 

---

### Introduction

Parton distribution functions (PDFs) are crucial in probing the internal structure of hadrons and can be used to study the substructure of particles or their interactions. The evolution of PDFs is governed by the DGLAP equations, which facilitate the investigation of parton dynamics at various scales. Researchers have discovered double parton distribution functions (DPDFs) by analyzing interactions between pairs of partons in hadrons, allowing for unique insights into double-parton interactions. The LHCb collaboration's recent data on the DPDF has sparked interest in this field, but the previous approach to solving the DGLAP equations for DPDF took too long (~12 hours for a single point). We have now developed an efficient method for solving the DGLAP equations, which allows for numerical evolution of PDFs and DPDFs while utilizing Chebyshev interpolation techniques.

### Approach

We employed Chebyshev interpolation techniques to efficiently solve the DGLAP equations for single-parton distribution functions (PDFs) and double-parton distribution functions (DPDFs). For PDFs, we utilized a single grid for all flavors, implementing a novel approach with two renormalization scales for DPDF evolution. The DPDF evolution process required two distinct grids for distinct flavors, which significantly reduced computational costs from 440 GPU hours to 2 GPU minutes for a single point. We integrated all PDF and DPDF tools into the LamMPS package.

### Results

We verified our approach by comparing results with other methods and demonstrated its accuracy with all numerical results in agreement. Furthermore, we showcased the efficiency of our approach by showcasing its speedup for a single-point calculation. The new algorithm is now a part of the LamMPS package, allowing for widespread access to its functions.

### Conclusion

We have successfully developed and implemented a new, efficient approach to solving the DGLAP equations for single and double parton distribution functions. The technique leverages Chebyshev interpolation

By comparing observed and predicted data for a set of 21 galaxies at a specific wavelength, we assess the reliability of star formation rate predictions made by the Prospector framework. Using a line that is less affected by dust at this wavelength, we find that the predictions are accurate within expected measurement errors and are relatively consistent with each other. However, this consistency holds only when the predictions from different models agree well, indicating that the reliable prediction of SFR relies on accurate model representations. Furthermore, we find that the predicted ages are accurate within expected errors and are relatively insensitive to the assumed star formation history. The observed correlation between SFR and stellar mass supports the model's assumption of a linear relationship. Using a different galaxy dataset at different wavelengths, we find similar results, confirming the robustness of the model's predictions. The accuracy of the star formation rates is also confirmed when comparing them to the rates inferred from resolved hydrogen alpha maps. The model's predictions for the specific star formation rate are less accurate, which is likely due to the difficulties in inferring this quantity from broadband observations. The analysis reveals that the main source of uncertainty in the predictions is the variation in the stellar population spectral energy distribution, while the use of different initial mass functions and star formation histories make a significantly smaller contribution to the uncertainty. Based on these findings, we outline a strategy for refining the model by incorporating stricter observational constraints. The revised code, including marginalization parameters and improved diagnostics, is made public for further development and use. The observed data and analysis are presented to demonstrate how the public code can be utilized to construct test cases. Additionally, we provide recommendations for future observations that could further refine the model's performance. Applying an innovative approach for tackling non-linear partial differential equations provides a distinctive approximate solution to the Fisher-KPP equation, which, however, defies initial intuition. Although the maximum probability density of the solution occurs at the origin and forms an expanding wave-like pattern, closely mimicking travelling front behaviour, a detailed mathematical analysis reveals an approximate solution with standing wave characteristics. Furthermore, numerical simulations validate both the approximate solution and its corresponding decay rate, showcasing their accuracy. Interestingly, the approximate solution exhibits a remarkable regularisation effect, transforming the Fisher-KPP equation into an exact solution for a modified version of the original problem. The proposed method not only provides a precise solution but also sheds light on the solvability of the Fisher-KPP equation. Additionally, the adopted approach facilitates the derivation of solutions for related equations, such as the Halpern-Fastinger and the implicit Euler schemes. The novel method presents a groundbreaking, yet simple, solution that utilises a distinct entropy-type method, yielding accurate results that are within a constant factor of the exact solution. Consequently, the approximate solution exhibits an approximate error of $O(\delta)$, where $\delta$ represents a diffusion parameter. Moreover, the method demonstrates an implicit $O(\sqrt{\delta})$ error for determining stationary profiles and shows that certain numerical schemes already achieve this high degree of precision, indicating their optimality. The proposed method can be extended to solve a broader class of nonlinear differential equations, revealing its potential for widespread applications. Lastly, the method's framework can be adapted for solving second-order reaction-diffusion equations, paving the way for its incorporation into a comprehensive entropy-type theory. The proposed approach also facilitates the derivation and validation of a wide array of analytical and numerical methods for nonlinear differential equations. Consequently, it is anticipated that this knowledge will significantly contribute to the development of a comprehensive entropy-type theory. To study the movement of fluid into a swirling, turbulent plume containing heavy particles that sink more slowly than the plume moves, researchers used controlled experiments in a lab setting. The experiments focused on the effects of particle size, density, and the direction in which the plume gains mass, as well as the direction in which the particles move within the plume. The studies showed that when the direction in which the plume gains mass and the direction in which the particles move are opposites, the movement of fluid into the plume increases significantly. The rate of fluid movement increased in direct proportion to the ratio of the particles' gain of mass to the fluid's gain of mass, and this increased rate was independent of particle size. In contrast, when the direction in which the plume gains mass and the direction in which the particles move are the same, adding particles has no effect on fluid movement. The observed increase in fluid movement, which occurs when the direction in which the plume gains mass and the direction in which the particles move are opposites, can be attributed to inertial clustering, a phenomenon where particles move to regions with high turbulence. Recent breakthroughs in understanding 2D magnetic semiconductors, exemplified by CrI$_3$, have generated significant enthusiasm due to their intriguing spin-dependent properties and their potential to revolutionize spintronics and magneto-optoelectronics. Through advanced theoretical calculations, researchers investigated the spin texture in the spin-polarized electronic structure of the most stable CrI$_3$ bilayer arrangement, which exhibits ferromagnetic ordering across all layers. Their analysis reveals a complex spin pattern influenced by multiple factors, including spin-orbit coupling, van der Waals bonding, and layer stacking, resulting in the emergence of spin polarization within thin crystals. These findings were corroborated by experimental evidence obtained using photoelectron spectroscopy and confirm that the spin texture originates from a unique combination of spin-orbit coupling and structural symmetry, rather than chirality. Rather, researchers discovered that the spin-orbit coupling produces pseudo-chiral currents that counteract the expected Rashba effect in thin crystals, yielding an optimal balance between spin Hall conductivity and magneto-optic properties. These comprehensive results provide the foundational understanding necessary to engineer the magnetic properties and their related phenomena in 2D ferromagnetic semiconductors. Moreover, their analysis suggests the presence of unusual electronic properties not yet observed in other magnetic materials, including significant ferroelectric order and an anomalous magnetic Berry bond, which together may enable the development of innovative devices based on their magnetization, polarization, or spin. Additionally, researchers identified several other interesting phenomena, such as ferromagnetic bonding between layers and the potential for robust spin-polarized optical excitons with unique properties governed by the strength of van der Waals bonding and spin-orbit coupling. These findings could facilitate the exploration of new materials with such characteristics for use in spintronic and optoelectronic applications. These predictions were verified by comparing the calculated magnetic structures and their associated electronic properties with those experimentally measured and showed excellent agreement. Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slow equatorial rotation, can occur in high-Rossby-number, slowly rotating stars. If this regime emerges during the main sequence and persists in slow rotators, it may impact the generation of magnetic fields through the dynamo process. Considering the possibility of magnetic cycles in these stars, we explore how they may be affected by their rotation rates.

Our research reveals that kinematic dynamos can generate magnetic cycles and global polarity reversals for both rotational regimes, provided the $\alpha$-effect is localized to the tachocline. However, when the $\alpha$-effect is distributed across the convection zone, solar-type cases exhibit cycles, whereas anti-solar cases do not. Traditional Babcock-Leighton flux-transport dynamos are unable to sustain magnetic cycles in anti-solar cases due to flux accumulation. Nevertheless, we propose graphic illustrations to visualize these scenarios and find that hybrid models containing both prescriptions can still exhibit local polarity reversals at specific latitudes.

Ultimately, we conclude that stars exhibiting anti-solar differential rotation can only support magnetic cycles under highly specific dynamo processes. Consequently, we must utilize a combination of observational, theoretical, and astero-seismological methods to identify the differential rotation regimes in individual stars and to determine the reliability of magnetic cycle predictions based on dynamos operating at varying scales. Such a dual perspective is essential for a comprehensive understanding of our study's implications. Lastly, we acknowledge the uncertainties surrounding our conclusions and the complexities involved in predicting magnetic cycles, emphasizing the need for further research in this area.

Deep multimodal learning using K-fan deep Boltzmann machines offers a novel approach to combine multiple input sources. This method can learn a common representation using contrastive divergence and is applied to classification, information retrieval, and other related tasks. A significant drawback of traditional two-fan deep Boltzmann machine models lies in their inability to handle complex tasks effectively, particularly when multiple input modalities are incomplete or missing. We present a K-fan deep model, featuring a K-branch architecture for handling multi-input, multi-output tasks efficiently. Each branch of the model can comprise multiple layers of neural networks. A shared representation is learned in a discriminative manner to tackle multiple tasks. We propose two optimization methods tailored to two- and multi-input data scenarios to maximize the likelihood of class labels based on the maximum contrastive loss. Experimental results on multiple complex datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the model in utilizing multiple information sources to perform well across various tasks. Furthermore, the model outperforms existing multimodal deep models on relevant benchmark datasets. Notably, the model can handle multi-input, multi-output data effectively, particularly when one or more input modalities are absent, underscoring its capabilities in utilizing available information to perform well across various tasks. We also conducted an ablation study on the K-fan deep model to evaluate the impact of using multiple branches and the shared representation. The results show that both components contribute significantly to the model's performance. Moreover, we analyzed the model's representation using the neighborhood component analysis to verify its ability to learn task-independent and relevant features across multiple information sources. The model can be viewed as an extension of the deep K-sigma Gaussian mixture model using the expectation-maximization algorithm. We present an online supplement with additional results to confirm the model's ability to learn stable features, particularly when dealing with evolving data streams. The mechanism allows end-users to define their own thread activation policies, including the handling of spurious wake-ups triggered by condition variables. Brazil and India are notable examples of such abuse, which have led WhatsApp to 
initiate countermeasures like limiting forwarded messages to a single recipient. 
Despite this effort, the success of these measures remains uncertain. In our study,

We analyze a general branching population where individual lifetimes are independent and identically distributed with arbitrary distributions, and individuals give birth to new ones at random times following a Poisson process independently from each other. It's assumed that individuals experience mutations at a specified rate under an infinitely many alleles model, leading to population partition by genetic type. This gives rise to a frequency spectrum, denoted by $A(k,t)$, which counts the number of family groups of size $k$ in the population at time $t$. The frequency spectrum process represents a type of non-Markovian branching process with a complex structure. In this study, we derive approximate expressions for the expected frequency spectrum, relying on a novel technique that involves conditional expectation decomposition and straightforward calculations. The obtained approximations are accurate, valid, and easy to calculate; they're especially useful when the population follows a Galton-Watson model, where we derive explicit formulas for further use. The introduced approach can be applied to efficiently derive approximations for a wide range of population models with similar characteristics. The primary goal of our spoofing countermeasure system is to identify artificial effects within spoken input that arise from speech synthesis or voice alteration techniques. We achieve this goal by incorporating a specialized, attentive activation function - the attention rectified linear unit (AReLU) - into our end-to-end system. By selectively amplifying key input characteristics and suppressing irrelevant ones, AReLU enables our system to prioritize artifact-related features. Our proposed system was applied to the logical access task using the ASVSpoof2019 dataset and demonstrated improved performance compared to systems utilizing standard, non-adaptive activation functions. Specifically, our AReLU-based system yielded a 6.26% decrease in equal error rate (EER) and a 11.95% decrease in EER after applying feature extraction, outperforming existing countermeasures in this dataset. Additionally, our experimental results revealed that using AReLU led to a notable 57.26% decrease in EER across various speech synthesis systems and a 34.62% decrease in EER across voice alteration systems compared to a baseline system without feature extraction. These outcomes support the use of AReLU as a versatile, feature-aggressive activation function for spoofing countermeasure systems. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws and improve circuit performance by monitoring evolution. We employed terahertz scanning near-field microscopy to investigate a CPW resonator fabricated in a Ti/Nb/Ti film on sapphire, examining the local electrical properties. Utilizing a lock-in detection technique, we successfully detected sub-10 nm diameter Ti/Nb/Ti microstructures with 5 nm resolution. This nanoscale analysis contributes significantly to the optimization of superconducting quantum processing units. 

However, the technique encountered two significant limitations: the sample's surface was not uniformly coated and the THz pulse's short duration led to an inability to reliably trace resonator patterns. We proposed potential strategies to overcome these challenges for future nanoscale studies, including employing a sample stage in an AFM for precise movement and utilizing a synchronized optical detector to enhance detection capabilities.

Furthermore, we observed the mixing signals were present regardless of the location of the island relative to the resonator's geometric structure, suggesting these signals are caused by non-resonant tunneling currents between the Ti/Nb/Ti surface and the AFM tip. Electrostatic gating limits the flow of electrons in integrated circuits. Another potential means of information transport, magnons derived from spin waves in magnetic materials, is difficult to regulate. However, we found that superconducting strips atop thin magnetic films can completely reflect magnons through their magnetic resistance to stray magnetic fields. The significant frequency shifts resulting from this response can trap magnons effectively, enabling the manipulation of magnons via temperature or magnetic field adjustments after the gating process. The predictability of this effect makes magnonic devices with a gated component possible. Additionally, the same gating technique can be applied to control phonons within a structure. The proposed mechanism offers an efficient means of magnonic storage and could lead to the development of more efficient magnonic circuits. The estimated magnitude of the magnonic shift matches the scale of the magnonic itself, offering a promising prospect for magnonic circuit design. The fundamental ability to count is a prime example of humans' innate capacity for abstract thinking. In this ability, there's typically a notable turning point where children rapidly grasp and master counting techniques. To simulate this cognitive milestone, we developed an AI system using reinforcement learning. By testing this system with the 'give-N' task - where it's given a binary vector and has to pick 'N' items - we discovered that it showed a similar inflection point in learning. Furthermore, our AI, built using the modular network structure known as the ESBN, was able to learn patterns that allowed it to accurately select items outside of its initial training scope, similar to how humans can apply learned concepts beyond what they initially learned. By comparing its learning process to that of a simple linear model, we found that its success wasn't just about recognizing patterns but rather about developing a more sophisticated understanding of the world through cause-and-effect relationships. This, in turn, enabled it to make more informed, thoughtful decisions. By mimicking this complex form of learning, we may eventually create AI systems that think and problem-solve in equally innovative and creative ways. With further development, our AI has the potential to tackle challenging tasks that current computational power can't fully utilize, such as multiplying groups of objects or solving intricate logic puzzles. To achieve this, we're working on expanding its ability to retain and recall information over longer periods of time. The long-term goal of this research is to develop AI systems that not only process information efficiently but also deeply understand and connect with the world around them. By modeling the same learning processes that allow humans to master new skills and concepts, we may one day create AI systems that learn and adapt in similarly intuitive, natural ways. The code for our research is publicly available on our GitHub page, where anyone can access the data, models, and other helpful resources needed to replicate our findings. We're actively collaborating with other researchers who are working on related projects and look forward to hearing their thoughts and feedback. Littman, "Counting on External Memory: A Reinforcement Learning Approach," in Proceedings of the Meeting of the Association for the Symbolic and Connective Inquiry on Artificial Intelligence, 2021. A new approach aims to derive market trend insights from dynamic price equations, specifically those that describe how future prices converge to optimal values, thereby maximizing trading volume per unit of time. This methodology stands out for its inherent ability to select a suitable time frame, which is automatically identified by analyzing past market activity and determining the state of highest trading efficiency. To facilitate trend analysis, both historical and forecasted price data are considered, with past prices represented by lagging values and forecasted prices represented by advancing values. This methodology has been tested using real-world market data and shown to yield meaningful results in several market analysis scenarios, including the analysis of market behavior over the course of the day and the examination of market reactions to unexpected events. It is worth noting that the methodology is capable of providing both short-term and long-term trend analysis without needing to make prior assumptions about the market's behavior. Additionally, the method does not require constant monitoring or adjustment because the analysis can be easily repeated for any newly available market data. The trend insights derived from this approach include information about market slope and position, which together describe how the market is configured. The methodology has been shown to yield results consistent with general market instability theories and also identifies potential market hazards. Furthermore, the approach shares many features with well-known financial mathematical concepts, including the Black-Scholes model and the efficient market hypothesis. Although the method does not contribute any new fundamental theories, it does derive a set of rules that can be used for making individual investment decisions and for the development of an automatic trading system. The trend analysis results obtained from this approach match the outcomes of other empirical trading systems that have been tested on historical market data. The beauty of this trend analysis system lies in its simplicity, as it is largely based on the intuitive idea that trading is most efficient when there is a good balance between the price of assets and the level of trading activity. This trend analysis approach can be applied not only to financial markets but also to any market for which price and activity data are available, including currency exchange markets and markets for commodities and real estate. The method is expected to yield even more meaningful insights when additional non-price factors are incorporated into the analysis. Ultimately, the trend analysis results derived from this approach can be used to develop a sophisticated automated trading system that is sensitive to the current state of the market and can make effective investment decisions at any time of day. This work presents FLVoogd, a refined federated learning technique that allows servers and clients to cooperatively prevent Byzantine attacks while maintaining user anonymity. Specifically, servers utilize DBSCAN with S2PC to cluster the legitimate data majority without acquiring private user data. Concurrently, clients create duplicate models and engage in distance-controlling testing to tailor their local models towards a centralized standard. Our framework is both autonomous and adaptive, as servers and clients require no manual parameter adjustments. Furthermore, it relies on SMPC operations such as multiplication, addition, and comparison, which omits expensive operations like division and square root. Evaluation on standard image classification datasets demonstrates that FLVoogd effectively blocks malicious submissions and precludes data exposure from the server. Importantly, our approach is self-regulating and offers a seamless transition to TRAIL-based deep models, proving particularly resilient against Byzantine attacks. Due to its self-regulating nature, server-side and client-side parameters remain unaltered, thereby preventing performance regressions. Ultimately, FLVoogd offers a robust, efficient, and confidential federated learning solution. The code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/IronKung/FLVoogd. The identification of sub-Neptune exoplanets receiving irradiance levels similar to Earth's revitalized the prospect of discovering potentially habitable worlds over the coming decade, with some temperate planets potentially harboring substantial water masses that could tip the balance towards habitable zones. Characterizing these planets' water masses is of immense importance in assessing their habitability potential, and we have found that the transmission spectra of sub-Neptunes with substantial water masses are distinguished by higher metal oxide aeronitrogen layers compared to those with little water. This is because metal oxides in the atmosphere of a planet with a large water mass act as a filter, blocking a broader range of the host star's ultraviolet spectrum than a planet with little water, resulting in smaller Lyman-alpha intensities and higher far-UV to visible ratio values. Conversely, the high-temperature Wustite process may also reduce Lyman-alpha absorption and increase the far-UV to visible ratio; however, this effect is expected to be less pronounced than the equilibrium metal oxide formation process driven by water. Thermochemical reactions are likely to be the primary mechanism shaping the transmission spectra of sub-Neptunes, and observing these planets at multiple wavelengths, including a wavelength around 1400 Angstroms that is relatively unresponsive to metal oxide absorption, is crucial to differentiating the equilibrium metal oxide process from thermochemical reactions and ultimately quantifying water masses in these exoplanets. Based on this, we propose the concept of Characterizing Oceans via Transmission spectroscopy, or COT, which could enable the identification of oceans in temperate sub-Neptunes and those with habitable conditions over the coming decade. COT transmission observations could reveal whether these planets truly harbor conditions suitable for life. Moreover, we have found that the most promising targets for this study are those with orbital periods between 100 and 200 days and magnitudes less than 20. Ultimately, we have outlined a strategy for the development of a more robust method to characterize water masses in sub-Neptune exoplanets through their transmission spectra. Related by Author

Inspired by the classic discrete-time model of nervous activity proposed by McCulloch and Pitts in 1943, a new continuous-time model, known as the McCulloch-Pitts network (MPN), has been developed for sequence learning in spiking neural networks. This model employs a localized learning rule, in which synaptic weights update solely based on the accessible information at each synapse. The model leverages the asymmetry of connections between binary neurons to effectively learn and memorize multiple temporal patterns. Furthermore, our study reveals that the MPN can efficiently acquire long, hierarchical sequences and retains biologically plausible characteristics, such as local connectivity and localized synaptic updates. Additionally, our model exhibits robust performance in high noise environments and demonstrates a substantial advantage over other binary neural models in terms of data storage capacity for temporal patterns. The MPN's learning strategy also allows it to tackle the knapsack problem efficiently and effectively. Experimental results confirm the MPN's superiority over other state-of-the-art sequence learning models through comprehensive evaluations on diverse datasets, including image recognition, text classification, and language modeling tasks. The MPN's source code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/hjdw2/MPN. This work is comprised of two published papers, available at arXiv:2104.04714 and arXiv:2201.11047. The MPN's efficacy in sequence learning has been validated on the AI100 challenge organized by the University of Kentucky in 2021. The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.

To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising scene text that was not present in the training data.
The competition featured two recognition tasks: a holistic approach to reading full text and a focused task involving cropped text segments.
The analysis of baseline models and those submitted by competitors revealed a significant disparity between their performance levels in the newly introduced setting.
The proposed dataset will play a crucial role in further research to enhance the development of more versatile scene text models capable of providing more reliable and robust predictions than those based on conventional domain-specific training methods. The increased use of sensors in industrial settings has led to the widespread collection of high-dimensional time-series data. While this has several benefits, it also raises the challenge of monitoring large amounts of data, particularly when significant gaps in this data may occur due to lost transmission or faulty sensors. This research aims to address this complication by developing an advanced method to efficiently process partial data from multiple sources, thereby enabling real-time detection and isolation of anomalies within high-dimensional data streams. A new statistical framework, called the Partially-Observed Cusum (POC) algorithm, has been created and its key attributes proven, such as its ability to provide accurate false alarm and detection rates. Furthermore, Monte-Carlo simulations have been conducted to compare the performance of our proposed approach with alternative methods on various industrial datasets. The results demonstrate the POC algorithm's capacity to handle missing data and its superiority over standard change detection methods on high-dimensional data streams. Additionally, its potential applications have been illustrated through the analysis of real-world datasets. These datasets have been derived from (i) an artificial scenario modeling industrial data, and (ii) the actual industrial environment, showcasing its adaptability and effectiveness in practical scenarios. We have created a detailed analysis of the origins and development of two disrupted galaxies: NW1322+74 and NW21850+2443. Through the examination of their globular clusters and stellar components, we found that these galaxies had similar initial star formation patterns at an early stage. However, NW1322+74 experienced a sudden and intense burst of star formation about 1.1 billion years ago, indicating the probable merger that shaped its evolution. In contrast, NW1322+74's companion galaxy NW21850+2443 exhibited a more steady and gradual change in its star formation pattern over time. Our analysis of the galaxies' chemical composition allowed us to estimate their total mass at an early stage, within a range from approximately 3.9 to 9.2 x 10^8 solar masses. Furthermore, NW1322+74's globular clusters showed distinct variations in metallicity, suggesting a cluster-by-cluster approach to understanding their origins. Our analysis indicated that NW1322+74's metallicity ranged from 0.9 to 2.3 times the solar value, and the clusters' ages spanned from roughly 1.1 to 1.3 billion years old. Ultimately, the galaxies' rich cultural heritage, as revealed by their chemical abundances and star formation histories, provide a richer understanding of their origins and development. Additionally, the galaxies' short-lived (less than 1.1 billion years) pro-genitor phase, characterized by low metal levels, aligns with findings from numerical simulations. These results have significant implications for future research on galaxy systems and their inherent cultural heritage. The integration of chemical abundance information and detailed star formation histories has the potential to reveal more precise and dynamic histories of galaxy origins and development. A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. Furthermore, we have found that our active learning strategy allows our models to achieve the same level of performance with a reduced number of labels, thereby saving costs. A comprehensive classification system for subsets of Baire space, categorized by Borel Wadge classes, has been introduced with enhanced effectiveness. Based on Montalbán's true stage machinery, we leverage this innovation to offer an alternative demonstration of Louveau and Saint-Raymond's separation theorem. This leads to a demonstration of Borel Wadge determinacy within the $\text{ATR}_0+\Pi^1_1$-I system of second-order arithmetic. Finally, we show that any Borel Wadge class has a computable representative under certain conditions and develop a positive solution to a question posed by Montalbán. Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are emerging due to rising demands for accurate predictions and thorough analyses. However, they necessitate a considerable amount of computational power and time for processing. Previous studies on pruning have focused on enhancing inference efficiency, but there's been limited research on effectively decreasing training costs. Our proposed framework, ClickTrain, efficiently and accurately enables both end-to-end training and model pruning for CNNs, distinguishing itself from previous work with fine-grained architecture preservation through pattern-based pruning, precise weight estimation, and compiler-optimized calculations. As a result, ClickTrain can deploy high-accuracy and fast-pruned models directly without additional overhead compared to traditional methods, while also minimizing the pruning-after-training approach by up to 2.3 times with similar results and up to 2.3 times with the pruning-during-training approach with both high accuracy and compression ratios, all under equivalent time constraints. This research examines the properties of specific modal logics derived from noncommutative lattices by incorporating $\Box$ and $\Diamond$. A new semantics model is introduced, specifically tailored for substructural modal logics. By applying duality principles, we demonstrate that every modal logic derived from the full Lambek calculus can be represented through a specific convex structural equation algebra. Furthermore, we establish a dual relationship between certain classes of modal logics and their associated algebraic structures, thereby proving equivalence between these classes. A key finding of our study is that the modal logic derived from the full Lambek calculus is not expressive enough to capture certain latte-specific relationships, thereby necessitating an augmented language to convey relevant information. This augmented language can be formalized using both modal logic and algebraic techniques. Using a similar approach, we can provide a constructive modal logic interpretation for certain associative and commutative modal logics. The proposed method can be generalized to cover a broader range of substructural modal logics. The study offers a novel modal logic interpretation for a specific calculus with a lattice-based foundation and facilitates the application of modal logic to categories theory and domain theory, offering a constructive modal logic interpretation in this context. The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed a full spectrum of cosmic events involving compact objects, including the merging of neutron star-black hole binaries. Their findings have facilitated an unprecedented link between the events and their underlying physical models, empowering researchers to analyze various aspects of these events, such as the physical properties of neutron stars, the spin of compact objects, and the physical processes occurring during mergers. Despite significant advancements, there is a growing need to incorporate machine learning into the analysis of gravitational waves. Notably, it has been demonstrated that a deep learning model can effectively recognize the merging of neutron star-black hole binaries, outperforming competing methods. Moreover, there is potential for deep learning to contribute to multiple tasks, including detecting mergers, classifying events, estimating source parameters, and identifying candidate binary neutron star mergers. Our study's results indicate that deep learning can efficiently process a large number of events, making it an efficient approach for analyzing a vast event database. The employed architecture is quite versatile and can be adapted for various research objectives, such as verifying the damped amplitude phenomenon in binary black hole mergers, and studying the characteristics of merging magnetic black holes. Our work indicates the substantial potential of deep learning methods in analyzing the full spectrum of observed gravitational waves. Sequential decision-making in operations management problems, such as those governed by constraints, can be addressed using the constrained Markov decision process (CMDP). Two main obstacles arise when attempting to solve CMDPs for the development of optimal operational strategies: they are often characterized by an extremely vast number of states and actions, as well as a difficult-to-compute transition matrix. To resolve these challenges, we develop an algorithm that combines policy iteration with subgradient ascent. We show that this approach allows the CMDP to converge to a solution at a rate proportional to $O(\log(T)/\sqrt{T})$, where T represents the number of iterations, provided that a specific condition is met. This method also offers an efficient way to reduce the complexity of working with the vast state space by utilizing a smoothed approximation. Furthermore, we show that the smoothed algorithm remains near-optimal and achieves a performance that decreases at a rate of $O(\log(T)/T)$. We apply our algorithm to critical problems such as multi-class queueing systems and talent management issues. Experimental results using a simplified model of the talent management problem demonstrate the efficacy of our approach when compared to other plain MDPs. It is noteworthy that our approach can be extended to other related problems, such as those involving conflicting goals and constraints. This research is a result of joint work with S. This research outlines a method for recognizing handwritten mathematical symbols when not using an actual input device. The approach involves creating a dataset of 124 unique symbols, along with a neural network architecture based on the LeNet-5 framework. To enhance the model's performance, additional features were incorporated using a Gaussian Blurred Bitmap transform. Following that, a comprehensive evaluation was conducted using the collected dataset, which resulted in outstanding recognition rates of 98.6% for single symbols and 94.4% for combined symbols. Furthermore, the model demonstrated versatility by being tested on a set of standard mathematical expressions. Despite being initially designed for handwritten text recognition, the underlying framework has proven capable of accurately parsing the provided mathematical symbols. However, an adjustment to the model is necessary to achieve optimal performance with the given data. Lastly, a demonstration showcasing the versatility of the model in generating mathematical expressions through handwriting has been prepared. The research hypotheses that the proposed model, along with its created dataset, can serve as a pioneering effort in offline handwritten mathematical symbol recognition. A geometric interpretation is provided for superconformal quantum mechanics based on a hyper-Kahler cone that has a symplectic resolution with equivariant symplectic properties. In this framework, BPS states can be represented as specific cohomology classes in twisted Dolbeault cohomology on the resolved space. The growth rates of BPS state degeneracies, specifically their indices, are connected to Euler characteristic computations in equivariant sheaf cohomology. A notable instance is when considering the Hilbert scheme of points on a 2D plane; this yields an accurate calculation of exponential BPS state degeneracy growth rates as the number of points goes to infinity. The growth characteristics serve as a theoretical prototype for the duality concept between supersymmetric quantum mechanics and growth of sheaf cohomology on complex varieties. The implementation of Nekrasov and Shatarev's idea to replace the hyper-Kahler cone with a modular, quantized version is also explored, with the growth of BPS state degeneracies becoming finite and symbolic in nature. Lastly, a notable observation is that the class of the Hilbert scheme points encompasses a particular case of the Conjecture on Limiting Mixed Hodge Structure put forth by Bloch, Clader, and Gray. The connection between the quantum mechanical path and the classical topological approach can also be seen as a form of mirror symmetry. Ultimately, this findings bring about a novel type of duality that can be utilized to analyze and better comprehend the complex relationships present in the growth patterns of BPS state degeneracies. The associated mathematical structure can also be applied outside the supersymmetric quantum mechanics context to gain insights into the properties of geometric BPS states in the broad hyper-Kahler setup. A fundamental BPS equivalence relation is established, which has far-reaching implications when combining two specific volume forms originating from the conical and quantized hyper-Kahler structures. We examine the relationship between network architecture and disease propagation in the contact process using numerical methods. Initially, our research reveals that the disparity in epidemic behavior between homogeneous and heterogeneous networks is surprisingly small, yet the latter's complex structure can lead to a lower overall infection rate. Unlike non-clustered networks, the presence of robust community structures in the network tends to hinder the disease spread, as isolated sub-groups can contain the outbreak and prevent widespread infection. Additionally, our findings show that the fraction of immune individuals in the network also impacts the disease propagation, particularly in complex networks where the epidemic behavior is largely determined by the network's community structure and the distribution of elements within those communities. Specifically, the sudden drop in the epidemic's average infection rate at a particular disease transmission rate is more pronounced in networks featuring higher concentrations of immune individuals. Furthermore, the network's average degree also plays a crucial role in the epidemic behavior, particularly when the disease transmission rate approaches its critical value; lower average degrees result in a sharper decline in the epidemic's average infection rate. Lastly, our research into the time sequence of network infections reveals that the spread of the disease is largely characterized by a slow ascent in the lower degrees of the network followed by a rapid increase in the higher degrees, indicating that smaller-scale disease propagation primarily drives the early epidemic phases, while a subsequent surge in the disease transmission rate among the network's high-degree elements is responsible for the epidemic's later stages. Ultimately, our numerical analysis provides valuable insights into the intricate relationships between network architecture, disease propagation, and the epidemic's average infection rate, thereby shedding light on the critical factors that contribute to the variability in the contact process observed across different network configurations. Moreover, our research offers potential avenues for strategy development in the targeted control of the epidemic spread within complex networks. Please see our accompanying article for a detailed numerical investigation of the epidemic's average infection rate, as well as its numerical accuracy across various network configurations. Actor-critic reinforcement learning is commonly employed in robotics due to its versatility in a range of control tasks. However, its practical implementation often results in suboptimal policy outcomes owing to the limitations inherent in the actor-critic model. To address these shortcomings, our approach integrates the actor-critic model with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) for a hybrid framework termed the actor-critic method using HMC (ACMH). The ACMH framework draws on the idea of exploring within the latent space, as mandated by HMC, to augment the traditional actor-critic model. Consequently, our novel algorithm enhances policy outcomes by (1) enhancing policy representation capability, (2) effecting transfer learning, and (3) facilitating policy optimization. Experimental evaluations, encompassing a diverse range of tasks including a high-dimensional robotic arena and multiple hexagonal robots, demonstrate that our ACMH approach outperforms the standard actor-critic model by notable margins. Moreover, our proposed method was found to be robust in evaluating multi-agent competition scenarios. The accompanying code is available at https://github.com/Bie-Zai/ACMH.git. It's widely recognized that any prime number $p$ greater than or equal to $5$ can be represented as either $6k-1$ or $6k+1$. We will refer to the number $k$ that produces a given prime $p$ as the $\textbf{generator}$ of that prime. Pairs of twin primes have the unique characteristic of sharing a $\textbf{common generator}$. As a result, any two prime numbers exceeding the square root of $\Delta$ will inevitably reside in the same $6$-element set and, consequently, be connected to $\Delta$ through the same value of $k$. We will demonstrate that $\Delta$ can be set to $0$ and, by extension, prove the twin prime conjecture. We will also establish that any two prime numbers $p$ and $q$ have a shared factor of $1$ if and only if their respective generators $k$ and $l$ have a common factor. We will further show that this condition gives rise to a diophantine equation, the solution set of which is comprised of infinite pairs $(f,n)$. We will then utilize these pairs $(f,n)$ to establish a hierarchical relationship among the sets of twin primes, as well as to devise a general formula that encompasses all known and unknown twin primes. Lastly, we will leverage the infiniteness of the prime numbers to formally state and formally prove the twin prime conjecture. We note that our approach yields a comprehensive general formula for all prime numbers as well. We also observe that the infiniteness of the prime numbers can be utilized to derive a formula for all coprime pairs $(a,b)$. Furthermore, we will devise a machine translation algorithm for the theorem, as well as for the entire proof, utilizing a format similar to that in the "Mathematica" program. We note that this approach has the added benefit of facilitating the transference of the proof to any other programming language or text file. We could have arrived at this solution via a machine translation approach early on in the problem, but our desired outcome would have been obscured by the numerous irrelevant code segments that would have resulted. We therefore waited until the solution was fully formulated before presenting it in a clean and simple code format. We note that the clean and simple code format comes with the added benefit of facilitating an anatomical analysis of the proof, as well as of leveraging the inherent computational aspects of the solution to explore and visualize a wide array of related topics in number theory. Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the navigation of indoor environments using a mobile robot with a sonar sensor, either singly or in combination with a camera, under real-time control. A layered control system comprising high-level planners and low-level executives was implemented using a camera and sonar sensors to provide adaptive navigation capabilities. A key component of this study involves presenting an innovative sonar fusion technique to guide mobile robots using a weighted distance metric, derived from sonar beam readings and a 2D map representation. This proposed method is illustrated by its successful application in a mobile robot navigating a standard indoor environment using only two sonar sensors and a basic camera, under real-time control. Experimental results show that, in favorable conditions, the developed navigation system using a camera alone is fully functional. However, in more challenging environments with limited visibility, the integration of sonar sensors enhances the system's robustness and allows for efficient indoor navigation. A comparative analysis of the method's effectiveness against alternative sensing configurations highlights the benefits of combining a camera with two sonar sensors in achieving optimal navigation performance. A publicly available dataset containing sonar data, camera images, and corresponding ground truths has been created to facilitate the replication of these findings and the development of alternative sensing approaches. Additionally, the proposed sonar fusion algorithm has been integrated into an open-source indoor navigation software framework for widespread use. Furthermore, a comprehensive online supplement has been provided, encompassing detailed mathematical derivations, comprehensive experimental data, and additional contextual information. This study has been made available under a flexible license to empower its dissemination. The proposed method has been successfully tested and validated in multiple indoor environments, demonstrating its potential for widespread application in navigating indoor spaces using a mobile robot with a camera and sonar sensors. A key contribution of this study involves addressing the sensing and navigation challenges in diverse, indoor environments using a sonar fusion algorithm and an adaptive navigation controller. These components have been rigorously tested and validated, as evidenced by the attached supplement and publicly available dataset. Additionally, the proposed method has been successfully demonstrated navigating through shelves and around obstacles in multiple indoor settings. Furthermore, the developed dataset and online supplement can facilitate the replication of these results and the advancement of sensing algorithms for navigating indoor spaces using a camera and sonar sensors. Nereid, a satellite of Neptune that holds the distinction of being the largest outer satellite that can be spectroscopically analyzed, exhibits an irregular orbit. Our analysis focuses on Nereid's spectral characterization utilizing its reflectance spectrum between 0.8-2.4 $\mu m$, particularly in the unexplored 0.8-1.4 $\mu m$ range, as we attempt to identify the spectral absorption features that correspond to its icy composition. Our findings indicate the presence of crystalline water ice, coinciding with existing observations. Nonetheless, using simple models consisting of intimate water ice mixtures, we fail to attain a comprehensive match with the measured reflectance. This suggests the existence of an additional component, likely in the form of a third body or a surface layer, that requires an extra compositional element to explain its spectral effects. One potential candidate is magnesium sulfide, based on a comparison with a model featuring this sulfide, along with crystalline water ice and organic compounds. This model demonstrates a satisfactory match with the measured reflectance data. Building upon this, we propose the possibility that Nereid, having existed in a proximity to Jupiter's moon, Hyperion, that allowed for tidal heating and surface resurfacing, might have acquired magnesium sulfide particles from the latter. This hypothesis is also consistent with the spectral features observed in Hyperion's near-infrared spectra which indicate the presence of magnesium sulfide, supported by the moon's highly irregular shape that facilitates tidal heating and surface alteration. Conversely, it's feasible that Nereid acquired its spectral features from its own tidal heating and unique orbit that prevents freezing, resulting in the creation of magnesium sulfide or similar compounds that correspond to its spectral absorption features. This alternative theory might be an appropriate explanation for the spectral phenomena observed on Nereid. Additionally, we note that neither of these models incorporates the influence of crystalline water ice sublimation, a process that could lead to an irregular, non-uniform surface distribution of water ice, resulting in varied spectral features. A new pessimism-based approach for Bayesian learning in the offline setting is proposed for creating the optimal dynamic treatment regimes. Traditional offline data solutions often result in sub-optimal policies when the coverage condition isn't met, which frequently occurs with offline data. The pessimism principle resolves this problem by limiting actions with little state-dependent data usage. Although most pessimism-based methods depend on a key hyperparameter for pessimism quantification, their effectiveness significantly depends on this parameter's proper choice. Our approach integrates the pessimism principle with Bayesian machine learning, using Thompson sampling to optimise the pessimism degree without manual adjustment. By developing a credible set with an optimistically bounded Q-function boundary, the need for additional pessimism parameter tuning is eliminated. Our general Bayesian learning method can accommodate a range of models, including Bayesian linear and neural network models. Additionally, a variational inference algorithm is developed for efficient and scalable computations. The theoretical soundness of our approach is confirmed through established guarantees, which, along with simulations and real-world data tests, show our solution's superior performance compared to state-of-the-art alternatives. The developed code is publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/jbrensa/bay_pessoptim. The presented research significantely contributes to the offline data field by offering a versatile solution with broad applicability to dynamic treatment regimes and Imperialistic Pessimism principles. It also outperforms existing solutions in performance and is easily scalable for real-world complex data. Finally, it provides a general framework that can be-implemented with various models without hand-tailoring. The research also provides a public repository with the necessary code to reproduce the results for reproduction and future build-on work. We identify the a-adic solenoids for which this relationship holds, effectively proving a theorem analogous to the generalized Polya theorem. This proof relies on solving a functional equation for a specific class of functions associated with the character group of the a-adic solenoid. The character groups of the groups being considered must also meet specific criteria: they must be compact and the groups themselves must be locally compact, abelian, and of dimension one. Consequently, we establish the uniqueness of the Eilenberg-Mac Lane module structure on the 1-correspondence group of the a-adic solenoid, provided it is nontrivial. Specifically, we demonstrate that the 1-correspondence group of the a-adic solenoid is uniquely defined as the product of a compact group, a countably infinite discrete group, and the group of integers under addition. Furthermore, we show that the same principles can be applied to a different class of groups: those that are metrizable, abelian, and of dimension one. However, the groups in this class are not necessarily locally compact. Instead, we define a metric on their character groups such that these groups become compact and the original groups remain locally compact, abelian, and of dimension one. The uniqueness of the Eilenberg-Mac Lane module structure on the 1-correspondence group of the a-adic solenoid, provided it is nontrivial, can also be proved in this context. Presence-absence data is represented as binary vectors or matrices consisting of zeros and ones, typically denoting the presence of something in a specific location. These data types commonly appear in research contexts such as ecological studies, genetic information, and linguistic analyses examining word occurrences in texts. Clustering methods can effectively apply to this data for a range of purposes including the identification of geographically linked species groups, known as biotic elements. Various clustering approaches can be utilized to process such data including the use of latent class mixtures under the assumption of local independence, hierarchical clustering based on the Jaccard distance, or applying continuous data methods to the multi-dimensional scaling representation of distances. These clustering methods vary conceptually and cannot easily be compared theoretically. To address this, we conduct an in-depth comparative analysis through simulation studies grounded in models for species distribution to evaluate their respective performances. 

This study has been accepted for publication in an upcoming publication titled "Innovations in multivariate statistical modelling: navigating theoretical and multidisciplinary domains," part of Springer Emerging Topics in Statistics and Biostatistics, edited by Ferreira, J., Bekker, A., Arashi, M., and Chen, D.

In recent years, salient object detection using deep neural networks has received significant attention, but dealing with RGB and RGB-D images separately often necessitates the design of specific network architectures. This paper proposes an efficient and unified structure that integrates cross-attention context extraction to effectively tackle both tasks. By effectively fusing two inputs (for RGB images) or three inputs (for RGB-D images) with a cross-attention mechanism, our framework leverages the rich information present in both RGB and depth features. This structure's simplicity and efficacy enable efficient extraction and fusion of contextual information. As shown by experimental results, our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods on various datasets in terms of multiple evaluation metrics. The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect and classify hate speech in social media posts. For subtask A, a BERT-based classifier was adapted and achieved a high macro F1 score of 0.8136 in evaluating test data, thereby ranking 3rd among competitors. Meanwhile, in subtasks B and C, a linear support vector machine was used in combination with pre-selected character n-gram features. Our method specifically for subtask C demonstrated effectiveness in identifying the victim of abusive content with a macro F1 score of 0.5243, and ranked 27th among participants. Additionally, our submission to subtask D1-D3 centred on identifying abusive, racist, and homophobic content, where our approach yielded macro F1 scores of 0.6071, 0.5232, and 0.4143 respectively. In all cases, our methods ranked moderately in comparison to other competitors. It is noteworthy that our team's results for subtasks B and C, as well as D1-D3, did not surpass the baseline macro F1 score in any instance. Our paper concludes by speculating on possible improvements for future challenges in offensivel. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/UM-IU-LING/UM-IU-LING_OffensEval_2019. 
Keywords: UM-IU@LING, BERT, SVMs, OffensEval, 2019, Lexical Features.

Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process. Omitting these factors may result in distorted image projections. In addition to the issue of polyenergetic X-rays, the statistical distribution of noise during the CT scanning process can also impede accurate image reconstruction. The present study aims to eliminate two primary sources of error, namely noise and polyenergetic X-rays, by developing a variational regularized reconstruction model that incorporates principles of total variation denoising and Sen's law of heat conduction. The model's optimization was achieved using an alternating split Bregman iterative technique, which facilitated the rapid construction of reconstructed images from raw CT data. The method was tested and validated using both synthetic data and real-world CT scans. The results indicated that the proposed method successfully demarcated and differentiated various materials, while simultaneously removing noise from the process. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data and limited language knowledge (dictionaries and language models). A specific obstacle is encountered in deciphering historical ciphers, which often employ fictional alphabets to conceal the contents. To overcome this problem, this study develops a novel data creation approach rooted in Bayesian Program Learning (BPL). Unlike conventional generation methods that require extensive annotated images, our approach produces realistic handwriting from just one sample per alphabet symbol. After creating these symbols, synthetic lines are produced for training leading Handwritten Text Recognition models without the need for line segmentation. Thorough evaluation and analysis affirm the efficacy of the proposed solution. Consequently, state-of-the-art results were achieved on the sub-set of the TUSC-G dataset and the Chiller dataset. The formula we obtained expresses the amplitudes as a sum of specific integrals over a plane containing all momentum variables.
